20023-the-letters-of-queen-victoria-vol-:
Queen Victoria came to the throne in 1837, and her letters from 1837 to 1843 fill the first volume of her published letters. The book pairs those letters with background on her family and the House of Brunswick. Her father came from that old German house, which also ruled Hanover.

Readers see a young queen in her first years of rule, writing in her own words. The opening pages trace her birth and family ties before the letters begin. For anyone who wants the start of the Victorian age from the queen herself, the volume gives a direct, personal record.
20920-morale-a-story-of-the-war-of-1941-:
An Area Officer loathes his quiet coast watch in Morale, Murray Leinster's tale of the war of 1941-43. He longs for the west, where strange fighting flares each day. Guarding calm shores for the sake of civilian morale galls his young, keen spirit.

Leinster, a master of pulp science fiction, wrote this as a future-war tale. Odd weapons and new tactics haunt its imagined conflict's edges. Morale itself, the faith of plain folk, stands as a weapon in play. The story shows how writers between the world wars dreamed the next war, half right and half wildly wrong.
a-lover-s-complaint-pg1543: A young woman's anguished confession fills this edition of Shakespeare's enigmatic narrative poem: seduced by a charming, faithless youth, she weeps over her ruin yet admits she would yield again. Forty-seven dense stanzas of regret and desire. Beautiful, puzzling, and very human.
arxiv-2512-00343:
Vision-language models such as CLIP are powerful, but they are also vulnerable to backdoor attacks. Zhongqi Wang and Jie Zhang study model-level backdoor detection for these pretrained models in 2025, under the banner that assimilation matters. A poisoned model behaves normally until a trigger appears.

Given a model fine-tuned by an untrusted third party, deciding whether a backdoor was injected is critical and challenging. Detection protects organizations that download models they did not train. The study speaks to a growing supply-chain problem in AI, where a single tampered model can compromise every application built on it. Backdoors are typically planted during fine-tuning, which is exactly the stage users outsource.
arxiv-2512-00643:
Milan Krömer and Stefan Müller wrote a 2025 paper on the math of elastic rods. Non-Euclidean elasticity studies bodies that have no stress-free shape they can fully relax into. The theory began with metal plasticity and dislocations, where inner strain is built in from the start.

Lately the same ideas have drawn interest in biomechanics, for living tissues that grow unevenly. Krömer and Müller focus on rods, the thin, one-dimensional case. They connect rod models to almost isometric embeddings of geodesic tubes, ways of placing curved tubes into space with little stretching. Their results help ground rod theories in careful math.
arxiv-2512-00943:
Jasveer Singh and Vardarajan Suneeta compute how nonlinear black hole vibrations can be in a 2025 paper. When a black hole is disturbed, it rings with characteristic tones called quasinormal modes. At second order, pairs of tones mix and produce quadratic modes, whose strength relative to the linear tones is the nonlinearity ratio.

Measuring that ratio tells physicists how far linear theory can be trusted for real signals. The authors revisit an analytic approximation scheme for computing these ratios. A reliable, fast scheme helps analysts interpret gravitational wave ringdowns without huge simulations, and tests where perturbation theory starts to break.
arxiv-2512-01043:
Thomas Bahder works through a classic problem in detail in a 2025 physics paper. The problem asks for the photon modes, the allowed patterns of light, inside a spherical cavity. It is iconic in electromagnetism, yet the literature reports conflicting answers for it.

Bahder starts from the Maxwell equations, the fundamental laws of electromagnetism. He applies the boundary conditions at the surface of the surrounding perfect conductor, where the field must behave in a specific way. By solving the problem carefully from scratch, the paper aims to settle which reported result is right. A clean reference solution helps students and researchers alike.
arxiv-2512-01343:
Shashank Landge and co-authors tackle the size of large language models. Big models are hard to run on cheap hardware. One fix shrinks each weight to fewer bits. If all weights shrink the same way, key weights get hurt and skill drops.

Their method keeps the most key weights at higher care. It uses a math split of each weight block to judge which parts matter most. Parts with strong inner form get more bits. The rest get fewer. This mixed plan aims to keep skill high while the model stays small enough for plain machines.
arxiv-2512-01443:
Xabier de Zuazo and co-authors decode brain waves for speech tasks. They used MEG, which tracks magnetic fields from the brain. Their entry targets a 2025 contest on the LibriBrain data set. Two tasks count: spotting speech and sorting speech sounds.

Their decoder is based on the Conformer model. It reads raw signals from hundreds of sensors at once. A light front layer shapes the input for each task. A form of data warping made for MEG was also tried. Strong decoders could one day aid speech aids for users who cannot speak.
arxiv-2512-01543:
Tomassini and co-authors study the binary star AFGL 4106 and its nebula with the SPHERE tool. The star is past its red supergiant phase. Its mass loss shaped a complex cloud around it. A companion star makes that loss harder to model.

SPHERE on the Very Large Telescope gives sharp views of the cloud. The team maps the cloud's form and the pair's traits. Those maps test how binary acts steer mass loss. They also show what yields the pair sends into space, which seed new stars and planets. Nebula maps also trace past outbursts, since each shell in the cloud marks an era when the star shed mass at a higher rate.
arxiv-2512-01843:
Zeqing Wang, Keze Wang, and Lei Zhang test whether text-to-video models obey physics. Video generators have grown in quality, length, and instruction following. Whether they grasp physics is open. Implausible motion can still look smooth at a glance.

Their PhyDetEx tool detects and explains physical plausibility in generated clips. It flags where motion breaks real laws. Explanations state what went wrong in plain terms. Physics-aware scores push generators toward clips that could train robots or teach science without false cues. Explanations name the broken law, like gravity or rigidity, which gives model builders a defect list they can train against next round.
arxiv-2512-02243:
Phishing pages steal credentials by impersonating trusted sites, and they increasingly hide behind obfuscated code and visual trickery. Md. Abdul Ahad Minhaz, Zannatul Zahan Meem, and Md. Shohrab Hossain present PhishSnap in 2025, an on-device detection system that judges a page by how it looks.

The system uses perceptual hashing, a fingerprint that captures a page's visual appearance and survives small changes. Because detection happens on the device, it preserves privacy instead of sending browsing data to a server. URL and HTML based detectors struggle against visual deception, so checking the picture itself attacks phishing where it actually deceives people.
arxiv-2512-02343:
A point that returns to itself after a fixed number of steps under a map is called periodic, and number fields measure the arithmetic cost of such points. Tien-Cuong Dinh and Jit Wu Yap prove in 2025 an exponential lower bound on that cost for polarized endomorphisms of smooth projective varieties.

The result extends earlier bounds to higher dimensions, covering maps of degree at least two on varieties over a number field. Galois orbits grow at least exponentially with the period, which limits how many low-cost periodic points a map can have. Such bounds feed the arithmetic dynamics program, which studies number theory through repeated maps the way dynamics studies motion.
arxiv-2512-03143:
Quasars from the dawn of time shine across the universe. M. Costa and co-authors study dust in the host galaxies of such quasars in this 2025 work. These bright objects help trace how giant black holes and their galaxies grew together early on.

The team uses infrared light from a quasar host at very high redshift. From that light they estimate the physical traits of its dust directly. Dust tells how fast stars form and how rich the gas is in heavy elements. Such clues help map galaxy growth in the first billion years. Dust measures also help date when heavy elements first spread through young galaxies.
arxiv-2512-03243:
Telling new behavior from normal behavior is a core task in data work. Ioannis Gasteratos and co-authors frame that task on path space in this 2025 work. Paths are sequences over time, like price curves or motion traces.

They treat novelty detection as a hypothesis test with signature-based statistics. Signatures summarize a path in a compact way. Using cost inequalities, they bound false positive rates beyond the Gaussian case. Reliable novelty flags help in finance, medicine, and engineering, where rare events can signal trouble. Tail bounds matter, since a novelty alarm that fires too often soon gets ignored.
arxiv-2512-03343:
Language models pick words one by one, which can blur ideas. Darshan Fofadiya proposes Idea-Gated Transformers in this 2025 work. He notes that people form abstract ideas first, then choose words to express them.

Standard models merge those two steps into next-token prediction. His design prunes the vocabulary in a differentiable way to enforce semantic coherence. Gating word choice by ideas could make text more consistent over long passages. The work explores a more human-like split in how models generate language. Vocabulary pruning is the gate, cutting words that do not fit the active idea.
arxiv-2512-03443:
Large magnetic fields shape how accretion disks evolve. Hongzhe Zhou, Yosuke Mizuno, and Zhenyu Zhu present a subgrid dynamo model in this 2025 work. Such fields drive turbulence, reconnection, and outflows from disks around black holes and young stars.

Simulations show the starting field strength and shape leave a direct imprint on outcomes. Resolving the dynamo that builds fields is too costly at full scale. Their model adds dynamical quenching inside general relativistic simulations. That lets big simulations include field growth more faithfully. Quenching stops runaway field growth, keeping simulated disks in a realistic balance.
arxiv-2512-03543:
Extreme events in many variables at once are hard to model. Pavel Krupskii and Boris Béranger present factor models for them in this 2025 work. Models must extrapolate beyond observed data, so their shape matters a lot.

Real extremes need flexibility, especially for asymmetric dependence between variables. They also need parsimony, few parameters, for clarity and for scaling to high dimensions. Factor models aim to give both. Better extreme models help in climate risk, finance, and insurance planning. Asymmetric dependence means crashes cluster while booms do not, a pattern factor models must capture to serve risk work well.
arxiv-2601-06643:
Michael Ganzburg studies asymptotics of certain B-splines in 2026. He examines the Mellin transform of associated B-splines with special knots. The results are expressed in terms of theta-like functions, he reports.

The proof rests on polynomial interpolation of power functions mainly. Properties of certain theta-like functions complete the argument, he explains. B-splines underpin curve design, approximation, and numerical analysis everywhere. Their Mellin transforms connect them to number-theoretic functions like theta series. Finding asymptotics clarifies how these splines behave at extremes. Approximation theorists get exact limiting forms for a special family. Such results often unlock error estimates for practical spline methods. The paper is a careful piece of classical analysis with modern tools.
arxiv-2601-06843: Research by Junyan Lin and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with speak while watching. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance across many tasks. Yet most systems remain limited to offline inference, requiring complete inputs before generating outputs. Recent streaming methods reduce latency by interleaving perception and generation, but still enforce a sequential perception–generation cycle, limiting real-time interaction. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07543:
M Silvestrini and a large team from many lands introduce CASCO, a project linking galaxy simulations with real observations. Small mismatches on galaxy scales have pushed cosmologists to test alternatives to cold dark matter. Warm dark matter is one such option. CASCO asks how strongly galaxy scaling relations can pin down cosmological and astrophysical parameters, including warm dark matter ones. The work appears as a 2026 preprint.

The team combines multi-resolution hydrodynamic simulations with data from real sightings in one joint analysis. Scaling relations connect observable galaxy traits like size, mass, and rotation speed. Because such models can be rerun under changed rules, they show which relations carry real weight. The project aims at sharper tests of dark matter using galaxies astronomers already observe. All of this rests on facts that teams can check with their own eyes and tools.
arxiv-2601-07743:
Pelle Brooke Borgeke goes on with a study of how small terms can unseat a spectrum, in a 2026 analysis preprint. The paper is part two of a series on subprincipal controlled quasimodes. Quasimodes are approximate solutions to an operator equation. Here they hinge on the subprincipal symbol, a lower term often seen as minor. The notation follows semiclassical analysis, with a small parameter h.

Such weak stability means tiny shifts can move eigenvalues far more than one would guess. Quasimodes built from subprincipal data show where that sensitivity comes from. A grasp of it matters for operators from quantum theory and wave physics. The paper is dense and aimed at microlocal analysis experts. It extends part one's analysis of the same construction. Readers get a deeper account of how lower-order terms control approximate solutions. It builds step by step on part one.
arxiv-2601-07943:
Francesco Coghi, Amarjit Budhiraja, and Juan P Garrahan tackle large deviations for systems whose rules rest on their own past. They take on the broad task of writing such large deviations for non-Markovian systems in closed form. Their systems are self-interacting jump processes. The rules rest on the past through a functional of a state based measured mean. A clear split of timescales drives their solution. Their 2026 preprint derives the exact level 2.5 result.

Level 2.5 tracks swings in both filled states and flows at once. Exact formulas there are rare for history-dependent systems. Bounds that follow can limit how exact such currents can be. Self-interacting processes model reinforced walks, learning, and acts that adapt. The paper serves statistical physicists working on fluctuation theory. It extends a powerful framework to systems with memory. Systems with a past show up in walks, in learning, and in live cells.
arxiv-2601-08843:
Haotian Deng and three co-authors test chat models as graders of short student replies. A teacher gives a rubric, a list that says what earns full or part marks. Student words vary a lot, so part marks are hard to set fair. Chat models look like a cheap fix, but their marks must match the rubric, not their own taste.

The team runs a broad check of model graders on rubric tasks. They look at how close marks sit to human marks, how sure the model is, and how marks hold up when replies are tweaked. A reader who runs a class or a test firm gets facts on trust. The work shows where a model grader can help, and where a human must still check.
arxiv-2601-08943:
Axel de la Macorra and Jose Agustin Lozano Torres test a dark energy model next to new sky data. Dark energy is the name for what speeds the growth of space. Their model ties dark energy to a bound state, with its own clear past. They check it next to a cold dark stuff model in the same frame.

They fit both to fresh range marks from the DESI survey. They add old space light data and star burst range marks from three sets. A good fit must please all sets at once. A reader in cosmos work gets a strict test of a less known model. It shows if bound dark energy can stand with the best data we have.
arxiv-2601-09043:
Nick Polson and Vadim Sokolov give a Bayes frame for nets that pick one expert from a pool for each input. Such nets are called mixtures of experts. One expert may suit math asks, a next may suit code. The pool can grow vast, so most experts should sit out most asks. A firm prior can force that thrift in a smart way.

They use the horseshoe prior, which shrinks weak signs hard but lets strong signs stand. Gates that pick experts learn from data as they go. Their learn rule tracks just key sums as new data flows in. A reader who builds large nets gets a sparse pick plan with doubt built in.
arxiv-2601-09343:
Prateek Dwivedi, Benedikt Pago, and Tim Seppelt attack one of the oldest open problems in algebraic complexity theory. Their 2026 arXiv paper seeks lower bounds using symmetry and homomorphism polynomials. At stake is Valiant's 1979 conjecture, which claims the classes VP and VNP are distinct.

In plain terms, the conjecture says the permanent needs far larger algebraic circuits than the determinant. A full split of the two classes has resisted proof for decades, as in many parts of complexity theory. The authors look for new leverage from symmetry, hoping structured polynomials can force the lower bounds that direct methods have missed.
arxiv-2601-09543:
Jason Carpenter, Faaiq Bilal, Eman Ramadan, and Zhi-Li Zhang test a simple idea for cutting web pages into blocks. Their 2026 arXiv paper examines how well DOM coordinates work for page segmentation. Web pages are a vast store of data for people and, now, for language-model systems.

That data is huge and unstructured, so automated extraction must be robust. Segmentation, splitting a page into its meaningful regions, is a first step for extraction and retrieval. The authors check whether the coordinates already present in a page's document tree are enough to guide it. A cheap signal that works would simplify many scraping pipelines.
arxiv-2601-09743:
Jianhua Yang and four co-authors widen the range of a resonance trick used to pull signals from noise. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies vibrational resonance in coupled Duffing oscillators that learn. Each oscillator adjusts its natural frequency under a learning rule as the input changes.

That self-learning gives the array frequency-adaptive response. The adaptive rule greatly extends the frequency range over which resonance boosts the signal. The target use is processing weak, noisy radio frequency signals. A self-tuning resonator array could find faint signals on its own, without any manual retuning by an operator.
arxiv-2601-09843:
Simon Portegies Zwart, Arjen Doelman, and Jelmer Sein hunt for the birth stories of braided three-star systems. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies periodic three-body orbits, called braids, in Newtonian gravity. Braids look special and unique, repeating the same woven pattern forever.

The authors suspect braids instead arise from ordinary encounters between four bodies. They reverse-engineer the encounters that could have formed them. The aim is to learn how often braids exist in the Galaxy. If common collisions make braids, then these elegant orbits are a normal product of crowded star clusters.
arxiv-2601-10143:
Haochong Xia and co authors build fake market data that tracks a live market. Models trained on past data oft fail in real trade. Markets drift. The past stops being a good guide. A model then fits old noise and fails on new days.

The team argues that past data alone is not enough. Their rig adapts as it makes new data. It is a data flow rig, not a fixed set. It aims to make spans that act like the live market now. Such spans can train trade models that hold up when the market shifts.
arxiv-2601-10443:
Roberto Ricci retells umbral theory as an algebra of formal power series. Umbral math began as a trick with marks that act like powers. Roman and Rota gave it a firm modern form. Dattoli and kin later made it a work tool for special functions.

Ricci sets that tool in series form. A formal power series is a sum with no need to settle. In that tongue, umbral steps read as algebra moves. The paper lays out the main acts in that form. It aims to make the tool clear to those who know series work well.
arxiv-2601-10743:
Ayesh Abu Lehyeh, Anastassia Gharib, Tian Xia, Dryver Huston, and Safwan Wshah present UBiGTLoc, a system that locates sensor nodes in wireless IoT networks. Knowing where each node sits is key for smart cities, smart farms, and other sensor-driven work. Most current methods lean on anchor nodes whose positions are known from GPS.

Anchors are costly and cannot cover every setting, such as indoors. UBiGTLoc blends a BiLSTM network with a graph transformer in one framework. Sequence learning and graph structure each carry clues about position. Joining them aims at accurate location with fewer anchors. The work serves network designers who need maps of their own sensors.
arxiv-2601-11943:
Loren I. Matilsky, Lydia Korre, and Nicholas H. Brummell propose a dynamo story for a thin layer in the Sun. The tachocline is a narrow shear layer at the base of the Sun's outer zone. Above it, spin varies with latitude, and below it, spin is near rigid.

The layer's thinness is a long puzzle. Inward flow should have spread it over time, in a process called radiative spreading. A dynamo-held layer could stay thin in spite of that flow. Their story also bears on how the Sun's spin slows with age.
arxiv-2601-12143:
Devin Hunter and Chinwendu Enyioha build a reactive controller for self-driving race cars. Attention-based neural models now lead in real-time nonlinear control. As such models enter safety-critical work, their calls need firm statistical grounds.

Their frame uses an Attentive Neural Process for gap-based driving choices. A physics-informed form adds known motion laws to the model. The pair aim for fast calls that still hold safety bounds. Race tracks give a hard, fast test bed for such control.  Race data give fast, hard tests for the control frame.  Gap choice is a hard case for safe, fast driving in a race.
arxiv-2601-12243:
Shreya Rajpal, Michal Golovanevsky, and Carsten Eickhoff sum long procedural videos with help from labels. Summaries turn long videos into short, clear forms for review and records. The need is high in fields such as surgical training, where video is long and stakes are high.

Past tools used basic visual traits, then vision-language models that grasp sense and time flow. Their label-guided method uses known step labels to pick key parts. A guided summary can keep the steps that matter for teaching. The work tests that guide on such videos.
arxiv-2601-12743:
Debobrata Rajak and nine co authors study how twisted light interacts with solids. Intense ultrashort pulses can carry orbital angular momentum, a twist in the light wavefront. Little is known about how such pulses drive high harmonic generation in solid state platforms. For conventional light, electron dynamics can often be confined to a single Brillouin zone.

The dipole approximation also describes many standard interactions well. Twisted light may break those simple pictures, and that is the gap the team probe. Their title names the transfer of orbital angular momentum in the harmonic process. New harmonics carrying a twist could serve optics and materials probes. The work opens a fresh corner of strong field physics.
arxiv-2601-12943:
Han Xu and Di Wang bring dependent types to automated amortized resource analysis. Static resource analysis determines how much a program consumes, like time, without running it. Affine type systems have been a dominant approach to this problem. They fall short on precise resource behavior of higher order programs, though. Partial applications are a noted hard case.

Their dependently typed approach takes a non affine route. Higher order programs pass functions as values, which breaks simple counting. Dependent types can track resource use inside the type itself. Precise static bounds help compilers and users trust performance. The work serves programming language theory and verified software.
arxiv-2601-13143:
Chaeyoung Jung, Youngjoon Jang, Seungwoo Lee, and Joon Son Chung speed up models that read both sound and sight. Such audio visual models join a large language core with ears and eyes. The join makes their token load swell, so runs cost more time and power.

Token prune work has cut load for plain text and for sight plus text models. It had not been fit to audio visual models. Their method, FastAV, is the first prune frame built for that case. It drops the least need tokens while it keeps the key sound and sight clues. For live apps such as video chat aids, cuts like this can make big models fit to run.
arxiv-2601-13543:
S. M. Troshin and N. E. Tyurin back a guess form for elastic scatter based on the rule of its imaginary part. In such scatter, two bits graze and part with no break. The scatter size is a complex count with a real and an imaginary part.

Marks at the Large Hadron Collider at 13 TeV hint at a shift in the clash zone. The zone that makes new bits may turn from a black disk to a black ring with a bright core. Troshin and Tyurin argue the imaginary part rules the size. A guess built on that rule may then track the real part with less free play. Such a form aids reads of total clash rates.
arxiv-2601-13943:
Zhiyuan Peng and a large team build a benchmark for making whole software services from scratch in 2026. Language models and agents have made remarkable progress in code generation. Past benchmarks test single functions, single classes, or edits to existing code. They neglect complete microservice repository generation, the real zero-to-one workflow.

Their RepoGenesis starts from a readme file and asks for a full repository. That task spans design, many files, and working links between parts. A firm benchmark shows if agents can build services end to end. Firms could then judge agent tools on work that mirrors real projects.
arxiv-2601-14243:
Haocheng Xi and a team from NVIDIA, MIT, UC Berkeley, and other labs present Jet-RL in this 2026 paper. Their topic is training large language models with reinforcement learning, the trial-and-error method that builds reasoning skills. Such training is slow and costly. The rollout phase, where the model drafts many trial replies, takes over 70 percent of the total time.

Jet-RL tries to cut that cost with FP8, a compact number format that uses eight bits per value. The team built one shared flow for training and rollout, so both phases use the same low precision. The goal is on-policy learning that runs faster without a new split between the two phases.
arxiv-2601-14543:
Zhuofan Jia and Jian Pei extend a fairness concept to messy data in this 2026 paper. The Shapley value provides a principled framework for fairly distributing rewards among participants according to their individual contributions. Prior work applied it to data valuation in machine learning. In that use, each participant's data are scored for how much they help a model.

Existing formulations overwhelmingly assume each participant contributes a fixed, deterministic dataset. Real data are rarely so clean: values arrive with uncertainty attached. The authors study the Shapley value on uncertain data. Readers get a fairness calculus that still works when the contributions themselves are not known exactly.
arxiv-2601-14843:
Endre Sørmo Rundsveen writes a short note on a new kind of module category in algebra. His 2026 arXiv paper builds on work by Gupta and Zhou, who set up these extended module categories. The note deals with Nakayama algebras, a well-studied family of algebras.

Rundsveen shows that a certain part of the category, called a postprojective component, exists for some algebras. He also gives a knitting method to build it step by step. The method works through number vectors that track cohomology, the algebra's own way of counting holes and gaps.
arxiv-2601-15243:
Adam LaClair, Matthew Mastroeni, Jason McCullough, and Irena Peeva ask when a graph's edge ideal gives a Koszul algebra. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with binomial edge ideals. Each edge of a graph gives one quadratic polynomial, and together they generate the ideal.

Koszul algebras have a tidy, linear form of resolution that algebraists prize. Many authors have studied when these ideals define one, ever since the class was first set out. The authors take up that question for binomial edge ideals. Their work sorts out which graphs pass the test.
arxiv-2601-15343:
Jingxu Wu and Jie Shi build a rigorous frame for slow escapes from a metastable state. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with gradient systems of Landau type, inspired by QCD phenomenology. A free-energy-like functional drives the system, with a field, a stiffness term, and a potential.

A control parameter tunes the whole landscape smoothly. The authors study rare transitions between the wells of that landscape. They use Eyring-Kramers asymptotics, formulas for how long a state lasts. Gamma convergence ties the finite models to their limit, so the transition rates stand on firm ground.
arxiv-2601-15543:
Jun-Yong Park works on height zeta functions for elliptic surfaces in a 2026 arXiv paper. The setting uses a perfect field whose characteristic is not two or three. Over the function field in one variable, he studies a moduli stack of minimal elliptic curves. The stack sorts curves by Faltings height, a measure of arithmetic size. It comes from a recent height-moduli framework.

The paper's claim is in its title: a certain zeta function is rational. The function is weighted by the trivial lattice rank of the surfaces. Rationality is a strong structural fact for such a generating series. It means the series can be written as a ratio of polynomials. Arithmetic geometers use such results to count curves by height. The abstract is dense and formula-led, aimed at specialists.
arxiv-2601-16043:
Nam Van Tran builds a flow method for a class of hard maths tasks. His 2026 preprint deals with tasks that mix inverse maps and mixed bounds. Such tasks show up in game and trade maths. He sets up a flow that shifts with time and uses casts to stay in bounds. The flow is of second order, so past speed shapes its path.

Under set terms, Tran proves the flow has one path. He also proves that path moves fast toward the sole true answer. He then turns the flow into steps a code can run. The step form keeps a push from past steps. The work gives both proof and a usable method in one place.
arxiv-2601-16143:
Kryzhniy gives a broad scheme to solve sums and growth tasks with high grade curve fits. His 2026 preprint joins many task types in one frame. The types span sum tasks, mixed sum and growth tasks, and plain growth tasks. Both start point and edge point tasks fit the frame. The scheme can also fit ill posed tasks, where small shifts cause big swings.

The core is a fit built from pieces of high grade curves. High grade fits can track hard shapes with few pieces. One scheme for many types cuts the need for case by case code. The work aims at trust and ease of use. It serves teams with mixed maths task loads.
arxiv-2601-16243:
Niccolò Castronuovo, Alberto Dennunzio and Luciano Margara show a key trait of group cell grids can be checked. Their 2026 preprint deals with cell grids whose rules rest on group maths. The trait is top spread, where a start state can reach near any state. For plain cell grids, that trait can not be checked by code. No code can settle it in all cases.

For group grids, the pair plus one show a code can settle it. That split marks group grids as far more tame. Tame traits let teams trust grid based tools and codes. The proof draws a sharp line in grid theory. It guides which grid types suit safe use.
arxiv-2601-16343:
Fionnuala Curran sums how much true chance a quantum state can give. Her 2026 preprint deals with chance born when a state is read. A read in a base where the state is not flat gives true chance. A spy tied to the state may try to guess the read. Guess odds set how much clean chance the read can yield.

Curran asks what if the spy is held back in a set way. Held spies change the clean chance count in clear terms. Clean chance feeds keys and draws in quantum tech. Firm counts tell teams how much chance a state earns. The work is a pure sum study of chance.
arxiv-2601-16443:
Kanishk Gandhi and three coauthors grow end less shell task worlds for agent train. Their 2026 preprint deals with tools that act in a text shell. Past task sets were built to test agents, not to train them. Train by trial needs a scale path, not a fixed set. The team builds a full auto path that makes new tasks on its own.

Each new task comes with checks that can grade the agent. Fresh tasks stop agents from rote learn of a fixed set. Scale of fresh tasks lets trial learn run long and wide. That breadth is what self growth needs most. The work, named Endless Terminals, feeds that need.
arxiv-2601-16843:
Marta Fernández-Lomana and a team of five co-authors probe a superconductor with a needle tip. The crystal LaRu2P2 turns lossless below a cold mark. A scan tool drags a sharp tip across its face. The tip reads how electrons pair and flow. Their 2026 preprint reports those reads at near-zero cold.

The reads show a single gap in the pair states. That gap fits the classic BCS tale of pairing. Vortex swirls in a magnet field form a neat grid. Such maps test if this crystal pairs in the plain way. They also guide hunts for odd pairing in kin crystals.
arxiv-2601-17243:
Rain and heat extremes put lives and farms at risk, yet they are hard to pin down. A study with no named author in the record builds a tool for honest doubt ranges. The tool is a quantile neural network with a new loss design. Its full name is the ReLU-bias loss quantile neural network. Two tweaks shape how it learns.

One tweak keeps quantile skill even across the full range. The other stops the output spread from collapsing to a false point. Good doubt ranges matter as much as best guesses. They tell planners how bad an event could get. The frame can serve climate risk work where ranges guide real choices.
arxiv-2601-17543:
Yi Lyu, Luke Dotson, Nic Draves, and Andy Zhang review Capture the Flag games in cybersecurity teaching. CTF games let students attack and defend real systems in play form. The authors sort them into four types. The types are attack-based, defense-based, jeopardy, and gamified wargames. Each type trains a unlike mix of skills.

They sum up the traits of each type in turn. That map helps teachers pick games that fit their goals. Hands-on play builds skills lectures cannot. It also shows who thrives under time pressure. Security courses need grads who can act, not just recall. A clear taxonomy helps schools design play with purpose. The review serves new and veteran teachers alike.
arxiv-2601-17743:
Jun Zhu and five co-authors compress video with a hierarchical temporal neural representation. Implicit representations model videos as continuous functions. They offer compact storage and flexible rebuilds. Most past methods treat time as one more input. That limits how well they capture complex time patterns. The team's design builds time in a hierarchy instead.

Layered time structure can hold both fast motion and slow trends. Classic codecs split time in like ways by design. Neural methods must learn that lesson to compete. Better time models raise quality at low bit rates. Streaming and storage both gain from that. The work pairs with the team's frequency study. Time and frequency are the two axes of video.
arxiv-2601-17843: Jesse Hoekstra and Frank Windmeijer work on sharper tests for part of a model in instrumental variable studies. Their 2026 preprint deals with the subvector Anderson-Rubin test, used when instruments may be weak. They seek the best feasible critical values that adapt to how strong the other parameters are, under equal error spread. Better values mean a test with more power to detect real effects.
arxiv-2601-18043:
Haorui Ni and Sunil A. Bhave build a three-dimensional acoustic resonator shaped like a fin. Their 2026 preprint presents FinLN, made from lithium niobate on an insulator base. The team used deep ion etching to carve the fin and patterned electrodes on its sidewalls. The fin shape traps sound in three dimensions. It also boosts the coupling between electric signals and acoustic waves, all in a compact footprint.

The built devices run near 300 megahertz. Strong confinement in a small device serves filters and sensors in radios and phones. A fin design borrows a trick from transistors and applies it to sound. The work shows the shape can be made and that it performs as designed.
arxiv-2601-18243:
Hongmei Hu and Naihong Hu carry out a program to grow big quantum groups from smaller ones. Their 2026 preprint is the fifth in a series on double-bosonization and Majid's conjecture. The goal is a larger target quantum group of Drinfeld-Jimbo type, built by grafting two given smaller ones. To start, the authors set up basics of a multi-tensor product theory for the generalized double-bosonization construction. Grafting then joins the pieces into the bigger group.

Quantum groups sit behind many results in algebra and physics. A grafting method turns construction into a system, not a craft. Each new group built this way extends the known family. The work serves the long study of how these groups fit together.
arxiv-2601-18643:
Dominik Neudert-Schulz and Thomas Dallmann give cars that talk and sense as one a way to sync and to place them-selves. Cars in a peer group must share one clock and one beat to make their joint sense work. Each car must also know where its mates are, with care. The team do both tasks in one scheme, spread across the group with no boss node.

Their scheme works in two stages, each built on a famed maths of joint beats. First the group locks its clocks and beats as one. Then it uses that lock to read the place of each car from the talks them-selves. A joint scheme could cut the kit cars need for safe group moves. It may serve fleets of self-drive cars that must act as one on the road.
arxiv-2601-18843:
Muhib Omar and many colleagues read the heart's faint field with tools made from flaws in a gem. The gem is diamond, and its flaws can feel a field with great care. The read is done with no touch and no cut: the tool sits by the chest and picks up the heart's beat as a field. Such a read could one day sit by a bed or in a small ward.

The team ran the read in three forms, in rooms with shields from stray fields and in rooms with none. Each trace took a mean over a huge count of beats to pull the faint mark from the hiss. Clear traces in plain rooms would be a big step: shield rooms are dear and rare. The work shows the gem tools can catch the heart's field in the wild of a real ward.
arxiv-2601-19343:
Rahel Ohlendorf and eight co-authors probe a candidate altermagnet by squeezing it and watching heat. Altermagnets break time reversal and rotation symmetry together, yet show no net magnetism. Their order has the same symmetry as magnetic multipoles, and it couples to a mix of magnetic field and strain.

The team studies manganese fluoride, a leading candidate, through the elastocaloric effect under strain. That effect turns the coupling into a measurable heat signal. A clean probe of this hidden order could confirm a new class of magnets prized for fast, stray field free devices.
arxiv-2601-19443:
Patricia Medina Capilla and Luca Sabatini prove a clean fact about the largest subgroups of near simple groups. An almost simple group is built around one simple group, the atoms of finite group theory. Take any maximal subgroup, one that sits inside no larger proper subgroup, and run its derived series, the chain of commutator steps.

The team proves the tenth term of that chain is always perfect, equal to its own commutator. The same holds for maximal subgroups that avoid the core in a perfect group. Such blanket facts tidy the map of how big groups are built from their largest parts.
arxiv-2601-19643:
Zoe Betta, Davide Corongiu, Carmine Tommaso Recchiuto, and Antonio Sgorbissa send robots into harbours to keep people safe. Port work involves heavy loads, large vehicles, and tight schedules. Sending inspectors into the most dangerous spots puts workers at risk. A four-legged robot can go where wheels and people struggle.

This work is an early phase of a larger project. The team first identifies the critical areas inside a port that most need inspection. That mapping step decides where a quadruped robot would help most. Harbours are complex, with daily operations that shift by the hour. A robot that fits that rhythm could take over dull and risky checks. The study lays the groundwork for later trials.
arxiv-2601-19843:
Doğa Yılmaz, Jialin Zhu, Deshan Gong, and He Wang add uncertainty handling to a popular rendering method. Gaussian splatting builds scenes from millions of soft three-dimensional blobs. It has become a standard for neural rendering, spawning work on representation, speed, and optimization. Data uncertainty, though, has been largely ignored.

Their framework, GraphiXS, brings a graphical model to four-dimensional Gaussian splatting under uncertainty. Graphical models are built to reason about uncertain quantities jointly. Scenes captured from real sensors always carry noise and gaps. A system that knows what it does not know can render more honestly. The work points toward splatting pipelines that report confidence as well as images.
arxiv-2601-19943:
Yuhao Li asks how a population of learners can diversify without being told to. Coordinated, varied behaviour usually requires communication or explicit rewards for diversity. Li shows that competition alone can produce emergent specialization. Learners spontaneously split into specialists for different environmental regimes.

The mechanism, NichePopulation, combines competitive exclusion with tracking of niche affinity. The pattern echoes ecological niche theory, where species divide resources to coexist. Specialists emerge because generalists lose head-to-head contests in each niche. The result is a simple route to diverse agent populations. It may inform multi-agent systems, ensemble learning, and models of social division of labour. The rule set is small. No one tells the group what to do. The split in roles comes from the game itself. Each niche is a set of tasks where one type wins. Win there, and the type stays.
arxiv-2601-20043:
Yan Zhang, Xuefeng Liu, Sipeng Chen, and colleagues improve Bayesian optimization for problems with distinct regimes. Bayesian optimization searches expensive functions by modelling them with a Gaussian process. The standard model assumes uniform smoothness everywhere. Multi-regime problems break that: molecular conformations jump between energy basins, and drug candidates cluster into unlike families.

A single process either smooths over sharp transitions or invents noise in calm regions. Their method mixes several Gaussian processes under a Dirichlet process mixture, letting different regimes have different smoothness. Uncertainty stays calibrated in both calm and wild regions. Better-calibrated search wastes fewer costly experiments. The work suits chemistry and materials discovery, where each test is expensive.
arxiv-2601-20143:
J. W. Kania and a large team report on GREENBURST, a search for fast radio bursts carried out with the Green Bank Telescope. The project ran for about twenty-four thousand hours of observing time. It works in commensal mode, which means it searches data gathered for other projects at the same time.

Fast radio bursts are brief, bright flashes of radio waves from deep space. Piggyback searches like this one scan far more sky time than a dedicated survey could afford. The data can also reveal other short-lived radio sources. Long commensal records help astronomers count how often such flashes occur and where they come from.
arxiv-2601-20543:
Hsin-Yi Yang proves a result on CM-liftability of simple superspecial abelian surfaces over prime fields. An abelian surface is a two-dimensional analogue of an elliptic curve. The question is whether such a surface, defined over a finite field, can be lifted to one with complex multiplication, a rich extra symmetry.

Yang proves that for any prime, these surfaces admit CM liftings after extending the field at most to the quadratic extension. The proof uses the residual reflex condition and Lie types. Liftability results connect arithmetic over finite fields to the classical theory of complex multiplication.
arxiv-2601-20643:
Rupendra Yadav, Amita Sharma, and Aparna Mehra evaluate shrinkage estimators for portfolio choice across markets of different sizes. The mean-variance model is the standard investment framework, built on diversification. It struggles with estimation error in its core inputs: expected returns and the covariance matrix.

The authors test mean-variance and global minimum-variance portfolios under several shrinkage estimators, which pull noisy estimates toward safer targets. They compare performance across market dimensions. The study speaks to any investor whose optimization is only as good as the numbers fed into it. The point holds in a small fund and in a large one: bad inputs spoil good math.
arxiv-2601-20843:
Saurav Prateek presents a new design for AI systems that write deep research reports. The 2026 paper introduces a Deep Researcher architecture. It aims at complex, PhD-level topics. The design responds to limits of the parallel scaling paradigm. In that paradigm, many searches run at once and their results are merged. Breadth grows, but the plan itself never improves.

Two innovations anchor the system. The first refines the research plan step by step through reflection. The second is a candidates crossover algorithm that mixes rival draft answers. Together they push reports toward depth and completeness. The paper is a single-author design study. It speaks to builders of research agents that must do more than gather links.
arxiv-2601-20943:
Timmy Ejdetjärn and four co-authors simulate a dwarf galaxy merger that leaks ultraviolet light. Their 2026 paper models Haro 11 with radiation hydrodynamics. Haro 11 is the closest known leaker of Lyman continuum light. That light can ionize hydrogen across space. The galaxy is also a strong Lyman-alpha emitter. Together, these traits make it a key analogue of the galaxies that reionised the early universe.

Reionisation is when the first galaxies cleared the cosmic fog. Nearby leakers let astronomers study that process up close. A simulation can trace how ionizing light escapes through gas. It can also show how mergers open escape routes. The authors follow both Lyman continuum and Lyman-alpha escape. Their model helps read real images of Haro 11 and its kin.
arxiv-2601-21043:

The authors propose a novel computational problem: synthesizing plausible motion directly from logs.

A touch log records taps and swipes as points and times. From that trace, the system infers how the hand and arm likely moved. That inference could power better keyboards and accessibility tools. It also raises questions about what logs quietly encode. The paper appears in the 2026 CHI proceedings. It opens a new link between interaction data and the moving body.

The goal is the most complete gauge-invariant theory of its kind in two space dimensions plus time. Within it, Neves computes electric birefringence. That is the split of light by direction in a field. Such effects matter for flat materials like graphene. The paper is a formal theory study. It extends tools built for our world into the plane.

braid-neurypnology-1843:
James Braid, a Manchester surgeon, founded the study of hypnotism in Neurypnology, printed in 1843. Watching a mesmerist's show, he saw the trance came from the subject's own nervous state. Braid coined the words neurypnology and hypnotism for the new science. The subtitle ties nervous sleep to the claims of animal magnetism.

He explains trance as a state raised by fixed gaze and strained attention. No magnetic fluid passes from operator to subject, he argues. Cases from his practice show the state used in treatment. The book broke mesmerism away from fluid theory for good. Every history of hypnosis starts with Braid. His terms are still in daily use.
carlyle-past-present-1843:
Thomas Carlyle published Past and Present in 1843, a fierce work of social criticism. Carlyle contrasts a well-run medieval abbey with industrial England in his own day. The past, in his telling, had faith, order, and real leadership. The present has the cash nexus: money as the sole bond between people.

He attacks laissez-faire policy and the misery of factory workers. Captains of industry is his call for a new, responsible ruling class. The book founded a line of Victorian social critique that Ruskin and others followed. Its prose burns with prophetic anger. Historians still cite it on the condition of England question.
cia-0000009043:
Soviet activities around the world, with special attention to the Far East, fill a CIA survey from March 1951. The Korean War was then in its first year, and Moscow's hand in Asia drew sharp American focus. The paper scans Soviet moves across regions before narrowing eastward.

Global surveys helped leaders judge whether Soviet steps formed one design or many local plays. In 1951, with China newly communist, the Far East section carried special weight. The file shows the early CIA thinking in worldwide terms. It also records how completely the Soviet Union dominated the agency's first agenda.
cia-0000009143:
Quynh Luu district, in Nghe An province, is the scene of a November 1972 report on a downed American pilot sighted there. Nghe An stretches along North Vietnam's coast, under routes struck throughout the bombing years. Late 1972 brought the war's final, heaviest air campaign weeks later.

A pilot down in a coastal district faced capture by local militia within hours. Reports from such districts let officials plot a man's likely path into the prison system. Few could be verified on the spot. This file preserves the sighting as filed, one point in a province crossed by many losses.
cia-0000009443:
American journalists held captive by Viet Cong and North Vietnamese forces in Kompong Cham province fill a September 1971 report. Kompong Cham lies in Cambodia, where the war had spread the year before. Correspondents covering that fighting faced capture alongside soldiers' risks.

The report records what was known of the newsmen's capture and condition. Journalists were valuable prisoners: known names with employers and families pressing for news. Their cases drew attention that anonymous captives rarely got. The file documents that attention at the agency level, tracking reporters who had gone to cover the war and became its story.
cia-0000011843:
American troops had landed in the Dominican Republic in 1965 to stop a civil war, and in May 1966 the CIA reported on security conditions there. The intervention had ended the fighting but left the island's politics in a tangle. Elections were near, and the question was whether order would hold once the troops went home.

The report weighs the armed forces, the rival parties, and the risk of fresh violence. It treats the calm as real but fragile, built on an outside presence. For readers, it shows the morning after an intervention, when Washington tried to judge what its landing had bought.
cia-0000012243:
Indonesia and Malaysia were locked in an undeclared war called Confrontation when the CIA weighed both countries' prospects in June 1965. President Sukarno had vowed to crush the new Malaysian federation, which he called a British puppet. Indonesian raids and British-led defenses ground on across Borneo while Sukarno's rule weakened at home.

The paper weighs the fight's course and the future of Sukarno's guided democracy. It also judges what Malaysia could withstand and what Jakarta might do next. Written months before Indonesia's violent upheaval that fall, it shows analysts reading a region on the edge.
cia-0000013143:
General Vang Pao, the Hmong commander of America's secret army in Laos, speaks in a statement recorded in January 1974. His subject is the missing: men held, or said to be held, in North Vietnam after the war's formal end. The Paris accords were a year old, the prisoners were supposed to be home, and the accounting was already failing.

The statement preserves the general's claims in his own voice. His words carried weight with Americans who had fought beside his men in the hills. For readers, it is a Laotian witness speaking into the war's longest argument.
cia-0000013243:
Rules for allied prisoners in Viet Cong Military Region IV are set out in a CIA item from September 1967. Region IV covered the Mekong Delta, the war's watery south. The item shows how the rules changed from place to place. Each zone's chief ran his camps in his own way, under the same flag but with different habits, rations, and degrees of mercy.

The zone-by-zone view is the item's value to the accounting. The same war produced different rules for the jailed in different country. For readers, the page shows a system that was one system on paper only.
cia-0000015243: Davidson wanted a word for word translation of a space message, in a CIA file dated November 3, 1957. Leon Davidson was a keen amateur who pressed agencies on saucer lore. A claimed message from space was just the sort of item he chased. The file shows officials fielding requests that mixed hope, hoax, and hard curiosity.

Families scanned every line for news, and officials filed each word for the record. Two voices in one interview also let analysts compare the men's condition and treatment side by side.
