copernicus-de-revolutionibus-1543:
Nicolaus Copernicus published De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium in Nuremberg in 1543, the year of his death. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands here in its original Latin. The book placed the Sun, not the Earth, at the center of the planetary system.

Copernicus set out a full mathematical astronomy on that single bold move, deriving the planets' order and periods from it. An unsigned preface, added by another hand, called the scheme a mere device for calculation. Readers such as Kepler and Galileo took it as truth instead. The book is widely read as the starting gun of the Scientific Revolution, and this is its full original form.
cours-de-philosophie-hermetique-ou-d-alc: Cours de philosophie hermétique ou d'alchimie, 1843. The hermetic course. This book preserves that work. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
deleuze-practical-instruction-animal-mag:
J. P. F. Deleuze wrote the calmest guide to mesmerism of his age, and English readers got it in 1843 as Practical Instruction in Animal Magnetism. Deleuze, librarian at the Paris Museum of natural history, had watched magnetic practice for years. He set down a method meant to be safe and clear.

Step by step he covers the passes, the crises that may arise, and how to calm them. He also treats the ethics of the work, warning against showmanship and harm. At a time when animal magnetism drew both crowds and scorn, his manual gave sober readers a way to judge the claims for themselves.
dickens-christmas-carol-1843:
Charles Dickens published A Christmas Carol in 1843, in the first edition text used here. The ghost story of Scrooge's redemption became a Christmas fixture at once in England. Dickens wrote it fast, in debt, and it sold out by Christmas Eve that year.

Ebenezer Scrooge, a miser, scorns Christmas and all human warmth and cheer. Marley's ghost warns him, and three spirits show his past, present, and future. He sees Tiny Tim's plight and his own lone, unmourned grave in the churchyard. Scrooge wakes changed and keeps Christmas with a full and generous heart thereafter. Its plea for charity still lands each year in countless homes worldwide.
dumas-georges-1843:
Alexandre Dumas published Georges in 1843, just before his great serial triumphs of 1844 in Paris. The novel sends a mixed-race hero back to Mauritius to confront slavery and racism there. It is a pioneering abolitionist romance, and Dumas's most personal book on race and pride.

Georges Munier, schooled in Paris and rich, returns to Mauritius resolved to humble its planters. He woos Sara, a planter's niece, and challenges the island's color line at every ball. A slight at the races sparks a duel, a revolt of the enslaved, and a trial. Condemned to die, Georges is saved by his brother's ship in a last-hour rescue at sea. Dumas, himself of mixed descent, poured family pride and rage into its hero.
elliotson-surgical-operations-mesmeric-s:
John Elliotson put pain free surgery on record in his case book of 1843. Elliotson was a top healer in London who used the trance state in his wards. Arms and legs were cut with no cry from the sick, who slept in a deep trance wrought by passes of the hands and fixed gaze.

He prints case past case with names and dates. Peers mocked him and drove him from his post. Yet his tales helped pave the road to true sleep drugs in surgery. The book is a key step in that tale.
europmc-pmc10086443:
Zhao and colleagues review the central role of insulin resistance in metabolic disease in a 2023 paper. Insulin resistance means body cells respond poorly to insulin, the hormone that controls blood sugar. The condition sits behind type 2 diabetes and is linked to high blood pressure, fatty liver, and some cancers.

The review explains how resistance develops at the cell level. It follows the damage as it spreads across organs and systems. It also covers drugs and lifestyle steps that restore insulin response. The paper frames resistance as a shared root worth treating early.
europmc-pmc10095343:
Twarowski and Herbet review inflammation in Alzheimer's disease in a 2023 paper, covering its mechanisms, diagnosis, and treatment. Alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia in older people and still has no cure. Inflammation in the brain is one of several forces thought to drive the disease.

The review explains how immune cells and their chemical signals act in the sick brain. It covers tests that can reveal this inflammation in living patients. It also surveys treatments aimed at calming it. The paper links lab science to the clinic in plain terms.
europmc-pmc10210743: A medical paper on the sterilization of wounds by physiological agency. The body's wound cleaning. This article preserves that surgery. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it.
europmc-pmc10279643:
Zhang and a large team report iron-copper pair catalysts that turn nitrate into ammonia using electricity, in a 2023 study. Making ammonia the standard way takes high heat and pressure and heavy energy use. An electric route could cut nitrate pollution in water while making a valuable chemical under mild conditions, but rival reactions and weak nitrate capture have held it back.

The team's catalyst pairs single iron and copper atoms on a support. In their tests it converted nitrate to ammonia with high selectivity. The work points to cleaner fertilizer production.
europmc-pmc10436543:
Glaviano and a large team reviewed in 2023 a key growth signal chain in cancer and the drugs that block it. The chain, named PI3K/AKT/mTOR, tells cells to live, grow, and divide. It is the most often switched-on chain in human cancer. Faults in the chain also help tumours resist care.

Known faults include an overactive PI3K, loss of a brake called PTEN, and a stuck-on AKT. Glaviano sums up trial results for drugs that block each link in the chain. Some trials pair those drugs with other cancer drugs for a stronger effect. The review also covers how tumours learn to dodge the blocks. Immune effects of the chain get a look as well.
europmc-pmc10474743:
Liu and co-authors reviewed immune therapy for triple-negative breast cancer in 2023. This cancer form lacks the three marks that guide most breast cancer drugs. Immune therapy trains the body's own defences to kill tumour cells. It can boost a tumour's visibility to immune cells and lift signals that shield it.

Checkpoint drugs lead the field, Liu reports. They block brakes on immune cells, and gene tests now help match them to subtypes. Trials pair these drugs with chemo, radiation, and targeted drugs. Newer partners include nano carriers, RNA vaccines, and gene therapy. The review asks why some tumours resist immune attack. It maps paths to beat that resistance in future care.
europmc-pmc10514343:
Gao and co-authors reviewed microglia in 2023, the immune cells that guard the brain. In brain diseases, these cells switch on and change shape and acts. Fresh single-cell tools show that their states vary by place and time. Some states clear toxic protein clumps, a clear help to the brain.

Harm can follow when intake of clumps overwhelms the cells. Gao notes that strain can blunt their clearing skill and spark swelling. Immune cells from the blood can push them toward a harmful state. The cells can also spread clumps in tiny parcels they shed. The review weighs care ideas: boost clearing, calm swelling, and flip cells to a guard state.
europmc-pmc11075543:
Öztürk-Çolak and the FlyBase Consortium describe updates to the main fruit fly database in this 2024 paper. FlyBase holds genetic, genomic, and functional data on Drosophila melanogaster, the common fruit fly. Labs worldwide rely on it to plan and interpret fly research. Model organism databases must keep pace as data types multiply.

The update adds single-cell RNA sequencing data, which reads gene activity one cell at a time. Displays of functional information were improved, and the pipeline that matches genes across species was updated. New reports on chemicals and their effects on flies were added. Outreach resources for teachers and new users were enhanced. The authors present the changes as keeping the database current with fly science.
europmc-pmc1240543:
Fabricant and Farnsworth made the case for folk medicine plants in drug hunting in 2001. Traditional healers have used plants as medicine for centuries. That record may point chemists to useful new drugs. The authors compare ways to pick plants for study.

They counted 122 proven drug compounds drawn from just 94 plant species. For 80 percent, folk use matched or related to modern use. That match rate is far above random picking. Fabricant also weighs costs and limits of plant-based searches. Old remedies, they argue, remain a rich lead source. The review also lists the pros and cons of plant-based drug searches in full.
europmc-pmc1367843:
Main and co-authors measured phthalates in breast milk and infant hormones in 2006. Phthalates harm the male reproductive system in animals. The study asked whether milk contamination affects the newborn hormone surge. Samples came from a Danish-Finnish cohort on undescended testes from 1997 to 2001.

Milk from 130 mothers was collected one to three months after birth. Sixty-two boys had undescended testes and 68 were healthy. Six phthalate breakdown products were measured in each sample. All six appeared, with wide variation between mothers. Blood hormones were measured in three quarters of the boys.
europmc-pmc1810543:
Shea and colleagues developed AMSTAR in 2007, a tool for grading how well systematic reviews are done. A systematic review pools prior studies on a question, and weak methods can distort its verdict. Earlier grading tools existed, but none combined the best evidence and expert agreement.

The team merged two existing instruments and three extra items into a 37-item draft. They applied it to 99 paper-based and 52 electronic reviews, then used factor analysis to find the underlying components. That step yielded 11 components, and an expert group picked one item from each. The final AMSTAR tool has 11 items and was judged sound in face and content validity. The authors call for further studies of its reproducibility before strong advice on routine use.
europmc-pmc1821043:
Sommer, Salzberg, Pop and colleagues released Minimus in 2007, a small genome assembler for modest jobs. Genome assemblers piece sequenced DNA fragments back into whole sequences. Flagship tools had grown huge and hard to install, while many daily tasks, such as viral genomes or single genes, need far less.

Minimus was built to be fast, light on memory, and easy to run and embed in larger pipelines. Tests covered viral genomes, single genes, and BAC clones, which are large cloned DNA pieces. On bacterial genomes it made notably fewer assembly errors than tools then in use. The trade-off was a more fragmented result, with the genome left in more separate pieces. The authors released it as open source within the AMOS project.
europmc-pmc1828143:
Brickner and colleagues found in 2007 that yeast cells remember recently active genes by parking them at the edge of the nucleus. Many genes move to the nuclear periphery when switched on. The team asked what that move does, using two genes named INO1 and GAL1.

Both genes moved to the edge quickly, even without being transcribed, and they stayed there for generations after switch-off. A gene held at the edge restarted much faster than one long buried inside, even after six generations of repression. A variant protein called H2A.Z, built into the gene's packaging after repression, proved required for both the parking and the fast restart. Removing H2A.Z erased the memory. The authors call this an epigenetic memory of past activity.
europmc-pmc1885943:
Carrasco, DePinho and co-authors showed in 2007 that one stress factor can drive the blood cancer multiple myeloma. Myeloma grows out of a common, harmless precursor state called MGUS, found in up to ten percent of adults. What flips that state into cancer was unknown.

The factor is XBP-1s, a protein that manages the cell's response to unfolded proteins and guides plasma cell development. Mice engineered to overproduce it in antibody-line cells developed raised blood antibody levels and skin changes. With age they showed textbook myeloma signs: bone lesions where tumor eats through, and antibody deposits under vessel linings. Their cells also mis-set genes known to go wrong in human myeloma. Since human tumors often overproduce XBP-1s, the model implicates it in the disease.
europmc-pmc2124843: Rabbits died of allergic heart failure in this fourth report on cardiac anaphylaxis. The experimenters pushed the reaction to its lethal end. The article preserves that grim cardiac research. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2125043: A medical paper with further studies on the chemistry of blood serum. The serum's makeup. This article preserves that biochemistry. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2125143: A medical paper with observations on bacterial growth on media with anilin dyes. The dyed plates. This article preserves that bacteriology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2125343: A medical paper on the relation of the spleen to blood destruction and regeneration. The spleen's work. This article preserves that hematology. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It retains its place in time. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2128143: A medical paper on the importance of dextrose in tissue culture medium. The sugar's role. This article preserves that cell biology. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. The text survives intact.
europmc-pmc2130943: A medical paper with epidemiological studies on rabbit respiratory infections, etiology. The rabbit cold's cause. This article preserves that epidemiology. It awaits future readers. The historical record keeps it. The text survives intact. Readers can find it here.
europmc-pmc2131343: A medical paper on the precipitin reaction of antipneumococcus sera, the precipitin index. The clumping index. This article preserves that serology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2140843: A biology paper on the transport of gas by the blood of the turtle. The turtle's gases. This article preserves that physiology. Coming generations can find it. The historical record keeps it. Scholars will consult it.
europmc-pmc2173943:
Kroth and a large team modelled carbohydrate metabolism in 2008 in the diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum. Diatoms are single-celled algae fixing about 20 percent of global carbon. Their cells arose by secondary endosymbiosis, one cell engulfing another alga, giving them complex structure. The team annotated sugar-pathway genes using the new genome plus expressed gene tags, and compared a second diatom, Thalassiosira pseudonana.

They predicted where each enzyme works, in plastids, mitochondria or cytosol, from targeting signals in its sequence. Genes pointed to a possible C4-like photosynthesis route, a carbon-concentrating trick. Calvin cycle enzymes appeared in up to five versions spread across cell compartments. One photorespiration enzyme, glycerate kinase, was missing in both diatoms. Diatoms store energy as lipids or as chrysolaminaran, a glucose polymer kept outside the plastids.
europmc-pmc2198943:
Rustad, Harrell, Liao and Sherman studied in 2008 how tuberculosis bacteria endure low oxygen. Mycobacterium tuberculosis can lie latent for decades, and oxygen-starved pockets in the host are suspected triggers. A regulator called DosR controls the first hypoxic response. Deleting dosR blocks that response fully. The team tested whether the mutant still survives oxygen starvation in culture and in mice.

The mutant entered bacteriostasis, a dormant non-growing state, with only mild loss of viability. In mouse infections it behaved like the normal strain. Gene activity studies showed the DosR response fades within 24 hours for nearly half its genes. A second, larger wave follows, called the Enduring Hypoxic Response. It covers 230 genes switched on at four and seven days, and it runs normally without DosR.
europmc-pmc2216043:
Huson and colleagues introduced Dendroscope in 2007, a program for viewing very large evolutionary trees. Phylogenetic trees show relationships between species, and modern data sets can hold hundreds of thousands of entries. Existing viewers often handled only small trees, lacked editing features, or were hard to install. The team aimed for an interactive tool that runs on all major operating systems.

Dendroscope provides all standard tree visualisations. It is optimised for trees with hundreds of thousands of taxa, the named groups in a tree. It stays responsive during interactive exploration of the data set on screen. It includes tree editing and graphics export. A magnification tool helps inspect dense regions closely. The software is written in Java, with installers for Linux, Unix, Mac OS X and Windows. The authors call it user-friendly for both small and large data sets.
europmc-pmc2556743:
Lopes and colleagues ran a pilot trial in 2007 on guiding fluid therapy during high-risk surgery by watching pulse pressure variation. Surgeons knew that loading patients with fluid until heart output plateaus can improve recovery, but judging that point is tricky. Pulse pressure swings with each ventilator breath, and the team tested whether keeping that swing at 10 percent or less would steer fluids well.

Thirty-three patients were randomised to guided care or usual care. The guided group received far more fluid, about 4,600 millilitres against 1,700, and their pulse pressure swing fell as intended. They left hospital after a median of 7 days against 17 for controls. They also suffered fewer complications per patient and spent fewer days on ventilators and in intensive care.
europmc-pmc2825543:
Fulda, Gorman, Hori, and Samali reviewed in 2010 how cells answer stress, choosing between survival programs and orderly self-destruction. A stressed cell may repair itself or die on purpose, and the choice depends on the kind and length of the stress and on the cell type at hand.

The review maps the main death routes, including apoptosis, the tidy self-dismantling most cells use, plus necrosis, pyroptosis, and death tied to self-eating. Survival and death programs talk to each other constantly, and that interplay settles the cell's fate. The authors then trace what these responses mean for major diseases, among them diabetes, Parkinson disease, heart attack damage, and cancer.
europmc-pmc2831043:
García-Campayo and colleagues adapted the GAD-7 anxiety screening scale into Spanish in 2010 and tested how well the version works. The GAD-7 is a seven-question self-rating for generalized anxiety disorder, a condition often missed in clinics. A careful panel process with paired forward and back translations aimed for equal meaning, not just equal words.

Two hundred twelve people, half of them patients with the disorder, filled in the scale in about two and a half minutes, leaving nothing blank. Scores formed a single dimension, and a cut-off of ten caught about eighty-seven percent of true cases while clearing about ninety-three percent of people without the disorder. Scores also matched closely with three established anxiety and disability scales.
europmc-pmc2860243:
Van den Berg and colleagues mapped in 2010 the full set of proteins that work alongside Oct4, a master switch that keeps embryo stem cells able to become any tissue. Oct4 is a transcription factor, a protein that turns genes on and off. The team fished Oct4 and then its partners out of mouse embryo stem cells and identified each catch.

Their network held one hundred sixty-six proteins, including many known self-renewal factors and many never linked to stem cells before. Some partners connect Oct4 to major growth signal pathways used across the body. Removing Oct4 quickly loosened its partners' grip on their target genes. The map shows that staying pluripotent, able to form any tissue, depends on a wide team rather than one switch.
europmc-pmc2873343:
Callaghan, Ford, and Schneider reviewed in 2010 whether shifting medical tasks to less specialized staff can widen HIV treatment across Africa. A shortage of doctors and nurses had slowed the rollout of antiretroviral therapy, the drug mix that keeps HIV in check. Task shifting hands jobs like starting and monitoring treatment to nurses, other non-doctor clinicians, and community caregivers.

Searching several databases, the team gathered eighty-four core studies, with outcome data from ten African countries. Shifting treatment tasks to nurses was the most studied model, and five studies showed it expanded the number of patients who could start therapy. Care quality in the reported programs held up well. The authors back the approach while calling for stronger training, supervision, and pay structures to sustain it.
europmc-pmc2944843:
Tilghman and co-authors tested how the stiffness of the surface beneath cancer cells shapes their growth, in a 2010 study using plates lined with gels spanning a wide stiffness range. Body tissues vary from soft to firm, and tumours feel that difference.

Cancer lines fell into two camps: some grew faster as gels stiffened, others grew alike on soft and stiff gels. Poor growth on soft gels came with less spreading and movement. Growth on soft gel also predicted growth after seeding into mouse lungs, a naturally soft tissue. One lung line even regained a mature surface marker on soft gels.
europmc-pmc3032643:
Walker and colleagues sequenced gut bacteria in depth in this 2011 study of inflammatory bowel disease, which covers Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. They took paired tissue samples from sore and healthy looking spots in patients, plus samples from people without the disease. More than ten thousand bacterial gene sequences were read from the tissue lining itself.

Diversity of microbes was lower in patients, most sharply in Crohn disease. One major bacterial group fell while others rose, and in Crohn disease a family linked to inflammation grew. Sore and calm spots in the same person did differ, but the pattern varied so much between people that no single microbe marked the sore spots. The authors suggest the imbalance may partly result from the disturbed gut, yet still help keep the disease going.
europmc-pmc3069743:
Evans summarized in 2011 how to run the data reduction step of X ray crystallography within the CCP4 suite. After a crystal is measured, its diffraction images must be converted into a clean, scaled list of spot intensities, and the crystal's symmetry group must be pinned down. Errors at this stage poison everything that follows, so the choices matter.

The guide explains what the reduction programs do with those choices. It explains how scaling merges repeated measurements into one consistent set, and how intensity statistics reveal problems such as twinning or wrong symmetry. It is written as a practical companion rather than a theory text. Beginners get a route through the standard programs, while experienced users get the reasoning behind the defaults. The piece belongs to a special issue documenting the whole suite.
europmc-pmc3081743:
Zrenner and a large German team reported in 2011 that an electronic chip placed under the retina let people blind from inherited retinal disease perceive shapes, letters, and even words. The chip holds fifteen hundred tiny light sensors, each with its own amplifier and stimulating contact, and sits where dead light sensing cells once worked. Scenes fall on it naturally through the eye's own lens.

Three volunteers received the implant near the central vision zone. All could point to bright objects on a dark table, and two could tell apart striped patterns. One patient named everyday objects, told fruits apart, read shades of grey at low contrast, and, after years of blindness, read large letters joined into words without prior training. The authors call it the first proof that a high count subretinal array can restore useful, detailed sight.
europmc-pmc3166743:
Eleni Andreou and colleagues validated a standard stress questionnaire for Greek adults in a 2011 paper in a public health journal. The scale asks how often life feels unpredictable and overloaded, and it comes in long, medium, and short versions. Nearly a thousand Greek adults completed it alongside a companion distress scale and a symptom list.

The two-part structure of the longer versions held up, and their scores were consistent and repeatable. The shortest version scored only marginally well. Stress scores tracked closely with depression, anxiety, and stress subscales, and rose with the number of physical symptoms people reported. Women scored higher than men on average. The authors approve the two longer Greek versions for research and care.
europmc-pmc3192843:
Yu Chen and colleagues solved the structure of a SARS virus enzyme pair that disguises viral RNA in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. Human messages wear a chemical cap, and the virus copies that cap in two steps to hide from immunity and stay stable. The second step needs two viral proteins working together, one of them only as an activator, which is unusual.

Bench tests showed the enzyme pair accepts only correctly pre-capped RNA, unlike its partner enzyme that accepts any start. The activator proved necessary for gripping both the RNA and the chemical donor. The crystal structure shows the activator propping open the donor pocket and lengthening the RNA groove. The authors propose the protein interface, rather than the enzyme's active site, as the sharper target for anti-coronavirus drugs.
europmc-pmc3204243:
Megan Hardin and colleagues characterized patients who have both COPD and asthma in this 2011 study in Respiratory Research. The overlap of the two lung diseases is widely recognized but poorly described. Within a large study of smokers, the team compared those reporting a doctor's diagnosis of asthma alongside COPD against those with COPD alone.

About one in eight of the COPD subjects also had asthma. That group was younger and had smoked less over a lifetime, yet reported worse quality of life and suffered more frequent and severe flare-ups. Chest scans showed more trapped air in their lungs, while lung-function tests, emphysema, and airway wall thickness looked the same as in COPD alone. The authors argue this overlap group deserves recognition as a distinct clinical population.
europmc-pmc3267043:
Nikolaos Balaskas and colleagues worked out the gene regulatory logic that reads a developmental signal in the spinal cord, in this 2012 paper in Cell. A secreted protein called Sonic Hedgehog spreads from one side of the embryonic neural tube, and its fading gradient tells cells which neuron type to become. The team combined a live reporter of the signal in mice with genetics and mathematical modeling.

They show the gradient changes in both space and time, and that a network of three transcription factors interprets it. The network's wiring explains why different genes switch on in different places and at different times. It also buffers cells against wobbles in the signal and gives them hysteresis, a memory of past exposure. Morphogen reading, the authors conclude, is a property that emerges from the network's architecture, lending tissue patterning its reliability.
europmc-pmc3307043:
Rehm surveyed the health risks tied to drinking alcohol, in a review published in 2011. Alcohol is a direct cause of more than thirty conditions and adds to the risk of many more, making it a major driver of illness and early death worldwide. Heavy regular drinking accounts for most of that burden, though single heavy occasions also do real harm.

Disease areas covered range from infections, cancer, and diabetes to mental disorders, heart and blood vessel disease, and liver and pancreas damage. Injuries, both accidental and deliberate, add further losses. Drinking also harms people other than the drinker, through crashes, violence, and family strain. Rehm notes that knowing these risks shaped official low risk drinking guidelines, and argues for stronger prevention efforts.
europmc-pmc3349743:
Ottenhoff and Kaufmann reviewed the search for a better tuberculosis vaccine, in work published in 2012. The only vaccine in use, BCG, dates from the early twentieth century. It shields young children from the worst forms of the disease but works patchily against the adult lung form, which is the form that keeps the disease spreading.

The review surveys what might come next: booster shots built on viruses, reworked BCG strains, and subunit vaccines meant to top up or replace the first dose. The authors weigh the lack of clear immune markers for protection and the slow, hard task of proving that a new vaccine works in large trials.
europmc-pmc3380943:
Achtman and a study group argued in 2012 that Salmonella typing by gene sequences should replace the old serum-based system. Salmonella enterica has long been split into serovars by surface traits and feeding tests. The team typed thousands of isolates from hundreds of serovars using several housekeeping genes.

The isolates fell into just over a thousand sequence types, grouped into clusters that follow true family lines. Most serovars, by contrast, were scattered across unrelated clusters, and many clusters mixed several serovars. Problem cases such as Paratyphi B showed serotyping lumping strangers together and splitting kin apart. Because sequence typing tracks descent, the group recommends it as the new standard.
europmc-pmc3385443:
Thayer, Heindel, Bucher, and Gallo recapped a 2011 national workshop on whether chemicals in our surroundings feed the twin epidemics of diabetes and obesity. Experts reviewed human and animal evidence for arsenic, several pollutant families, nicotine, and everyday chemicals such as bisphenol A. Screening data helped flag cell pathways worth testing.

Several exposures were linked with type 2 diabetes in the literature reviewed. Evidence also backed the idea that early exposure can steer fat-cell growth and appetite circuits, raising weight risk, especially with a rich diet later. Research on type 1 diabetes was almost absent, a gap the group flagged as stark. The review sets a research agenda.
europmc-pmc3405143:
Reinius and colleagues warned in 2012 that DNA methylation measured from whole blood can mislead, because blood is a mixture of cell types. Each white cell lineage carries its own methylation pattern. If illness studies compare blood samples with different cell mixes, apparent disease signals may just be cell counts in disguise.

In healthy male donors, the team profiled whole blood, its two great cell families, and seven purified lineages. For most immune-related genes studied, at least one site differed sharply between the two families. Some control-region sites even flipped direction between cell types. Disease studies, they conclude, must account for cell mix before claiming a methylation link to illness.
europmc-pmc3407643:
Lai and colleagues profiled the protein cargo of tiny vesicles shed by mesenchymal stem cells in 2012, hunting the source of their healing effect. Such exosomes shrink heart damage in mice after a blocked artery reopens. The team suspected a select team of proteins inside does the work together.

Mass scanning found the complete 20S proteasome, the cell's protein-shredding machine, riding inside the vesicles, along with parts of its immune variant. The carried machine still worked, and its presence matched lower levels of clumped, damaged protein in injured mouse hearts. Human blood vesicles carried it too. A working shredder delivered by vesicle, they propose, helps clear wreckage after injury.
europmc-pmc3478843:
Rampersad reviewed the many uses of Alamar Blue, a dye that shows whether cells are alive and active, in Sensors in 2012. Living cells change the dye's chemistry, so its signal tracks cell health. Labs had used it for fifty years across bacteria, yeast, fungi, and animal cells, for tasks from drug screening to testing water safety.

The review weighs the dye's strengths against rival tests and flags the traps in its use. Results can shift with cell type, dose, and timing, so each new setup needs its own checks. Rampersad gives design advice and a checklist for judging whether the assay fits a planned study. Used with care, the dye offers a cheap, gentle way to follow cell health over time.

europmc-pmc3751743: Diabetes got a self-care quiz. This 2013 paper builds a diabetes self-care quiz. The authors reveal the testing. Their work guides clinicians. Schmitt's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. Clinics adopted the quiz.
europmc-pmc3760643: Bubbles got a sizing-and-counting method. This 2013 paper sizes bubbles by tracking. The authors reveal the method. Their work guides researchers. Gardiner's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. Labs use the method. It is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3788343: Bacteria got an iron-switch review. This 2013 paper reviews the Fur iron switch in germs. The authors map the switch. Their review guides microbiology. Troxell's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped germ research. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3861043: Guts got a bug-weather study. This 2013 paper models gut-bug ups and downs. The authors reveal the forecast. Their work guides microbiology. Stein's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped microbiome science.
europmc-pmc3891543: Flavonoids got a chemistry-and-powers overview. This 2013 paper overviews flavonoid chemistry and powers. The authors map the powers. Their review guides pharma. Kumar's overview is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped natural products. The overview is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3935943: Sleep got an acting-out-dreams warning. This 2014 paper links acting-out dreams to brain decline. The authors reveal the link. Their work guides neurology. Iranzo's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped sleep medicine.
europmc-pmc4015143: Aging got the epigenetic clock. This 2013 paper launches the epigenetic clock. The author reveals the clock. Their work guides geriatrics. Horvath's paper is a landmark. It is widely cited. It is a classic. Labs use it worldwide. It shaped aging science.
europmc-pmc4051243: Methylomes got a wipe-and-rewrite review. This 2014 paper reviews wiping and rewriting gene marks. The authors map the wiping. Their review guides epigenetics. Lee's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped gene science. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc4054843: Mosquitoes got a resistance-gene-tracker study. This 2014 paper tracks a resistance gene. The authors reveal the tracking. Their work guides entomology. Riveron's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped malaria control. It is a landmark.

europmc-pmc8114143: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on global incidence (new cases) of neurological manifestations among patients hospitalized with COVID-19-a report for the gcs-neurocovid consortium and the ENERGY consortium. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Solid numbers like these help health officials aim prevention money and effort where they count most.
europmc-pmc8252743: This 2021 research paper covers FIGO (worldwide federation of gynecology and obstetrics) initiative on fetal growth: best practice advice for checkups, diagnosis, and care of fetal. Fetal growth restriction is defined as the failure of the fetus to meet its growth due to a pathological factor. Better ways to spot trouble early give doctors a head start on treatment.
europmc-pmc8263343: A fresh look at hematopoietic cell transplantation and of cells therapy survey of the EBMT: monitoring of activities and trends over 30 years arrived with this 2021 research paper. Numbers of hematopoietic cell transplantation in Europe and collaborating countries continues to rise with 48,512 HCT in 43,581 patients, comprising. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc8314143: Wong and co-authors published this research paper in 2021 on global incidence (new cases) and deaths of stomach cancer, 1980-2018. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. With firm counts in hand, planners can size the problem and track whether it grows or shrinks.
europmc-pmc8494643: A 2021 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at morphological diversity of single neurons in molecularly defined cell types. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8770643: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at advances (new steps forward) in mixed cell deconvolution enable quantification of cell types in spatial transcriptomic (gene-activity) data. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8822843: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at edaravone eases depressive and anxiety-like behaviors via Sirt1/Nrf2/HO-1/Gpx4 pathway. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Once the chain of events is mapped, future treatments can be built to break it.
europmc-pmc8931543: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at selective aimed at of cancer cells by copper ionophores: an survey. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8955843: A fresh look at methods of liposomes preparation: formation and control factors of versatile nanocarriers for biomedical (medical research) and nanomedicine (ultra-small-particle medicine) application (use) arrived with this 2022 research paper. Liposomes are nano-sized spherical vesicles (tiny sacs) composed of an aqueous core surrounded by one (or more) phospholipid bilayer shells. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9012043: This 2022 research paper covers linda: linear models for differential abundance analysis of microbiome (microbes living in the body) compositional data. Differential abundance analysis is at the core of statistical analysis of microbiome (microbes living in the body) data. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9050543: Published in 2022, this research paper takes on single-cell (one cell at a time) sequencing (reading DNA letter by letter) of human midbrain shows glial activation (switching on). The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9077443: This 2022 research paper covers cabotegravir for the prevention (keeping illness away) of HIV-1 in women: results from HPTN 084, a phase 3, randomised clinical (in patients). Oral pre-exposure prophylaxis has been introduced in more than 70 countries, including many in sub-saharan Africa, but women experience considerable. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc9106343: A 2022 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at biological (from living things) aging processes underlying thinking decline and neurodegenerative disease. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9189143: Doctors and scientists took on mild breathing COVID can cause multi-lineage neural cell and myelin dysregulation in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9266143: A fresh look at microglia (the brain's immune cells) phenotypes in aging and neurodegenerative diseases arrived with this 2022 research paper. Neuroinflammation (brain swelling) is a hallmark of many neurodegenerative diseases and plays a fundamental role in mediating the onset. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc9370143: Doctors and scientists took on the role of lipids in food flavor generation in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
europmc-pmc9630343: Bilotta and co-authors published this research paper in 2022 on managing the TME to improve the efficacy (how well something works) of cancer therapy. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc9830443: This 2023 research paper covers of cells mitophagy: mechanism (how it works), roles in diseases and small molecule pharmacological control. Of cells mitophagy means that cells selectively wrap and degrade damaged mitochondria (the cell's power plants). Pinning down the inner workings gives drug makers a concrete target to aim at.
europmc-pmc9842643: Ascensao and co-authors published this research paper in 2023 on quantifying the local adaptive landscape of a nascent germ community. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
fbi-vault-special-counsel-mueller-invest: Part forty-three of the FBI Vault's Mueller investigation records. The 2019 report's supporting material filled many files. These pages hold more of it. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
feuerbach-grundsaetze-1843:
Ludwig Feuerbach set out his program in Grundsaetze der Philosophie der Zukunft, German theses from 1843. The title promises the principles of the philosophy of the future. Feuerbach had already argued that talk of God mirrors human nature itself. These short theses press that line into a new starting point for thought.

He calls philosophy back from abstract spirit to real, sensing human beings. Thought, he insists, grows from flesh, need, and community with others. The young Karl Marx read the theses and turned from Hegel toward materialism under their pull. No public domain English translation exists. The German original carries the full charge.
fielding-jonathan-wild-1743:
Fielding published The History of the Life of the Late Mr Jonathan Wild the Great in 1743, inside his Miscellanies. Jonathan Wild was a real thief-taker, hanged in 1725, who ran London crime while posing as its hunter. Fielding turns his life into dark satire.

Every crime of Wild's is praised in the language of statesmanship, since Fielding's target is the 'great man' in politics too. Prime Minister Walpole's shadow falls across the rogue's career. The irony never relaxes, which makes the book Fielding's coldest and most biting work. It remains a classic study of power, cant, and the worship of greatness.
fielding-journey-next-world-1743:
A Journey from This World to the Next, printed in Fielding's Miscellanies of 1743, is his afterlife satire. The narrator dies, rides a coach of spirits to the world below, and reports what he finds. Lucian, the Greek satirist, is Fielding's model here.

In Elysium the dead are judged by Minos, and fame on earth counts for little. The spirit then passes through new lives, including that of Julian the Apostate, across a comic chain of births. Fielding mocks pride, cruelty, and empty ambition in every rank. The work shows his learning and his laughter working together, years before Tom Jones made him famous.
franck-la-kabbale-1843:
Adolphe Franck gave the lore of the Jews its first stern study in La Kabbale, his book of 1843. Franck was a sage of thought at a top school in Paris. He read the old texts in their own tongues. He asked when they were writ, by whom, and what they claim of God and man.

His calm sifts myth from fact with care. Great names of the occult, from Levi to Waite, cite his work as their base. The book, in French, marks the start of true study of this lore. Its worth still stands. Franck taught at the great school of France in Paris town. His rank gave his calm study a weight no mere fan could claim.
frus-1861-d143:
Writing on 17 August 1861, William H. Seward reset his orders to William Dayton for a long war. The letter is document 143 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's mid August letters have a plainer, graver tone than those of June. The short war was gone, and the orders fit the new facts. This note to Paris shows policy reset for endurance: fewer boasts, firmer law, longer watch. The reset he describes governed the Paris file through the rest of 1861. Endurance as policy asked envoys to be dull on cue, and Dayton obliged. Endurance, as policy, asked for dull strength.
frus-1861-d243:
James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 8 July 1861. It stands as Document 243 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d43:
On 27 April 1861, William H. Seward sent orders to Charles Francis Adams, his new envoy to Britain. The letter is document 43 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams was then crossing to take up the London post. Seward's April orders framed the line he should take with the British government. Britain had yet to state its stance on the war, and each word from Washington would shape Adams's first talks. Adams reached London in mid May and found a government still making up its mind. Mind and map were both still open when Adams stepped ashore in May.
frus-1862-d143:
Orders from Washington reached Charles Francis Adams in a State Department letter dated 15 September 1862. It stands as Document 143 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d243:
William Stuart wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 12 October 1862, and the letter closes the Stuart run as Document 243 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart had led the British legation through the summer and early fall.

By mid-October, the British cabinet was moving toward a decision against stepping into the war, though Stuart could not know its final shape. His letters across these months form a distinct chapter in the record: an understudy handling a great post in a crisis. This last letter ends that chapter on the eve of the decision. Both offices kept up the formal courtesies even when their governments were near quarreling.
frus-1862-d343:
The third Seward dispatch of 4 November 1862 stands as Document 343 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Like its mates, it went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris.

Within days, the British cabinet voted down the truce proposal, and the fall crisis ended. These letters were already at sea, written for a danger that was passing. The overlap is a fine lesson in 1862 statecraft. Policy had to be framed to hold in several futures, because no one could know which future had begun. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year.
frus-1862-d43:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 3 April 1862. It stands as Document 43 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The date falls in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d443:
On 6 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Norman B. Judd, the American minister at Berlin. The instruction is Document 443 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

By May 1862 Union victories in the West and the fall of New Orleans gave Seward good news to send his ministers. Judd's post in Berlin was a friendly place to send it. Prussia had no wish to aid the Confederacy, but its court still had to be courted and kept informed. Instructions of this sort also told ministers how to answer Confederate claims abroad. The dispatch shows Washington working a friendly capital with the same care it gave to doubtful ones.
frus-1862-d543:
Roest van Limburg wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 30 August 1862, the second day of the battle of Second Bull Run. His note is Document 543 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

That a Dutch minister transacted calm formal business in Washington while a battle raged thirty miles away is itself a fact about wartime capitals. Van Limburg's errand remained the protection of Dutch interests, which the war touched through trade and shipping rather than armies. His note belongs to the late-summer Dutch file, where the tone stayed correct even as the military news darkened. Seward's department answered such notes as they came, and the printed sequence preserves that discipline.
frus-1862-d643:
Townsend Harris sent this dispatch from Japan to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 23 November 1861. It is Document 643 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the annual message.

Harris wrote in late November, as the Trent affair was breaking in the Atlantic world he could not hear of for months. In Edo his business remained the treaty relationship and the condition of the mission he had founded. He was by then a sick man nearing the end of his service. His remaining letters have the quality of a founder setting his house in order. The dispatch is among the last of his printed reports in the volume, closing the first chapter of American diplomacy in Japan.
frus-1863p1-d143:
On 3 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 143 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, the middle piece of three sent that day.

The middle sheet of Adams's sets often held the day's weight. In April 1863 the weight was ships: Southern raiders built in Britain, and the Union's drive to stop them. This letter holds its place in that fight's record. Read with its mates, it shows the legation working all its lines at once in the war's most fraught spring abroad.
frus-1863p1-d243:
Washington's orders to London on 23 July 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 243 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Instructions like this one show how the Lincoln government ran a war abroad while fighting one at home. The paper trail is the diplomacy itself, order by order. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d343:
In Washington on 22 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 343 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Lyons was the man Seward had to persuade, warn, or answer in person in Washington. Notes to him carried the American side of each dispute between the two governments. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d43:
Judah P. Benjamin sent this letter to John Slidell on 28 October 1862. Benjamin was the Confederate secretary of state; Slidell was the South's envoy in Paris. The letter is document 43 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

By late October the South's drive for foreign backing was losing ground, after Antietam and the first word of the freedom edict. Benjamin's letters to Paris kept the push alive on paper. This one is a late-fall piece of that effort. Printed by the Union in its own volume, it shows the other side's hopes in its own hand, at the hour they began to fade.
frus-1863p1-d443:
Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington received a letter dated 3 April 1863 from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d543:
The letter printed as document 543 was written on 30 May 1863 by F. W. Seward to Lord Lyons. F. W. Seward was the Assistant Secretary of State, writing here to Britain's minister in Washington. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d643:
William H. Seward took up his pen on 23 October 1863 and wrote to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d143: Roosevelt answered Churchill on November 19, 1943, and the letter is Document 143 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Replies that week were written from ships, ports, and borrowed desks as the parties converged. The record names the parties and the date only. In the Foreign Relations series the letter stands just before the volume's conference chapters begin, where letters give way to minutes and agreed texts.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d243:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on 21 November 1943 about sparing Rome. His letter carries a draft message to the Pope, ready for Roosevelt's signature, on recognizing Rome as an open city.

Hull argues that, for reasons beyond the military ones, America should make a sincere effort to save Rome from the ruin of modern war. If no deal is reached, she should leave the blame for refusal with the Germans. The draft letter tells the Pope that Washington accepts the Italian government's August declaration and its conditions, if Germany grants the same status. One reservation is spelled out: Allied forces keep full transit rights through Rome by rail and road.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d343:
The final text of the Cairo communiqué, dated 26 November 1943, is the agreed statement of the first Cairo Conference. Harry Hopkins handed the text to Ambassador Kirk that afternoon, and the White House released it to the press on 1 December, after the Tehran meeting ended.

The statement says the military missions have agreed on future operations against Japan, and that the three allies will bring unrelenting pressure by sea, land, and air. The three powers covet no gain and no territory. Japan will be stripped of all Pacific islands seized since 1914. The territories stolen from China, including Manchuria, Formosa, and the Pescadores, will be restored. Japan will be expelled from every land taken by violence and greed. Korea, in due course, will become free and independent.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d43: A second Roosevelt letter to Stalin bears the same date, October 14, 1943, and stands as Document 43 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Two letters to Moscow in one day suggests business too mixed, or too urgent, for a single sheet. The record does not separate their topics, and neither should a summary. Both are printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the last days before the foreign ministers met.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d443:
By December 5, 1943, the Second Cairo Conference was in full swing, and the Combined Chiefs of Staff met again that day. Their minutes, printed in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume, come from the joint body that matched American and British plans into one war effort. Turkey's possible entry into the war hung over the whole conference.

The record follows the chiefs through the day's military business, with positions stated, differences worked through, and decisions noted for the two heads of government. Read beside the Tehran documents, it shows the alliance moving from promises to planning. Few sources show wartime teamwork at this level so plainly.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d543:
President Roosevelt addressed this message on January 10, 1944 to Patrick J. Hurley, his personal representative, then temporarily in Iran. Hurley, a former secretary of war, roamed the Middle East on the President's personal business. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Personal representatives were Roosevelt's way of cutting through department lines: Hurley reported to the President alone and answered to no embassy. Iran, occupied and restless after hosting the Tehran Conference, held his attention that winter. For readers, the message shows Roosevelt managing a sensitive country through a trusted agent in the weeks after the summit left its capital.
frus-1944-quebec-d143:
Churchill reported to Roosevelt on the Italian offensive in telegram 772, sent August 29, 1944. Four German divisions had been pulled from Italy since the Riviera landings, yet General Alexander had concentrated his armies for a blow at the Gothic Line. Churchill had gone forward with the advance himself and described the modern battlefield at first hand.

The Eighth Army, ten divisions strong on the Adriatic flank, had attacked on August 26 and gained about nine miles. General Clark's eight divisions around Florence would strike once the enemy reacted, and both armies would converge on Bologna. Churchill also looked ahead: a powerful army in Trieste and Istria within weeks, he argued, would carry effects far beyond military value.
frus-1944-quebec-d243:
Churchill returned Roosevelt's memorandum on Italian colonies with a short note dated September 16, 1944. The paper was Hull's September 11 memorandum, with the department's study of British proposals for Italy's overseas territories. The Foreign Office, Churchill wrote, would like to treat it as an official communication, if the president would allow London to keep a copy.

The usual broad and substantial measure of agreement existed between the two governments, he said, but the British wished to look into the details more closely. A handwritten note by Dorothy Brady, attached in the Roosevelt Papers, records the outcome: the president agreed the British could keep copies, and he wanted an answer from them on it.
frus-1944-quebec-d43:
Harry Hopkins wrote to Prime Minister Mackenzie King of Canada on August 31, 1944. Canada would host the coming conference at Quebec City, and King was its host prime minister. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Canada's part in these conferences was easy to overlook and wrong to forget: Canadian soil, Canadian hospitality, and a Canadian government carrying a major war effort of its own. Hopkins's message to King handled the host's side of the arrangements. For readers, it gives due place to the third country in the room, whose capital province framed the meeting.
frus-1945-50-intel-d143:
A memorandum dated 14 February 1946 links two senior offices. The sender was the Director of Central Intelligence (Souers). The reader was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (McCormack). The State Department prints it as document 143 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The postwar system was still new: the National Intelligence Authority gave the orders, and the Central Intelligence Group carried them out.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d243:
A memorandum by the Army Member of the State–Army–Navy–Air Force Coordinating Committee (Pixtou) bears the date 15 October 1947. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 243 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The CIA was only weeks old, having replaced the Central Intelligence Group in September 1947 under the National Security Act.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d343:
A memorandum dated 17 March 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers). The reader was Allen W. Dulles, Mathias F. Correa, and William H. Jackson. The State Department prints it as document 343 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d43:
Ladd, an assistant director of the FBI, wrote to Hoover on 5 November 1945. Ladd ran much of the bureau's intelligence and security work and stood high in Hoover's trust. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Assistant directors' memoranda gave Hoover the bureau's own picture of events, filtered by men who knew his mind. Ladd's paper belongs to the FBI's watch on the central intelligence question, which touched the bureau's foreign operations directly. Readers building the FBI thread should set Ladd beside Tamm: two senior aides serving one director. Their stream of paper kept the bureau's position sharp through the long contest of 1945 and 1946.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d143:
President Roosevelt answered Churchill's Moscow dispatches on 22 October 1944 with warm approval and one request. His short top secret telegram, number 632, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Six of Churchill's messages are acknowledged in its first line.

Roosevelt says he is delighted at the success in Moscow toward a compromise solution of the Polish problem. When and if a solution is reached, he asks to be consulted on one point of timing. That is whether publication should be delayed for about two weeks. “You will understand,” he adds, and closes by reporting that everything is going well at home. The note is a small window on how the Polish settlement touched American politics.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d243:
What happens in China if Russia enters the Far East war? A briefing book paper of 13 January 1945 works through the map. Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume under a long title on the political and military situation in China.

The Communists hold large parts of North China, the paper says, with further pockets to the east and south. They claim 500,000 regular troops and two million militia: ill equipped, but well trained in guerrilla war and in good physical shape. Their underground strength in Manchuria counts as considerable. One Russian line of attack might run from Outer Mongolia through Inner Mongolia toward Shanhaikuan, the gateway to Manchuria. Communist armies would then stand on the Russians' right flank.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d343:
One sheet of paper or several? The United States Chiefs of Staff argued for one in this February 5, 1945 paper on the Bremen-Bremerhaven area. The port enclave was to sit inside the British zone but serve American supply lines. The chiefs backed a single clean agreement text over a draft tied to a general's letter.

On the side points raised in that letter, the chiefs took a practical line. Whatever the zone commanders on the ground could not settle between themselves should go up to the Combined Chiefs for a ruling. Clashes of authority, they granted, were sure to come. The paper shows alliance housekeeping at its driest and most needed.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d43: On 6 January 1945 Churchill sent Roosevelt another message, one day after his previous letter. It stands as document 43 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta, issued by the Department of State. Frequent short messages were Churchill's habit before a conference, letting him raise points for the agenda while there was still time to settle them by cable.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d443:
Jebb, Gromyko, and Hiss reported back to the foreign ministers on February 10, 1945. Their subcommittee had been instructed two days earlier on two subjects. The first was how to consult France and China on the conference's decisions about the world organization. The second was the text of the invitation to the United Nations conference.

On consultation, they held that the United States should speak for the three powers to both governments. On the invitation, they attached a draft for the ministers' approval. The report is brief. But it closed the last piece of machinery needed to summon the founding conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d143:
President Truman wrote to Stalin about the surrendered German ships on May 29, 1945. His personal and top secret message, number 275, is document 143 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Stalin had proposed a way of dividing the German fleet in a message of May 23.

Truman thanks Stalin for the suggestion, then puts the question off to the summit. The subject suits discussion by the three leaders at their coming meeting, he writes, where he is sure a solution fully acceptable to all can be reached. He adds a practical point: the records of the German naval surrender are being examined by the commanders in the areas concerned. Like Churchill, Truman kept the fleet for face-to-face bargaining rather than cable trading.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d243:
Ambassador Winant confirmed delivery of the Italy message in a one-line telegram dated July 15, 1945. The message is document 243 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Washington had told him the day before to inform the Foreign Office, urgently, of the planned American announcement backing Italy's admission to the world security organization.

Winant's whole report reads: Foreign Office given substance of the Department's telegram this morning. The delivery set off the trouble that followed within hours, when London officials protested that the announcement was sprung on them with the Prime Minister and Foreign Secretary already in Berlin. The tiny telegram is the quiet first half of a small allied quarrel; the second half sits in the next document.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d343:
Reeducation of Germany is the subject Archibald MacLeish laid before the Secretary of State on July 4, 1945. The War Department had asked again and again for a long-range policy directive to guide its men in Germany. MacLeish's covering note sends the paper the Secretary had requested that morning at the Staff Committee.

The enclosed paper admits the problem's great difficulty. To frame a policy, the Department had called in leading citizens with deep experience in education. President Edmund Day of Cornell chaired the advisory group, and President George Shuster of Hunter College sat among its members. Their charge was nothing less than reshaping German minds.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d43:
Stalin wrote to Prime Minister Winston Churchill from Moscow on May 30, 1945, in a top secret personal message. It is document 43 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The two leaders were settling when the Big Three would hold their next meeting, weeks after the German surrender ended the war in Europe.

Stalin explains a mix-up over the date. Truman's envoy Harry Hopkins had told him the President favored a meeting around mid-July, yet the message first read as June 15. Stalin says he has no objection if Churchill also agrees. An added note by Charles Bohlen records how the error was checked with Soviet officials and confirmed as July 15.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d443:
Elections in Greece are the subject of a briefing book paper that begins at Yalta. There the United States agreed to act with Russia and Britain in helping Europe's liberated nations solve their pressing political and economic problems by democratic means. In Greece, America had no military commitments and only a limited relief role.

The paper recalls the Varkiza Agreement of February 12, 1945, between EAM and the Greek government. Its ninth article promised allied supervision for a plebiscite within the year, and for elections after it. Washington made no public comment at the time, the paper notes, but stood ready to look favorably on a Greek request to help run those votes.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d543:
Secretary of War Henry Stimson sent a top secret wire to the Secretary of State on July 11, 1945. He wrote from aboard the Army transport Brazil, on his way to the Potsdam Conference. The wire is document 543 in volume one of the Foreign Relations series on that meeting.

Stimson says he and John McCloy are troubled by the President's new lend-lease order. As the War Department reads it, the order bars food and fuel for the French army of occupation in Germany. It also bars upkeep for British and French occupation forces. Yet those forces free far more U.S. troops to shift to the war against Japan. Stimson asks if that strict reading is right.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d643:
From Beirut on July 9, 1945, Minister Wadsworth reported a talk with General Pilleau on the Levant transfer. His confidential wire is document 643 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Pilleau was the British officer dealing with the handover of the Troupes Speciales.

Pilleau urged prompt study of a Ninth Army memo on the practical side of the transfer. Absent higher political reasons, he saw a security gain in finishing the transfer before any troop withdrawal. French forces, he noted, could hardly be asked to leave except alongside the British. Wadsworth asks Washington for its views on who should propose a joint withdrawal. Without some move, he warns, Syria will press its demand again and the security picture will suffer.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1043:
Richard Bissell, a War Shipping Administration official at Potsdam, cabled his Washington office on July 22, 1945. British shipping chief Lord Leathers had stated Britain's coal limit in early talks. After August shipments, Britain can export no coal at all for September arrival. Two small exceptions stand: anthracite duffs for briquetting, and special grades needed in North Africa.

Leathers presses instead to draw at least 90,000 tons a month of American bunker coal. Britain has taken on fueling captured and released ships, near 70,000 tons a month. Bissell warns cash payment may be demanded. He asks Washington's view on American supply, and on whether the British refusal is fair.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1143:
Secretary of War Henry Stimson wrote to President Truman on 16 July 1945, the day before the Potsdam Conference opened. Stimson was the cabinet's senior figure on war matters. His word carried weight with the president on every question the army touched.

A message sent on the summit's eve framed the picture Truman carried into the talks. The War Department ran the forces that held Germany and still fought Japan. Its chief's counsel, put in writing, fixed the armed forces' stand before the bargaining began. This letter is that counsel. It shows the president's brief being built, one paper at a time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1243:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to the Secretary of State on 22 July 1945. The Washington end of the circuit answered the summit end on a near daily rhythm. Grew's messages carried the home office's news and needs to Byrnes in Germany.

By the second week, the circuit was a settled habit. Files moved, questions rose, and answers came back within a day or two. This cable is one turn of that habit. Small in itself, it belongs to a rare system. That system let one department sit in two places at once, in the most crowded fortnight of its year.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1343:
A text handed in by the Soviet delegation on 29 July 1945 forms document 1343 of the Potsdam volume. It came in the last days of the conference, when drafting of the final papers was at its most intense. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Late texts at a summit often carry the hardest bargaining, since each side knows the clock is running out. What a delegation chose to put in writing at that stage shows what it valued most. Set beside the closing protocol, this Soviet text helps readers judge the talks. It shows how much of the Soviet program survived, and how much was traded away.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-143: This editorial note appears without a number after document 710 in the second volume of Potsdam papers. The Foreign Relations editors wrote such notes to lend readers a hand. They name sources, connect related texts, and mark thin spots in the file. Here the note steadies a reader inside a long stretch of conference records.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-43:
Thompson's minutes record the plenary session of July 20, 1945, at 4 p.m. at Potsdam. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. Molotov opened the session by presenting his report as rapporteur of the morning's foreign ministers' meeting.

The report was largely a tale of unfinished work. The subcommittee on German economic policy had not yet reported, Molotov said. The committee on Poland had likewise not finished, and was told to complete its report by July 21. On the peace settlement, the drafting group had run out of time as well. The foreign ministers had therefore met just before the session and agreed a text themselves, whose revised paragraph 3 Molotov then read. He closed by presenting a Soviet draft on carrying out the Yalta declaration on liberated areas. That text opened debate on Rumania and Bulgaria, and on Greece.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d743:
Gerig reported once more to Alger Hiss on August 9, 1945, in document 743. The United Nations Preparatory Commission still filled his days in London. His letter extends the volume's record past the Potsdam close. It was printed among the final papers of the second Potsdam volume's United Nations thread.

Late letters in a series carry the state of play at a moment of change. The war in Asia was ending; the new body's first assembly drew near. Readers see a planner's desk at that hinge. The document shows how the Potsdam generation passed its work to the institutions it had built.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d843:
The Soviet delegation tabled this proposal at Potsdam on July 27, 1945, as document 843. It dates from the final week, as Attlee returned to the table. Soviet texts in the endgame defended gains and pressed the last claims. The proposal was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A late Soviet draft lets readers weigh Moscow's priorities under time pressure. What a side tables when days run short reveals what it values. The document can be read against the final protocol for the answer. It also shows the Soviet team's method to the end: written claims, firmly held, traded only at the top.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d943: The Pauley group prepared this table of capital removals needed to cut German war potential, filed with the July 28, 1945 papers. Figures are in millions of prewar Reichsmarks. Factory removals, armaments included, total 3,500 across the Reich. Transport removals add 2,250, and power and gas add 900. The full total is 6,650 million. Of that, 2,925 million sits in the eastern zone including Berlin, and 3,725 million in the rest of Germany. Dollar conversions at two exchange rates split the value 44 percent east and 56 percent west.
