gao-gaoreports-b-298143: Lawrence C. Drake took his April 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. He said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Individuals get the same full hearing as the firms.
gao-gaoreports-b-298543: STG took its October 2006 contract fight to GAO — two more case numbers in the docket — and this ruling is the call. The firm challenged the awards, and the ruling tests the claims. The docket's tangle got one careful answer. The tangled docket got one answer.
gao-gaoreports-b-311143: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Harris Enterprises, Inc. Decided March 27, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-b-311343: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Singleton Enterprises- GMT Mechanical, A Joint Venture. The April 23, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-243: Missile defense's 2004 status got a GAO check in 2005, and the report covers the program's year. The review reads the scorecard closely. The shield's progress was measured. The measure was taken. The year was graded. The scorecard was read. The year was recorded.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-343: Head Start's new test needed development in 2005, and GAO's report says further work could let results guide decisions. The findings demand the refinement. The report warns that the little learners deserved honest tests. The development had to continue. The little learners deserved honest tests.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-543: Border air and marine assets needed coordination in 2005, and GAO's report says opportunities existed to increase teamwork. The findings demand the coordination. The report warns that the borders deserved joined-up patrols. The opportunities had to be seized. The borders deserved joined-up patrols.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-943: Smart traffic systems fell short on congestion in 2005, and GAO's report says the intelligent systems' promise was unmet. The findings deliver the verdict. The report warns that the gridlocked drivers deserved working tech. The promise had to be kept. The gridlocked drivers deserved working tech.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-143: Consumer-directed federal health plans got an early review in 2005, and GAO's report examines the first experience. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the workers' new health choices needed watching. The experience had to be studied. The workers' new choices needed watching.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-343: The Civil Rights Commission needed better quality control in 2006, and GAO's report says the commission should strengthen its assurance policies. The findings demand the rigor. The report warns that the rights watchdog needed watching. The policies had to be strengthened.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-43: Laid-off workers mostly got help in 2006, and GAO's report says most workers in five layoffs received services, though outreach on new benefits needed work. The findings balance credit and prodding. The report warns that the displaced deserved to know their options. The outreach had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-643: The military's Katrina response needed better plans in 2006, and GAO's report says better plans and exercises should guide responses to catastrophic storms. The findings demand the preparation. The report warns that the next storm would not wait. The plans had to be ready.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-943: The Pentagon's surplus gear was a security risk in 2006, and GAO's report says control breakdowns presented significant danger and waste. The findings sound the alarm. The report warns that the excess property should not arm the wrong hands. The controls had to be restored.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-143: The Army's chemical defense units were not ready in 2007, and GAO's report says management action was needed to close the preparedness gap. The findings target the shortfalls. The report warns that the gas masks and suits had to match the threat. The readiness gap could not stand.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-43: Welfare-to-work transit aid was improving in 2007, and GAO's report says the Job Access program had progressed, though evaluation and outreach lagged. The findings balance credit and prodding. The report warns that the rides to work needed both riders and results. The buses had to be counted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-643: The Navy's repair shops could not trust their own numbers in 2007 — GAO's report says the air warfare center's books needed management action. The findings target the working-capital fog. The report's moral: a repair depot that cannot count cannot price.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-243: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on emergency Transit Assistance: Federal Funding for Recent Disasters, and Options for the Future. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-343: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on information Security: Protecting Personally Identifiable Information. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-43: Another 2007 Government Accountability Office report on the nation's switch from analog to digital television. It argues that federal agencies needed stronger planning and risk management to keep the transition on track — particularly around public education and the converter-box coupon program. The findings warn that without tighter coordination, millions of households could lose over-the-air TV service when analog signals went dark.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-443: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at international Trade: US Trade Preference Programs Provide Important Benefits, but a More Integrated Approach Would Better Ensure Programs Meet Shared Goals. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-643: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at small Business Administration: Additional Actions Are Needed to Certify and Monitor HUBZone Businesses and Assess Program Results. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
liebig-familiar-letters-chemistry-1843:
Justus von Liebig published Familiar Letters on Chemistry in 1843, a popular book grown from letters on science for a general audience. Liebig wrote to show lay readers that chemistry touches their daily bread, farms, and health. The letters avoid formulas and argue in clear prose.

Liebig explained how chemistry serves agriculture and physiology, the themes of his two great technical books of 1842. He attacked the old idea that living things obey wholly separate laws, and he praised experiment over authority. The letters sold widely and were often reprinted and expanded. They made Liebig a public figure and stand as a model of how a working scientist can address the whole reading public.
matter-histoire-critique-du-gnosticisme-:
Jacques Matter's Histoire critique du Gnosticisme, published in French in 1843, was the first great documentary history of Gnosticism. Earlier writers had treated the subject in fragments; Matter assembled the scattered ancient evidence into one coherent story. His two-part study also traced the movement's influence on later religious sects.

Working through the church fathers and the sects' own traces, he built the field's first real archive. Modern study of early Christian heresy effectively begins with his volumes. The French text demands effort from English readers, but historians still respect its groundwork. Matter founded a discipline almost single-handedly. Anyone tracing how Gnosticism became a subject of scholarship should know his name.
mill-system-logic-vol-1-1843:
John Stuart Mill's System of Logic, Volume 1, appears here in a separate entry for the 1843 first edition's first volume. Mill's full title adds Ratiocinative and Inductive, naming the two kinds of reasoning he treated. Volume 1 covers names, propositions, and the start of induction.

Mill defined the words and statements logic works on, then asked how we prove anything at all. His answer gave pride of place to induction, learning general laws from observed cases. That focus made the book the founding text of the philosophy of science in English. Readers who use this entry get the original 1843 wording of the opening books, before Mill's many later revisions.
mill-system-logic-vol-2-1843:
John Stuart Mill's System of Logic, Volume 2, completes the 1843 first edition in this entry. The second volume carries induction forward and then turns to error and to the study of society. Mill wrote it as the payoff of the whole system.

Chapters finish the methods of causal proof, catalogue the fallacies that spoil argument, and defend a logic for the moral sciences. Mill claimed that history, politics, and the mind could be sciences, though softer ones than physics. That claim shaped how universities later built social science. Together with Volume 1, this entry preserves the complete first edition of a founding work.
mill-system-of-logic-1843:
John Stuart Mill published A System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive in 1843. Mill, then in his thirties, set out the rules of proof for both math-like reasoning and the sciences of observation. The book made him a leading thinker of the Victorian age.

Mill defined terms, tested syllogisms, and then built his famous methods for finding causes by experiment and comparison. He argued that even the laws of nature rest on induction, reasoning from cases seen to cases unseen. Later parts applied logic to the study of society. Generations of students learned scientific method from Mill, and his methods are still taught by name.
mill-system-of-logic-vol-1-1843:
John Stuart Mill published Volume 1 of A System of Logic in 1843, the first half of his treatise on reasoning. This entry holds the first edition's first volume, Books 1 to 3 in part. Mill set out to ground all proof, including science, in experience.

Book 1 treats names and propositions, and Book 2 tests the syllogism and its limits. Book 3 begins induction, Mill's central subject, with his methods for finding causes. He held that logic is the science of evidence itself. The volume founded the modern study of inductive logic, and its account of how we learn from cases shaped the philosophy of science.
mill-system-of-logic-vol-2-1843:
Volume 2 of Mill's System of Logic, first edition of 1843, completes the work begun in Volume 1. John Stuart Mill carried induction through its harder cases and then turned to error and to society. Books 3 through 6 fill this second half.

Mill finished his account of causal proof, then catalogued fallacies, the stock errors of reasoning he thought corrupted debate. The last book treats the logic of the moral sciences, arguing that history and society can be studied scientifically. That defense of social science as science drew wide notice. The two volumes together formed the founding text of inductive logic in English.
moneta-adversus-catharos-1743:
Moneta of Cremona, a Dominican friar, finished his Adversus Catharos et Valdenses, Against the Cathars and Waldensians, around 1241. It is the great scholastic summa of the anti-heresy war in five books. Tommaso Agostino Ricchini edited the Latin text at Rome in 1743. Moneta wrote in Lombardy, where the Cathar churches stood strongest in Italy.

Book by book he states the heretics' claims on God, matter, marriage, and the church, then answers them from scripture and reason. His reports of Cathar teaching are full enough that scholars mine the attack as a source for the attacked. The work shows the schools of Paris turned into weapons. It is the high medieval counter-offensive in full armor.
openalex-w1995770643: Fish get skin cancer too — even in the wild. Sweet and colleagues' 2012 study found evidence of melanoma in wild marine fish populations. The discovery linked novel diseases in marine ecosystems to climate shifts and new pathogens.
openalex-w2054012543: A tiny RNA steers plant aging. Schommer and colleagues' 2008 study found miR319 targets control jasmonate biosynthesis and senescence. The work traced how a microRNA's targets regulate leaf aging and the hormone signals behind it.
openalex-w2135168743: Maize diversity got a SNP map. A 2009 study characterized a global maize collection and estimated gene links. The SNP assay genotyped 632 inbred lines from breeding programs — corn's gene map, drawn at last for breeders everywhere.
openalex-w2136669243: Reef resilience needs measurable indicators. A 2012 paper prioritized key resilience indicators for coral reef management. The work cut through theory with hard evidence for climate-ready reefs — management's toolkit, assembled at last for managers now.
openalex-w2140214243: Chagas' main Central American vector has deep diversity. A 2008 study mapped the gene geography of Triatoma dimidiata. The work documented wide physical, genetic, and behavioral diversity — the kissing bug, mapped at last for control teams now.
openalex-w2474124643: Tithonia diversifolia is an invasive weed sprawling across tropical ecosystems — and its chemistry shifts with its surroundings. This 2016 Scientific Reports paper uses spectral data and multivariate statistics to map how abiotic factors reshape the plant's secondary metabolites. The environmental metabolomics approach reveals how invaders tune their chemistry to conquer new ground.
openalex-w2542984143: Fuel cells could run clean if cheap catalysts replaced platinum — and iron-nitrogen-carbon materials are candidates. This 2016 Nature Communications paper develops an in situ electrochemical method to count the actual active sites in Fe–N/C oxygen-reduction catalysts. Knowing how many sites do the work, not just how much material is there, is key to making non-precious catalysts viable.
openalex-w2616925143: During the Zika emergency, sequencing the virus straight from patient samples was slow and fiddly. This 2017 Nature Protocols paper, by Joshua Quick and colleagues, presents a multiplex PCR method that prepares Zika and other virus genomes for MinION and Illumina sequencers directly from clinical samples. The protocol helped bring rapid, field-ready genomics to outbreak response.
openalex-w2947890843: Glioblastoma feeds on glucose and glutamine — so why not starve it? This 2019 Communications Biology paper tests combining a calorie-restricted ketogenic diet with glutamine targeting in late-stage experimental glioblastoma. Attacking both fuels at once, the study finds therapeutic benefit against a tumor that has resisted decades of therapy.
openalex-w3036495543: COVID-19 showed pandemics can shatter supply chains worldwide. This 2020 Annals of Operations Research paper maps the research agenda on epidemic impacts on supply chains through a structured literature review. The agenda fills a gap the pandemic exposed.
openalex-w4318071643: ADHD is a prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder with a major genetic component. This 2023 Nature Genetics meta-analysis — 38,691 cases, 186,843 controls — identifies 27 risk loci, refines the genetic architecture, and implicates several cognitive domains. The findings deepen the biology of attention.
openalex-w7133357343: Chest cancer treatment is advancing fast. This review covers new drug milestones for lung malignancies: next-generation targeted pills and immune checkpoint drugs with striking survival gains. The authors surveyed both small-cell and non-small-cell disease. An oncology review of a field in rapid motion.
openalex-w7204169643: Medical students took their lessons to a quilombola community in southwest Bahia, teaching mosquito-borne disease and viral hepatitis prevention. This experience report describes the outreach project: what the students did, what the community taught them back, and how health education works outside the classroom. A first-hand account of medicine as service.
openalex-w7204566843: After bowel surgery, a leak where the intestine was rejoined can be deadly. This paper studies a technique that helps surgeons check blood flow during the operation: injecting a green dye that glows under special light. The authors review how this fluorescence imaging prevents leaks and guides decisions on the table. A surgical innovation where seeing better means healing better.
openalex-w7204757643: Virus-killing materials need not rely on rare earths. This paper reports iodate compounds built from common elements, tested for antiviral power and coated onto textile fibers. The authors also checked the powder forms. A materials study of everyday elements fighting germs.
phreno-magnet-and-mirror-of-nature-a-rec: The Phreno-Magnet of 1843 mirrored nature with facts and experiments. The magnetic mirror of discovery. The phrenological record. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open. Scholars prize such firsthand sources from long ago.
plos-pbio-0020243:
Anne E. Bygrave, Kirsten L. Rose, Josefina Cortes-Hernandez, and their team raised a caution about mouse research in PLOS Biology in 2004. Two common lab mouse strains, called 129 and C57BL/6, can develop signs of autoimmune disease on their own as they age. Autoimmunity means the immune system attacks the body itself.

That background noise can confuse studies of gene-targeted mice. If a normal mouse of the same strain shows the same signs, a removed gene may not be the cause. The authors urge care in picking control mice and in reading results. Their warning helps labs avoid false claims about which genes cause lupus-like disease in mice.
plos-pone-0000043:
Olivier Neyrolles, Rogelio Hernández-Pando, France Pietri-Rouxel, and co-authors asked a pointed question in 2006: does tuberculosis hide in fat? Mycobacterium tuberculosis can sleep inside the body for years before waking to cause disease. Its hiding places were thought to be mainly in the lungs and immune cells.

The team tested adipose tissue, body fat, as a place of persistence. Fat is plentiful, long-lived, and laced with immune cells, which makes it a plausible bunker. If the germ truly shelters there, treatment must reach it there too, and relapse after cure becomes easier to explain. The question opened a line of research into fat as an overlooked reservoir in chronic infection.
plos-pone-0000143:
Peter Caley, Niels G. Becker, and David J. Philp published this modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It asks a pointed question for pandemic planning: once influenza erupts in one country, how long is the waiting time before it spreads to others? The authors build a model of that inter-country spread.

The answer shapes how much time health agencies have to react with travel measures, vaccines, or alerts. The authors weigh factors that shorten or lengthen the delay. Their work belongs to the planning literature that tries to turn the chaos of the last pandemic into numbers the next response can use.
plos-pone-0000243:
Margarita Gutova, Joseph Najbauer, Anna Gevorgyan, and colleagues published this lung cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Small cell lung cancer is aggressive and often resists chemotherapy. The authors identify a set of tumor cells marked by the protein uPAR that survive chemotherapy, chemoresistant cells that can regrow the cancer.

Finding the cells that outlast treatment is the key to stopping relapse. The authors show these uPAR-positive cells carry that resistant role. The marker gives drug developers a defined target: kill this subpopulation, and the tumor's comeback route may close.
plos-pone-0000343:
Olivia Carter and Patrick Cavanagh published this vision study in PLOS ONE in 2007. When two different images are shown to the two eyes, perception rivals: one image wins, then the other. The authors study onset rivalry, the contest at the very start of viewing. They show that a brief presentation isolates an early, independent phase of that perceptual competition.

Isolating the opening phase lets researchers study competition before slower influences pile on. The authors use very short displays to catch it. The result sharpens the picture of how the brain chooses what we see when the eyes disagree.
plos-pone-0000443:
Alexander Maye and colleagues searched for order in behavior with no instructions, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. When animals or people act spontaneously, their choices look random at first glance. The team analyzed spontaneous behavior for hidden structure, patterns that would show the behavior is organized rather than coin-flip random.

Finding order in spontaneity matters for how scientists interpret free behavior in experiments, from flies in a chamber to people at rest. Structured spontaneous behavior suggests the brain generates patterned activity on its own, rather than merely reacting. The paper joins a growing challenge to the idea that unprompted behavior is noise.
plos-pone-0000543:
John R. Talbott argued that the scale of sex work shapes the global AIDS pandemic, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper titled Size Matters. His analysis linked the number of prostitutes in a population to the spread of HIV/AIDS across countries. Commercial sex networks can carry the virus efficiently between high-risk and general populations.

The claim directs policy toward the structure of epidemics, not only individual behavior. Where sex work is extensive, targeted prevention may decide a country's trajectory. Such ecological analyses are debated because country-level patterns can mislead, but they force attention on drivers that clinic-based studies overlook.
plos-pone-0000643:
Timothy H.-C. Hsiau, Claudiu Diaconu, Connie A. Myers and colleagues mapped the control logic of the eye's light-sensing cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Photoreceptors, the retina cells that catch light, carry more genetic diseases than any other cell type. Most of the more than 120 cloned human blindness genes are highly expressed in photoreceptors.

The team studied the cis-regulatory logic, the DNA switches near genes, that runs the photoreceptor gene network. Their aim was an integrative framework, one map joining the switches to the genes they control. Such a map helps explain how photoreceptors become what they are, and why so many mutations blind.
plos-pone-0000743:
Garret Suen, Barry S. Goldman and Roy D. Welch worked on predicting where a bacterium lives from its genome alone. When they wrote in 2007, automated sequencing was so fast that analysis had become the rate-limiting step. Hundreds of prokaryotic genomes were publicly available, with new ones arriving at roughly 20 per month. Each genome is a parts list without an address.

An ecological niche describes the environment an organism occupies and the life it leads there. If gene content predicts the niche, researchers can infer lifestyle for microbes never cultured in a lab. Most microbes refuse culturing, so genome-based prediction opens the majority of bacterial life to study.
plos-pone-0000843:
Yossi Buskila, Yasmin Abu-Ghanem, Yifat Levi and colleagues reported brain support cells making a signaling gas in a mutant mouse, for PLOS ONE in 2007. It was well accepted that glial cells in the central nervous system produce nitric oxide through the enzyme NOS2 only in response to various insults. The team had recently described rapid astroglial, NOS2-dependent nitric oxide production under other conditions, challenging that rule.

In a NOS2 mutant mouse, they report enhanced astrocytic nitric oxide production and neuronal modifications in the neocortex. Astrocytes are the brain's housekeeper cells, and nitric oxide is both messenger and potential toxin. Rewriting when this gas is made changes accounts of brain inflammation and injury.
plos-pone-0000943:
Konrad Kording, Ulrik Beierholm, Wei Ji Ma and colleagues framed perception as the brain drawing conclusions about causes, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A sensation matters to an animal because of what it says about the world. Smells, sounds and sights are clues, and the brain must infer what caused them.

The authors apply that idea to multisensory perception, where several senses report at once. The brain has to decide whether two clues share one cause or come from separate events. That decision shapes whether we merge the clues or keep them apart. Their causal inference view gives a single logic for many puzzling perception results.
plos-pone-0001043:
Sherine Abboud, Pekka Karhunen, Dieter Lutjohann and colleagues linked a cholesterol gene to a major stroke type, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The gene PCSK9 helps set blood levels of LDL cholesterol, the harmful kind. Its variants were already tied to cholesterol levels and coronary heart disease severity.

The team asked whether PCSK9 also raises the risk of large vessel atherosclerosis stroke, the kind caused by clogged big arteries. A gene that links cholesterol to stroke as well as heart disease widens the case for targeting it. Drugs against PCSK9 were a live idea at the time. Genetic evidence from patients helps judge that idea.
plos-pone-0001143:
Long-term cocaine use is known to impair a person's ability to stop a behavior once started. Lorenza Colzato, Wery van den Wildenberg, and Bernhard Hommel asked whether casual users show the same problem, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Recreational users are a growing group, and findings from heavy users may not apply to them.

The study compared recreational cocaine users with non-users on tasks that require inhibiting and executing responses. Their title states the result: inhibitory control is impaired in the recreational users tested. That finding extends concern about cocaine's effects on self-control beyond chronic addiction.
plos-pone-0001243:
Insecticide-treated bed nets and sprays are mainstays of malaria control, but mosquitoes evolve resistance. João Pinto and colleagues studied knockdown resistance mutations in Anopheles gambiae, the chief African malaria mosquito, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. How often such mutations arise in wild mosquito populations is a basic question for resistance research.

The authors report multiple origins of the knockdown resistance mutations in this mosquito across the Afrotropics. Resistance did not spread from a single source; it evolved repeatedly. That changes how control programs should expect resistance to emerge and spread.
plos-pone-0001343:
Thiacetazone is an old antitubercular drug whose precise action was unclear. Anuradha Alahari and colleagues report how it works against mycobacteria, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The mycobacterial cell wall is rich in mycolic acids, complex branched fatty acids that make the wall highly hydrophobic and hard for drugs to cross.

Pathogenic mycobacteria carry mycolic acid subtypes containing cyclopropane rings. The authors show that thiacetazone inhibits the cyclopropanation of these cell wall mycolic acids. Weakening the wall's chemistry explains the drug's effect and suggests related targets for new TB drugs.
plos-pone-0001443:
Cecilia Poderoso and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how cells make steroid hormones. A signal chain known as ERK helps drive hormone based steroid making, but its exact role was vague. Both the signal and steroid making can be sparked by a cell messenger. The team traced a protein complex inside the cell power units.

They show this complex is vital for the chain to tag a key control protein. That tag is a step the cell needs to make steroids. The finding places part of the control inside the power units themselves. It refines the map that drug and hormone research relies on.
plos-pone-0001543:
Jens Schwachtje, Susan Kutschbach, and Ian Baldwin published a 2008 PLOS ONE essay on gene tests in field ecology. By tweaking single genes, labs can test what each gene does for a plant in the wild. That power could reshape plant ecology. But fears of side effects from the tweak method had held the field back.

The authors weigh those fears against the gains and set terms for sound use. Field tests with single gene changes can split gene effects from soil and weather noise. The essay urges the field to move, with care, from lab pots to real ground. It frames rules for that step.
plos-pone-0001643:
Carla Lucia Esposito and co-authors studied how two receptor proteins talk to each other in nerve tumor cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The receptors are TrkB and Ret, both tyrosine kinases, enzymes that pass growth and survival signals into the cell. How signals from several such receptors combine to set a cell's final state is a key question for drug design.

The team worked with neuroblastoma cells, a childhood nerve cancer, treated with retinoic acid, a drug that pushes these cells to mature. Their results show cross-talk: Ret treatment also brings TrkB into play, and together they drive the cells to differentiate. The full text gives the signal measurements and cell outcomes. Mapping this kind of cross-talk helps explain why some tumors resist drugs aimed at a single receptor.
plos-pone-0001743:
Hamish A. Campbell, Keiron P. P. Fraser, Charles M. Bishop, and their co-authors reported hibernation-like behavior in an Antarctic fish in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians actively suppress metabolism ahead of winter. Fish were thought different: their metabolic rate simply falls in step with water temperature, with no active suppression.

The team's fish, studied on the ice through winter, showed an active metabolic suppression in anticipation of winter conditions. The full text gives the activity and metabolic measurements across seasons. A fish that truly hibernates rewrites a chapter of physiology. It hints at how animals first evolved winter dormancy, and it was found in one of the harshest seas on Earth.
plos-pone-0001843:
Hung Tseng, Weichin Chou, Junwen Wang, and their co-authors catalogued variants of mouse ribosomal RNA genes in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Earlier cytogenetic studies suggested the various rDNA chromosomal loci are not equally active in different cell types. Consistent with this variability, rDNA polymorphism is well documented in humans and mice.

Attempts to identify molecular rDNA variant types had lagged. The team reports that mouse ribosomal RNA genes contain multiple differentially regulated variants. The full text gives the variant sequences and their activity patterns by cell type. Ribosomes build all proteins, so regulated rRNA variants add a hidden layer to how cells tune protein production.
plos-pone-0001943:
Liora Shamgar and co-authors probed a partner protein that reins in a key channel, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The channel, Kv7.1, helps set heart rhythm and nerve firing, and faults in the Kv7 family cause heart and nerve disorders. Kv7.1 rarely works alone; a small partner, KCNE1, joins it and changes how it acts.

The team studied how KCNE1 holds back the channel's voltage sensor, the part that feels charge and works the gate. As the title states, KCNE1 constrains that sensor. Knowing the brake's grip helps explain rhythm disorders tied to this channel, and it may guide drugs that ease or tighten the hold.
plos-pone-0002043:
Wendy Stevens and co-authors checked the baseline health of African volunteers for future HIV vaccine trials, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Safe trials enroll healthy people, and lab safety values are used to screen them. Knowing the normal health profile of local volunteers is key to running such trials well, yet data from Africa were thin.

The team recorded morbidity at baseline in two thousand nine hundred ninety adult volunteers recruited to set lab reference intervals. Local reference values stop healthy Africans from being barred by norms drawn from other continents. The study lays groundwork for vaccine trials across several sites.
plos-pone-0002143:
Petteri Ilmonen, Alexander Kotrschal, and Dustin Penn asked whether fighting infection can wear down the ends of chromosomes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Those ends, called telomeres, act as protective caps. They grow shorter as a person ages, and many scientists think that this shortening plays a part in aging itself.

A leading idea holds that inflammation is a main cause of telomere loss, since immune defense is costly for the body. Infection is one strong source of that inflammation. The authors test the idea that infections speed up telomere shortening. If true, a lifetime of fighting germs would leave a mark written into the chromosomes themselves.
plos-pone-0002243:
Anne Schulp, Mohammed Al-Wosabi, and Nancy Stevens reported the first dinosaur tracks found on the Arabian Peninsula, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The Mesozoic land animals of Arabia were almost unknown when they wrote. Despite wide rocky outcrops, only a handful of fossils had been described from the region.

Near Madar in Yemen, the team documented a track assemblage left by more than one kind of dinosaur. Footprints record living animals in motion, including herd behavior that bones alone cannot show. The find opens a blank page in the region's fossil record and suggests far more waits in Arabian rock.
plos-pone-0002343:
Inken Beck and co-authors removed an enzyme in mice to learn what it does for the immune system. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. MMP19 is a matrix metalloproteinase, an enzyme that cuts the scaffolding between cells. It affects cell proliferation, adhesion, and migration in the dish, but its real role in the body was poorly understood.

The team generated mice lacking MMP19 by disrupting its catalytic domain. They report that MMP19 is essential for normal T cell development and for T cell-driven immune responses in the skin. A scaffolding enzyme turning out to be required for immunity widens its interest for inflammation research.
plos-pone-0002443:
Mattson led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Christine L. Mattson, Richard T. Campbell, Robert C. Bailey, among others. Its subject is risk Compensation Is Not Associated with Male Circumcision in Kisumu, Kenya. The title goes on to note a Multi-Faceted Assessment of Men Enrolled in a Randomized Controlled Trial. Three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have confirmed that male circumcision (MC) significantly reduces acquisition of HIV-1 infection among men.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002543:
Rueda and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Patricia Rueda, Karl Balabanian, Bernard Lagane, among others. Its subject is the CXCL12γ Chemokine Displays Unprecedented Structural and Functional Properties that Make It a Paradigm of Chemoattractant Proteins. The CXCL12γ chemokine arises by alternative splicing from Cxcl12, an key gene during development.

This protein binds CXCR4 and displays an exceptional degree of conservation (99%) in mammals. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002643:
Taichi E. Takasuka and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was sequence information encoded in DNA that may influence Long-Range chromatin structure correlates with human chromosome functions. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Taichi E. Takasuka, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Little is known about the possible function of the bulk of the human genome. It goes on to note a further point. We have recently shown that long-range regular oscillation in the motif non-T, A/T, G (VWG) existing at ten-nucleotide multiples influences large-scale nucleosome array formation. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002743:
Eun Jig Lee and co-authors studied a cancer-related protein called AFX in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. AFX, also known as FOXO4, belongs to the forkhead family of transcription factors, proteins that switch genes on and off. In its alpha form it acts as a tumor suppressor. It pushes damaged cells toward apoptosis, or programmed cell death.

The paper asks what happens when altered splice variants of AFX appear. As the title reports, these variants act as dominant negatives. They block the alpha form's work, so tumor cells stay alive that would otherwise die. The authors set this against a known pattern: losing apoptosis genes helps tumors grow. They compare the alpha form, at 505 amino acids, with the shorter zeta form, at 450.
plos-pone-0002843:
Sascha Sauer and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008 on classification and identification of bacteria by mass spectrometry and computational analysis. Authorship is credited in the record to Sascha Sauer and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. In general, the definite determination of bacterial species is a tedious process and requires extensive manual labour. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002943:
Jonathan Esteve-Lanao, Alejandro Lucia, Jos deKoning and co-authors measured strain in endurance runners in 2008. Distance running offers a clean model of human movement under load. The team asked how people control bodily strain during hard, long exercise across races from 5 to 100 kilometers.

They analyzed heart rate records from 211 competitive runners. Strain was judged as a share of each runner's maximum heart rate. Published in PLOS ONE, the records show how pacing holds strain within bounds even as race length grows hugely. Coaches and physiologists get rare data from real races, not lab treadmills.
plos-pone-0003043:
Jaqueline Ferreira, Betânia Drumond, Maria Guedes and co-authors compared vaccinia virus strains from Brazil in mouse tests in 2008. Brazilian vaccinia had been isolated from sentinel mice, rodents, and lately from people and cattle during dairy farm outbreaks. Those outbreaks carried high economic and social impact.

Phylogenetic studies had hinted at distinct groups. Virulence tests in a murine model show two distinct populations of strains, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, the split matters for tracing outbreaks and judging risk from a virus related to the old smallpox vaccine. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003143:
Laurent Mereghetti, Izabela Sitkiewicz, Nicole M. Green and colleagues track how group B streptococcus reacts to human blood in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Streptococcus agalactiae can cause invasive infection, and the team wanted to know how it adapts once inside the body. They ran a whole-genome transcriptome analysis after the bacteria were incubated with whole human blood.

Global changes in gene activity appeared fast in response to blood, as the title's claim of extensive adaptive changes suggests. Readers see which bacterial systems switch on during a key step of infection. That picture may help find weak points for new treatments.
plos-pone-0003243:
Andrija Tomovic and Edward J. Oakeley present a structural analysis done by computer in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Crystal structures of protein-DNA and protein-protein-DNA complexes are now publicly available in growing numbers. From them, it is now possible to extract structural, physical-chemical and thermodynamic parameters. Those values are enough to support general observations and predictions about their interactions.

The authors study multiple proteins bound to DNA as a class. Readers get rules drawn from many structures at once, rather than one complex at a time. General rules help predict how transcription factors cooperate on DNA, a core step in gene control.
plos-pone-0003343:
Yasuhiro Kitazoe, Hirohisa Kishino, Masami Hasegawa and colleagues study amino acid change in primate mitochondria in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The mitochondrial gene tree of placental mammals reveals a very strong acceleration of amino acid replacement rate. It also shows a change in amino acid compositional bias in the lineage leading to higher primates. This stands in contrast to the nuclear gene tree. Whether this acceleration reflects adaptation was the question.

The title reports an adaptive threonine increase in transmembrane regions of mitochondrial proteins in higher primates. Readers see a specific chemical shift tied to membrane proteins. Mitochondrial adaptation may relate to the high energy demands of large primate brains.
plos-pone-0003443:
Claire Cenciarini and co-authors tested how long bacterial RNA lasts in bottled water in 2008. Labs judge whether germs are alive partly by their RNA. Two germs were studied: Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Escherichia coli. Both were heat-killed, then stored for a long time in mineral water.

The team tracked how fast each germ's RNA broke down in storage. Earlier work on other species had given mixed answers. RNA survival affects how water safety tests should be read. If dead cells keep their RNA, tests may overstate the living risk. Water plants must decide how much weight such test results deserve.
plos-pone-0003543:
Renée E. Haskew-Layton and co-authors studied swollen brain cells in rats for this 2008 paper. Many injuries and illnesses make brain cells swell. Swelling opens channels that release small molecules from the cell. That release lets cells shrink back toward normal volume.

Under low-salt swelling, cells released excitatory amino acids and taurine. The releases ran through two distinct modes, not one. Separating those modes clarifies how the brain vents pressure. The work bears on swelling after stroke and head injury. Brain swelling is a top cause of death after severe head injury.
plos-pone-0003643:
Pauline Dupaigne, Christophe Lavelle, Anthony Justome, and colleagues published this DNA study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Rad51 is a protein central to homologous recombination, the repair process that swaps matching DNA strands. It was known to coat single-stranded DNA and form a filament there.

The authors studied how Rad51 chains form on DNA and what that does to chromatin, the packed form DNA takes in cells. Rad51 polymerization on double-stranded DNA turned out to reshape that packing. The team presents this as a new way cells remodel chromatin during repair.
plos-pone-0003743:
Charlotte H. Lenselink, Willem J. G. Melchers, Wim G. V. Quint, and colleagues published this health survey in PLOS ONE in 2008. Human papillomavirus infection is a required step on the road to cervical cancer. Little was known about the course of infection in unscreened young adults. Vaccines against HPV were then being developed.

The team studied Dutch women aged 18 to 29 in the pre-vaccine era. They linked sexual behavior patterns to HPV infection in that group. The baseline shows what the virus was doing on its own, before shots changed the picture for later generations.
plos-pone-0003843:
Constantin T. Yiannoutsos, Ming-Wen An, Constantine E. Frangakis, and colleagues published this statistics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. HIV care programs lose many patients to follow-up, and those losses distort reported death rates. Tracing every lost patient is not feasible in large programs. The team worked in a PEPFAR-funded program in western Kenya.

They developed sampling-based methods to estimate mortality among patients who dropped out. Sampling a fraction of the lost patients corrects the rosy bias of counting only those who stay in care. The approach gives big treatment programs honest numbers about survival.
plos-pone-0003943:
Maroun J. Beyrouthy, Karen E. Alexander, Amy Baldwin, and co-authors listed genes active in the first cell-cycle phase in 2008. Cell-cycle studies need cells moving through phases in step. Common tricks to sync cells, like starving them, distort later events. Early events in the G1 phase are especially easy to disturb.

Their PLOS ONE article used normally cycling human cells instead. From those cells they identified genes governed by the G1 phase. An undistorted list gives a truer picture of cell growth control. Other labs can use it to study how cells commit to dividing.
plos-pone-0004043:
Sabine Ohlendorf, Andreas Sprenger, Oliver Speck, and co-authors scanned motion-sensitive brain areas in 2008. Motion in one side of vision activates the opposite brain side. It suppresses activity in the matching areas on the same side. Real life, though, fills both sides of vision whenever we move.

Their PLOS ONE article used optic flow stimuli near the center of vision. Group fMRI showed how motion regions handle that central flow. The pattern differs from simple one-sided motion results. It better matches the visual world people navigate daily. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004143:
Laura Gioiosa and colleagues published this animal behaviour study in PLOS ONE in 2009. In mice, how an animal responds to pain shifts with its social rank. Recent work also showed that the social setting itself can change pain sensitivity.

The team paired up male CD-1 mice and studied how rank and setting interact to shape pain responses. Their work tests the idea summed up in the title: a trouble shared is a trouble halved. The results matter for animal welfare and for lab studies, where the cage mate beside a mouse can quietly change the data.
plos-pone-0004243:
Peyman Björklund and colleagues published this breast cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Breast cancer arises when genes are deregulated by changes in the genome or its packaging. The WNT and beta-catenin signalling pathway is often over-active in breast tumours, yet mutations in the pathway's own parts are rare there.

The team studied an internally truncated form of the receptor LRP5, a shortened version missing a middle section. They present it as a therapeutic target in breast cancer. A shortened receptor that tumours depend on offers a mark that healthy tissue may lack.
plos-pone-0004343:
Arnaud Beduneau and colleagues published this nanomedicine study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mononuclear phagocytes, the immune cells that eat particles, serve as target cells and vehicles for many microbial infections. These eating cells patrol the blood and tissues. The authors posit that these same cells can help doctors find disease and deliver drugs, ferrying cargo where it is needed.

They theorised that particle shape, size, and coating govern uptake. Their study of superparamagnetic iron-oxide nanoparticles examines facilitated uptake by monocyte-macrophages and the particles' tissue distribution. Such particles can both carry drugs and light up in magnetic scans.
plos-pone-0004443:
Eight unlike proteins work as one machine in the exocyst, and Nicole Croteau, Melonnie Furgason, Damien Devos, and co-authors compared their shapes in PLOS ONE in 2009. The exocyst guides tiny cargo sacs to the cell surface and fuses them there. That delivery step is basic to how cells grow and release material.

Oddly, the eight parts share less than a tenth of their building blocks in common. Yet solved structures hinted that they might still fold in alike ways. The authors report that a bundle of spiral-shaped parts, called a helical bundle, is conserved across the subunits. A shared fold beneath unlike surfaces can reveal common ancestry, and it helps explain how the parts lock together into one working machine.
plos-pone-0004543:
A protein called C/EBPbeta pushes cartilage cells from dividing into their swollen final form, show Makoto Hirata, Fumitaka Kugimiya, Atsushi Fukai, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The switch from proliferation to hypertrophic differentiation in chondrocytes is a crucial step in endochondral ossification, the process that builds bone on a cartilage scaffold. It matters in normal skeletal growth and in diseases like osteoarthritis.

How that switch is thrown was still an enigma. The team shows C/EBPbeta acts through p57Kip2, a brake on cell division, by switching its gene on. Turning on the brake and the growth program together moves cartilage cells into their bone-building stage. The mechanism gives osteoarthritis research a concrete control point to study.
plos-pone-0004643:
Regulatory T cells rush in fast enough to stop a dangerous immune storm in mice, show Tea Gogishvili, Daniela Langenhorst, Fred Luhder, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Superagonistic CD28 antibodies are highly effective activators of regulatory T cells in rats. But a first-in-man trial of the human version, TGN1412, caused an unexpected cytokine release syndrome that nearly killed the volunteers.

Using a new mouse antibody of the same class, the team studied what protects mice from the same storm. A rapid regulatory T cell response prevents the cytokine storm, as the title reports. Understanding that safety mechanism could let doctors use these powerful immune activators without repeating the TGN1412 disaster.
plos-pone-0004743:
Jean-Philippe Couture and colleagues named a kinase as a key driver of fat cell formation, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The kinase DLK belongs to a family tied to cell change in many tissues. Its role in making fat cells, though, had not been tested before this work.

The team used a standard lab fat cell line that can be pushed to mature. They tracked DLK levels and blocked its action to see the effect. DLK proved central to the shift from precursor to fat cell. That makes it a lead for obesity research and drug screens. Follow up work can check whether the same pattern appears in other settings.
plos-pone-0004843:
Alexis Bretteville and colleagues used two dimensional electrophoresis of tau mutants revealing phosphorylation patterns linked to early conformational changes, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Role of tau phosphorylation in neurofibrillary degeneration linked to Alzheimer disease remains to be established. Transgenic mice based on FTDP-17 tau mutations recapitulate hallmarks of degeneration, while cell models could help exploratory studies of early molecular events preceding tangle formation.

Specific patterns mark early shape changes in tau. Early markers precede overt tangles. That window may be best for intervention. Cell models enable rapid screening. Future studies can use these results to refine both methods and theory.
plos-pone-0004943:
Mouse researchers often need a gene on a clean genetic background. They breed it into a chosen strain for many generations. This congenic breeding can take three to four years. Narumi Ogonuki and co-authors described a faster version in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their high-speed strategy uses first-wave male germ cells.

The trick uses sperm-forming cells from the first wave of production. Young males produce that wave early in life. Breeding from it shortens the scheme sharply. The recipient background stays clean. Faster congenic strains mean faster answers for gene-mapping studies. Many trait and disease projects depend on such strains.
plos-pone-0005043:
Smoking injures the whole airway, not just the lungs. Gene-level changes from smoking were already known. Protein-level changes were less clear. Katrina Steiling and colleagues compared both layers in PLOS ONE in 2009. They profiled the bronchial airway lining of current smokers. Never smokers served as the comparison.

The proteomic and transcriptomic profiles tell partly different stories. Some changes appear in proteins but not in gene messages. Others appear in messages only. Where the layers agree, the signal is strongest. The side-by-side view sharpens the picture of smoking's harm. It also warns against reading gene data alone. Proteins are what cells actually run on.
plos-pone-0005143:
The heartbeat's timing depends on potassium channels. One channel pairs the protein KCNQ1 with a tuner, KCNE1. Mutations in either cause long QT syndrome, a dangerous rhythm disorder. Jerri Chen and colleagues mapped their interaction in PLOS ONE in 2009. They focused on KCNE1's C-terminus, its tail end. The pair forms the slowly activating current that resets the heart.

The tail end grips and controls the channel through specific contacts. The contact map explains how the tuner shapes electrical recovery. Each heartbeat needs that recovery to finish on time. The finding clarifies a molecular partnership behind a healthy rhythm. It may help interpret patient mutations. Knowing which contacts break tells doctors which variants are dangerous.
plos-pone-0005243:
A receptor called GluRδ2 sits only in the cerebellum, in the spines of Purkinje cells where they meet parallel fibers. Mice called hotfoot lack working GluRδ2 and move poorly. Mandolesi and colleagues restored the receptor in adult mice in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Even in the mature cerebellum, adding GluRδ2 back promoted new parallel fiber connections. It also revived competition between axons for contact space. The adult brain region, it turns out, can still rewire when the right part is returned, which matters for repair research. A brain area that can still grow new links in adult life gives hope for repair after stroke or injury in that part of the brain.
plos-pone-0005343:
Babies whose growth was restricted before birth often gain weight fast after birth, a pattern called catch-up growth. That sequence has been suspected of promoting belly fat and insulin resistance later. Beltrand and colleagues checked the outcomes at one year of age in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Catch-up growth did promote rapid restoration of fat mass, as the title states. Yet at one year there were no metabolic consequences to match the suspicion. The finding softens one worry about small babies' fast growth, though longer follow-up remains important.
plos-pone-0005443:
Daniel Datiko and Bernt Lindtjørn tested a community approach to tuberculosis in southern Ethiopia in a 2009 PLOS ONE trial. Finding and treating people with active tuberculosis is a main way to control the disease. Yet in many countries, too many cases are never found.

Health extension workers in villages were asked to help find cases and support treatment. The trial compared areas with their help against areas without it. Case finding and treatment success both improved where the workers were active. The result supports using local health workers to close gaps in tuberculosis care.
plos-pone-0005543:
Rowena Beecham, Robert Reeve, and Sarah Wilson studied how people picture ideas in space, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Many abstract ideas seem to be laid out in the mind like objects in space. Numbers, time, and social rank are often placed along lines or maps.

The authors asked whether the same spatial habits serve every topic, or whether each topic has its own pattern. They also asked whether a person uses the same pattern across topics. Answers matter for teaching, since a lesson that matches a student's inner map may be easier to learn.
plos-pone-0005643:
Stefano Di Santo and co-authors tested a cell-free approach to growing blood vessels in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Progenitor cells are used to repair tissue starved of blood, partly by releasing helpful factors. Transplanting the cells themselves carries risks and practical problems.

The team collected the fluid the cells had grown in, holding the factors they released. That fluid alone improved vessel growth in tests, without any cells being transplanted. A bottled factor mix would be easier to store, dose, and approve than living cells. A fluid treatment also travels and stores like a normal drug, unlike living cells that must be kept alive.
plos-pone-0005743:
Chaogan Yan and co-authors tested in 2009 how steady the resting brain's default network stays when the mind is given light tasks. Even at rest, a set of brain regions works in sync, called the default mode network. Its hubs include areas at the back and front of the brain.

Earlier work disagreed on whether small changes in rest conditions alter the network. The team compared several low-demand states with brain scans. They asked which parts of the network hold firm and which shift. The answer matters because many studies use resting scans as a baseline for disease.
plos-pone-0005843:
Efstathios Karathanasis and co-authors tested in 2009 whether a tiny imaging probe's leakage from tumor vessels matches the tumor's growth signals. Tumors build leaky vessels as they grow, under signals like VEGF. Its receptor, VEGFR2, is a major driver of that leakiness and growth in breast tumors.

The team measured how much nanoprobe escaped tumor vessels and compared it with angiogenic marker levels. Permeability tracked the markers, they report. A scan that gauges leakiness could thus report a tumor's aggressiveness without a biopsy. The work is an early step toward imaging-based tumor grading.
plos-pone-0005943:
A tiling microarray reads a whole genome in fine detail, tile by tile. Gard Thomassen, Alexander Rowe, Karin Lagesen and colleagues tackled the two hard parts of using such arrays on bacteria in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper covers how to design a custom array and how to make sense of the flood of data it returns.

Genome size and makeup change the design choices, so a fixed recipe will not fit every germ. The team's methods aim to give labs a sound way to plan arrays and read results. Better arrays mean sharper maps of which genes are active, a basic need in the study of bacteria and their behavior.
plos-pone-0006043:
Recreational cocaine users often insist the drug leaves their thinking untouched. Lorenza Colzato, Wery van den Wildenberg and Bernhard Hommel tested early attention in such users in 2009. Cocaine is Europe's second most used street drug after cannabis, yet the thinking costs of light, monthly use were barely known when their PLOS ONE study ran.

The users showed a reduced attentional scope, meaning their early selection of what to heed covered a narrower field. A cost found in casual users carries more weight than one found only in heavy users. The work warns that monthly use is not free of effect, and it gives attention research a clear measure of the narrowing.
plos-pone-0006143:
The first fork in a mammal embryo's road splits the outer shell from the inner mass. Srinivas Viswanathan, Craig Mermel, Jun Lu and colleagues asked in 2009 which microRNAs mark that fork. Their PLOS ONE paper profiles microRNA expression during trophectoderm specification, the step that makes the outer layer that will form the placenta, while the inner mass forms the body.

The transcription factors for this first fate choice were known; the microRNA layer was not. Small regulators at the first fork could set much of what follows. Mapping them serves both fertility medicine, where embryos fail at just this stage, and stem cell work, which steers the same fork in a dish.
plos-pone-0006243:
Brain-machine interfaces turn brain signals into commands for prosthetic limbs and cursors. Zheng Li and colleagues improved the decoding step with an unscented Kalman filter, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Earlier real-time methods read commands from groups of neurons but handled signal quirks poorly.

A Kalman filter tracks a changing system while discounting noise; the unscented version handles curves in the data better. Better decoding means smoother, more accurate control for users. The work is one step toward prostheses that feel natural to operate. It also suits other neural recording tasks.
plos-pone-0006343:
Mouse stem cells need a factor called LIF to stay young and able to form any tissue. Yumi Kawahara and her team grew such cells in fake low gravity for a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Growth in dishes also tends to need feed from animal cells, which must be cut out for use in care of people.

In fake low gravity the cells stayed young with no LIF at all. That swap of a drug for a state of the body is a neat trick. Clean growth with no animal feed is a step toward safe stem cell care. The work also hints that cells sense pull and weight as they choose what to be.
plos-pone-0006443:
Laurent Mamelli and colleagues worked on new antibiotics for drug-resistant germs in PLOS ONE in 2009. Bacteria that resist many drugs have become a major worry in hospitals worldwide. One promising target sits inside the cell: peptide deformylase, an enzyme bacteria need. The problem is getting drugs past the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria to reach it.

The title reports their fix: bypassing that membrane barrier raises the activity of deformylase-blocking drugs. In other words, entry is half the battle. The study points to designs that pair a blocker with a way in. Such designs could revive a whole class of candidate antibiotics.
plos-pone-0006543:
Edward Eivers, Luis Fuentealba, Veronika Sander, and colleagues studied signal integration in fruit fly development for PLOS ONE in 2009. A key question in developmental biology is how growth factor signals are integrated to generate pattern. The team investigated integration of BMP signaling with Wingless signaling in the fly. They focused on wing development and segment patterning.

Their title reports that a protein called Mad is required for Wingless signaling in these processes. Signals thought to run in parallel turn out to share parts. Such cross-talk explains how embryos make precise patterns from a few signals. The fly wing is a classic place to learn these rules.
plos-pone-0006643:
Thomas Krahe, Weili Wang, and Alexandre Medina tested a drug approach in a fetal alcohol model in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders are the leading cause of mental retardation in the western world. Children with FASD present altered somatosensory, auditory, and visual processing. The team studied orientation selectivity, a visual cortex property, in their model.

Their title reports phosphodiesterase inhibition increases CREB phosphorylation and restores orientation selectivity. CREB is a gene-switch protein tied to plasticity. Restoring a visual function in the model suggests plasticity can be rescued after alcohol exposure. That hope motivates further treatment research.
plos-pone-0006743:
Anna N. Panek and colleagues raised a growth factor in heart muscle cells of mice and rats in PLOS ONE in 2009. The factor is connective tissue growth factor, or CTGF. It rises strongly in human and experimental heart failure. CTGF is usually described as promoting fibrosis, or scarring. Its precise job in the heart stayed unclear.

The team made transgenic animals with extra CTGF only in cardiomyocytes. The heart muscle grew thicker, a change called hypertrophy. Surprisingly, the hearts were also protected under pressure overload. Protection clashes with the simple view of CTGF as harmful. The results suggest CTGF can help the heart adapt to strain, at least for a time.
plos-pone-0006843:
Ke Ma and colleagues disrupted the body clock and watched bile chemistry go off balance in PLOS ONE in 2009. Bile acids can be toxic in excess. Their production, uptake, and export in the liver are tightly regulated. Circadian rhythm is one of the regulating inputs. The team tested what happens when the peripheral clock breaks.

Disrupting circadian control disturbed bile acid homeostasis. Several steps of bile handling shifted together. The result ties clock genes to liver chemistry directly. It may help explain metabolic problems in shift workers. It also suggests timing matters in treating bile-related disease.
plos-pone-0006943:
Arnaud Florins, Michal Reichert, Becca Asquith, and colleagues studied retrovirus leukemia timing in PLOS ONE in 2009. Delta-retroviruses include HTLV-1 in humans and bovine leukemia virus in cattle. Infection is mostly without symptoms. Fewer than five in a hundred infected hosts develop disease, after a long latent period.

The team asked whether removing the spleen changes that timeline. After splenectomy, leukemia from these viruses began earlier. That result points to the spleen as a brake on disease development. It may help explain why only some infected hosts progress to leukemia or nerve disease.
plos-pone-0007043:
Mathias De Roo, Paul Klauser, Adrian Briner, and colleagues studied anesthetics and the developing brain in PLOS ONE in 2009. Early brain wiring depends on activity driven by experience. It also rests on a balance between excitatory and inhibitory signals. General anesthetics are powerful drugs that disturb that balance.

The team found anesthetics rapidly promote the growth of new synapses. The effect appeared during a critical window of brain development. Rapid extra wiring could reshape circuits in unwanted ways. The finding feeds concern about anesthesia in very young children, and it gives researchers a model to test that concern.
plos-pone-0007143:
Fabrice Not, Javier del Campo, Vanessa Balagué, and colleagues surveyed tiny marine life in PLOS ONE in 2009. Picoeukaryotes are the smallest complex cells in the sea. Culture-free surveys using 18S gene libraries had spent a decade revealing them. Many sequences belonged to entirely new high-rank groups. That flood reshaped views of marine food webs.

The team synthesized what the new diversity means. Organisms once invisible now appear central to ocean ecology. Their synthesis sets out how much of marine life was missing from older counts. It argues the base of the ocean food web is richer than textbooks said.
plos-pone-0007243:
Jaime Clausell, Nicole Happel, Tracy K. Hale, and colleagues studied linker histone variants in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Histone H1 subtypes sit throughout chromatin, the packaged DNA inside cell nuclei. Their exact functions were partly unknown, and published studies had reported contradictory properties for different subtypes.

The authors test whether H1 subtypes change chromatin condensation in different ways. They also check whether subtypes block ATP-dependent remodeling by complexes called SWI/SNF and NURF. They report differential effects on condensation without preventing remodeling. Their work helps explain how cells fine-tune DNA packaging.
plos-pone-0007343:
Mark J. Kohler, Kurt Lushington, Cameron J. van den Heuvel, and colleagues studied surgery for childhood sleep breathing problems in 2009. Sleep disordered breathing is common in childhood. It covers a range of upper airway obstruction during sleep, and children with the condition show significant neurocognitive deficits in attention and learning.

Adenotonsillectomy, removing tonsils and adenoids, is the first-line treatment. The authors assess neurocognitive outcomes after that surgery. Their PLOS ONE paper asks how much thinking ability recovers. The answer matters for parents deciding between surgery and watchful waiting for affected children.
plos-pone-0007443:
Serdar Korur and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer. Many tumors are maintained by stem-like cells that copy themselves without limit. Those cells form a reservoir that can rebuild the tumor. The team studied a signaling protein called GSK3β and its effect on these cancer stem-like cells.

Raising GSK3β activity pushed the cells to mature and stop growing. Instead of endless self-renewal, they took on a more settled, differentiated state. That switch attacks the tumor at its source rather than its bulk. A treatment that drains the reservoir of self-renewing cells could make other therapies work better. The study identifies GSK3β as a lever for forcing that change.
plos-pone-0007543:
Steven Stanton and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on voters' bodies on the night of the 2008 United States vote for president. Elections are contests for rank and power. In such contests, the winners' testosterone tends to hold or rise, while the losers' falls. No one knew if that held for voters too, who only watch the fight. The team tracked backers of each man through election night.

Voters' testosterone moved with their man's fate. Men whose side lost showed the same drop seen in beaten rivals. So the body's rank chemistry answers even to losses felt at a distance. Seeing your side lose is, in hormone terms, a kind of defeat of one's own. The study takes a known animal pattern and finds it in mass politics. It hints at why election night feels so sharp in the body.
plos-pone-0007643:
Cheng Hu and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on type 2 diabetes genes in a Chinese population. Genome studies, mostly in Europeans, had confirmed a growing list of risk loci for the disease. Whether those loci matter in other populations must be tested, not assumed. The team analyzed variants from seven known loci, including PPARG and KCNJ11. They looked at each variant's effect alone and at the joint effect on diabetes and glucose traits.

The seven loci were associated with type 2 diabetes in the Chinese sample as well. That confirmation extends the markers' reach to East Asia. It also shows the biology of diabetes risk is shared across ancestries more than it differs. Shared risk genes point to shared mechanisms, which drug research can target. The study is part of genetics' necessary second step: checking discoveries in every population they will serve.
plos-pone-0007743:
Marianne Nymark and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines how a marine diatom adjusts to bright light. Diatoms are tiny photosynthetic algae that drift in the sea. Light at the surface can swing fast and unpredictably.

To survive, diatoms must retune their light-harvesting systems on short notice. The molecular steps behind that acclimation were largely unknown. The team combined several kinds of data into one integrated analysis. They tracked genes, proteins and cell responses together. The picture they built helps explain how ocean algae cope with a shifting light climate.
plos-pone-0007843:
Dennis Rodder and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It questions a model that placed an invasive turtle in an unexpected home. The red-eared slider is an alien invader in many waters. Species distribution models map a species' niche and project it onto geography.

Those maps help predict where invaders can spread. One model put sliders in habitat that seemed unsuitable. The authors ask whether the turtle truly shifted its niche. Or did the result reflect the predictors the model used? The distinction decides how much managers should trust such forecasts.
plos-pone-0007943:
Osamu Ogasawara and Kousaku Okubo weighed luck against selection in gene activity, in a PLOS ONE theory paper from 2009. Genes do not just turn on or off; their activity levels shift over ages of evolution. Experts argue over how much of that shift is chance drift and how much is true selection.

The authors built models that let both forces act and checked what each force leaves behind. Their math shows how to tell the two apart in real data, at least in part. The work gives the long debate a firmer base and helps readers judge claims about why gene activity changed.
plos-pone-0008043:
Katie Barott and colleagues watched corals and algae fight for reef space with fine light tools in PLOS ONE in 2009. On a crowded reef, every inch of rock is claimed. Corals and algae meet at borders where one side slowly gains or loses ground.

Light-based imaging that reads many colors at once, paired with health measures, showed what happens at those borders cell by cell. Some corals hold their edge; others yield as algae press in. The fine view helps reef managers tell which stresses tip the fight toward algae.
plos-pone-0008143:
Sandeep Ravindran and colleagues stopped a parasite mid-break-in with one chemical in PLOS ONE in 2009. Toxoplasma, a single-celled parasite, forces its way into host cells by firing protein sacs called rhoptries. The firing is a key step in its invasion sequence.

The chemical 4-bromophenacyl bromide blocked that firing and little else, leaving other steps untouched. A clean, single-step block is a fine tool: researchers can freeze invasion at that instant and study what follows. It also proves the firing step can be drugged, a hint for future treatments. The parasite infects people and animals worldwide.
plos-pone-0008243:
Miguel A. Fuentes, Austin Gerig, and Javier Vicente studied extreme stock price moves in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many models treat stock prices as a smooth random walk. That view, called geometric Brownian motion, is roughly correct. It fails, though, to explain frequent extreme movements such as crashes. The authors used a large collection of data from three markets.

They looked for universal behavior shared by those extreme movements. A pattern that holds across markets hints at a common market mechanism. Such findings challenge standard risk models used in finance. They matter for anyone who prices or guards against market crashes.
plos-pone-0008343:
Gavin Andrews, Alice Kemp, and Matthew Sunderland published reference data in PLOS ONE in 2009 for a disability scale. The WHO Disability Assessment Schedule measures disability from health conditions. It covers diseases, injuries, mental or emotional problems, and substance problems. The twelve-item version was used in a large Australian survey. Normative data tell users what scores are typical in the population.

With norms, a patient's score can be judged against a healthy baseline. That makes the short scale more useful in clinics and surveys. The paper provides those benchmark values. It supports consistent disability measurement worldwide.
plos-pone-0008443:
Zongjin Li and co-authors report stem cell work in PLOS ONE in 2009. They turn human embryonic stem cells into endothelial cells. Endothelial cells line blood vessels. A ready supply of them could help treat heart attack and like diseases. New vessels could bring blood back to damaged tissue. But making pure, useful cells of this type is hard.

The team describe how they make the cells and test them. They check what genes the cells turn on and how they act. They also test use after heart attack. The work moves cell therapy for heart damage one step closer.
plos-pone-0008543:
Keisuke Nagao and co-authors delete a surface protein in mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The protein is EpCAM, also known as CD326. It is expressed by many normal and malignant epithelial cells. Prior lab experiments suggested EpCAM acts as an adhesion molecule between cells. It has been studied extensively as a cancer marker. The team breed mice that lack EpCAM entirely. They watch development from the earliest stages.

EpCAM-null mice show abnormal placental development. They also die early as embryos, before birth. That lethality proves EpCAM is essential, not merely a marker. Its placental role explains why loss cannot be compensated in development.
plos-pone-0008643:
Kucku Varghese, Peter Molnar, Mainak Das, and co-authors published a brain research study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Small soluble clumps of amyloid beta protein are widely blamed for much of the harm in Alzheimer's disease. Most drug work had aimed at damage done right at the synapse, where nerve cells meet. The team looked for another place to intervene.

They tested a fresh target using patch clamp recording, which tracks tiny electric currents in single cells. A high-throughput version let them run the same checks at far larger scale. Both methods backed the target as a real site of amyloid beta harm. That gives drug hunters a validated target, plus a faster way to screen candidate treatments.
plos-pone-0008743:
Yann Cheli, Shirley Williams, Robert Ballotti, and colleagues studied a repeating stretch that tunes a human gene. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene, ITGA2, builds part of a cell-gripping protein on platelets and other cells. Before the gene sits a run of C and A letters of varying length. Longer or shorter runs might change how much protein gets made.

Two DNA-handling proteins bound more strongly when the repeat ran long. Those proteins were PARP-1 and the Ku70/80 pair. Stronger binding links repeat length to gene output. The dial may help explain person-to-person differences in the protein.
plos-pone-0008843:
Lili Jing, Laura Gordon, Elena Shtibin, and colleagues mapped when a wiring protein is needed as zebrafish muscles meet nerves. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. A neuromuscular junction links a nerve ending to a muscle cell. Its first step is clustering the receptors that catch nerve signals. The gene unplugged, also called MuSK, starts that clustering. It also shapes where junctions may form later.

Timed experiments showed distinct windows when MuSK function is essential. Early and late jobs differ in timing and place. A schedule of one protein's duties refines models of synapse building. The work informs diseases where junctions fail.
plos-pone-0008943:
Janarthanan Krishnamoorthy, Victor Yu, and Yu-Keung Mok presented a computer program called Auto-FACE in PLOS ONE in 2010. The program helps chemists map where a small molecule binds on a protein. It works with NMR spectroscopy, which watches atoms inside a protein as a drug-like molecule attaches. Mapping the binding site by hand is slow, expert work.

Auto-FACE reads a common kind of NMR experiment and marks the likely binding surface. It is built for systems where the molecule hops on and off the protein quickly. That fast exchange makes signals shift in ways the program can track. Faster mapping helps drug designers see how a candidate compound fits its target.
plos-pone-0009043:
Guillaume Sarrabayrouse and co-authors dressed up melanoma cells so the immune system could see them, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Melanoma cells often hide by showing few flag molecules to T cells. Without those flags, killer T cells pass the cancer by. Two treatments were combined to force the flags back up.

A drug called GGTI plus the signal interferon-gamma restored the cells' visibility. Mice vaccinated with the treated cells mounted stronger defences. Killer responses against human melanoma cells also grew sharper. The approach could turn a patient's own tumour cells into a teaching vaccine.
plos-pone-0009143:
Clara Touriño, Andreas Zimmer, and Olga Valverde paired two party drugs in mice to test brain protection, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most users of MDMA, or ecstasy, also use cannabis. The two drugs push the body in opposite directions on several measures. MDMA overheats the body and damages serotonin neurons, especially in warm rooms.

The team gave mice THC, cannabis's main active compound, alongside MDMA. THC prevented much of the MDMA neurotoxicity in their tests. The pairing is common in real life, rarely studied in the lab. The result adds a twist to debates about combined drug harms.
plos-pone-0009243:
