Cedric Bouzigues, David Holcman, and Maxime Dahan published this cell sensing study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Growing nerve fibers must steer toward chemical cues. Their tips, called growth cones, read faint differences in cue levels between one side and the other. To steer well, the tip must amplify that tiny difference.

The authors describe a mechanism in which receptors gather on one part of the tip's membrane. That clustering, called polarity formation, sharpens the contrast the cell senses. A small external gradient becomes a large internal difference. Their model explains how growth cones manage the accurate steering that wiring a nervous system requires.
plos-pone-0009343:
Giuseppe Geraci and co-authors published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Large studies had catalogued the mutated genes found in human cancers. Those catalogues said little about how varied the mutations are inside any one tumor. Variety matters, because mixed tumors resist treatment in mixed ways.

The team looked for genetic instability in tumors and in the normal tissue right beside them. Finding instability in nearby healthy-looking tissue would change the picture. It would mean the soil around a tumor is already unsettled before cancer shows. Their evidence speaks to how early the genome starts to wobble in the making of a cancer.
plos-pone-0009443:
Kirsty Flower and colleagues set out a computer based plan in PLOS ONE in 2010 for work on Epstein Barr virus. Most people carry this virus for life after a first infection. It hides in memory B cells, a type of immune cell. At times it can help drive cancers by resetting how genes are switched on or off.

Their plan predicts which host genes the virus is most likely to reset in this lasting way. Epstein Barr virus is known to leave such chemical marks on DNA. A short list of likely targets lets lab teams test the best leads first. That saves time in the search for how the virus helps start cancer.
plos-pone-0009543:
Darren Yuen and co-authors tested cell therapy in rats with kidney disease in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chronic kidney disease scars the kidneys with fibrous tissue. The heart is often scarred too, and both organs fail over time. Bone marrow cells had shown hints of fighting such scarring. The team grew marrow cells in a special culture, then gave them to sick rats.

Treated rats showed less injury in both heart and kidneys. The benefit came through an anti fibrosis action not described before. The result gives cell therapy a concrete lead against scarring. Scarring drives much of the harm in kidney disease, so a way to slow it matters.
plos-pone-0009643:
Edwin Leeansyah and co-authors checked immune cells in treated HIV patients in PLOS ONE in 2010. Natural killer cells are front line defenders against viruses. They rely on signaling proteins, among them one called FcR gamma, to pass activation orders. Earlier lab work showed HIV lowers this protein in macrophages. The team measured it in natural killer cells of people on combination antiretroviral therapy.

Even with the virus suppressed by therapy, the cells carried less FcR gamma. That shortfall could blunt the cells' killing function. The study documents a lasting immune alteration in the treatment era. Suppressed virus, it shows, is not the same as a fully restored immune system.
plos-pone-0009843:
Synapses can weaken with use, a change called long-term depression. Jean-Marie Billard revisited that change in aged rats, focusing on the CA1 area of the hippocampus. The single-author review appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The CA1 area is a much-studied layer of the hippocampus.

The hippocampus is a brain region central to memory. Billard argues the measured effect depends on temporal constraints tied to slice preparation, meaning how and when brain slices are made. Preparation timing can distort what counts as an aging effect. The paper urges care before blaming age for weaker synapses.
plos-pone-0009943:
Turning stem cells into heart cells is a goal of regenerative medicine. Anca Chiriac and colleagues streamlined that conversion using a conserved network of signals. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pluripotent stem cells can become almost any body cell type.

Cardiogenic induction means steering the cells toward heart muscle. The network integrates three signals: SDF-1, VEGF, and BMP2. Conserved means the same network works across species. Heart cells made in the lab serve drug testing and repair research. A streamlined route through one network could make heart cell production steadier.
plos-pone-0010043:
The authors were Sophia Vijay, Prahlad Kumar, Lakbir Chauhan, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study asked why tuberculosis patients in India stop treatment early. Stopping raises the risk of drug resistance, relapse, and death. It also leaves patients infectious to others for longer, weakening control programs.

Working with new patients under the national DOTS program, the team identified risk factors for default. DOTS uses watched, regular doses to keep treatment on track. Knowing who is most likely to quit lets programs add support where it will help most. Their findings rest on records from patients starting standard treatment.
plos-pone-0010143:
The authors were Natasha Mott, Wilson Chung, Pei-San Tsai, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used neuronal cell lines to study growth signals. Fibroblast growth factors guide much of brain development, from early patterning to cell survival. Yet how cells control those signals themselves was less well described in the literature.

The team focused on FGF8 and its two receptors, Fgfr1 and Fgfr3. They found FGF8 regulates its own receptors, and does so differently for each one. That self-tuning may keep brain development signals within safe bounds as tissue grows.
plos-pone-0010243:
The authors were Kathleen Brown, Ted Witte, W. Elaine Hardman, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study tested chili pepper compound against an aggressive lung cancer. Small cell lung cancer progresses fast and has low survival rates. New treatment agents are urgently needed for it, since standard therapy often fails within months of diagnosis.

Capsaicin, the compound that makes peppers hot, slowed this cancer's growth. It worked in cell culture and in nude mouse tumor models. The effect ran through a growth control route called the E2F pathway, which the team traced in their experiments.
plos-pone-0010343:
Jan Martel, Cheng-Yeu Wu and John Young took a hard look at claims about tiny bacteria-like particles in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some labs had grown so-called nanobacteria and calcifying particles from body tissues. Those cultures relied on cow serum that had been treated with strong gamma rays. The treated serum was thought to feed the particles while killing normal germs. Martel's team questioned that standard recipe.

They tested whether the irradiated serum itself could create misleading results. If the feeder serum produces mineral grains on its own, past claims may rest on an artifact. Careful checks of this kind rarely make headlines, but they guard a whole field. The study asks readers to separate real living things from lab-made look-alikes. Its caution applies well beyond one disputed particle.
plos-pone-0010443:
Peila Chen and co-workers probed one stress enzyme's role in breast tumors driven by a cancer gene, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cancer genes force cells to copy DNA fast, causing stress and damage. Stress switches on a family of enzymes called JNK. Whether each family member helps or hinders tumors was unclear. The team focused on Jnk2 in a mouse model of mammary cancer.

They tracked tumor growth, genetic instability, and copying stress with and without Jnk2. Sorting one member's role from its siblings' is painstaking but necessary. Drugs that block whole families can backfire if one member restrains tumors. This study helps aim future drugs more precisely. It also deepens the picture of how stressed cancer cells survive.
plos-pone-0010543:
David Greene, Duen-Wei Hsu and Catherine Pears studied control of cyclin C levels during development of a slime mold in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cyclin C partners with an enzyme, Cdk8, inside the mediator complex. That complex links gene regulators to the core transcription machinery. The pair fine-tunes a subset of genes and has been tied to development in many organisms. The team used Dictyostelium, a social amoeba, to watch cyclin C across development.

How cyclin C levels are set may decide when its gene subset can act. Dictyostelium develops in a simple, visible sequence, ideal for timing questions. Basic control of a universal complex in a simple organism informs all eukaryote biology. The study adds a developmental time course to a molecular story. It also hints at layers of control beyond gene switching.
plos-pone-0010643:
Cristiane Squarize and colleagues tested a growth switch to speed wound healing in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Slow wounds are a growing problem for older people and people with diabetes. Tumor cells use growth circuits that healthy tissue keeps tightly controlled.

Turning on the mTOR growth pathway in defined mouse models made wounds close faster. The treated skin rebuilt its layers more quickly than untreated skin. The same pathway can drive cancer when left on, so timing and dose would be critical. Still, a short, controlled boost may one day help wounds that refuse to heal.
plos-pone-0010743:
Rui Dilão and Daniele Muraro presented software for modeling gene control networks, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Genes switch each other on and off in webs that decide cell fate. Writing the math for such webs by hand is slow and error-prone, especially as webs grow.

Their tool builds the equations automatically from a network sketch. It rests on classic chemistry rules and the operon model of gene control. Test cases reproduced sharp thresholds and striped patterns in fly development. Automating the math lets biologists try more network designs and compare them fairly, instead of wrestling with algebra for each new idea.
plos-pone-0010843:
Rikard Fred, Claus Bang-Berthelsen, Thomas Mandrup-Poulsen and co-authors published this diabetes study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Long exposure to high blood sugar harms the pancreas islets that make insulin, but the steps behind that harm were not settled. The team focused on PTB, a protein that helps keep insulin's message stable inside islet cells.

Human islets were kept for a day in low or high glucose, and the researchers measured small regulatory RNAs thought to target PTB. High glucose raised one of them, miR-133a, while PTB levels and insulin production fell. Fat and inflammatory signals, which also strain islets, were tested for comparison. Fred and colleagues outline a chain from sugar overload to a small RNA switch. That chain offers a concrete target for protecting insulin output in type 2 diabetes.
plos-pone-0010943:
William Netzer, Craig Powell, Yi Nong and co-authors published this Down syndrome study in PLOS ONE in 2010. People with Down syndrome carry high levels of beta-amyloid, the protein that builds plaques in Alzheimer's disease, throughout their lives. That load is blamed for dementia in older adults with the condition, but whether it also harms learning in the young was unknown.

The authors gave young mice that model Down syndrome a drug that blocks an enzyme needed to make beta-amyloid. Lowering the protein corrected the learning problems typical of these mice. Netzer and colleagues argue the same protein may drag down thinking long before dementia begins. Their result raises the possibility that amyloid-lowering treatments, developed for Alzheimer's, could also help younger people with Down syndrome learn.
plos-pone-0011043:
Gabriel Rosenblum, Philippe Van den Steen, Sidney Cohen and co-authors published this enzyme imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Matrix metalloproteases are molecular scissors that remodel the tissue scaffold, and one of them, MMP-9, digests collagen fragments during inflammation. How it recognizes and grips triple-helical collagen was unclear, so the authors filmed single enzyme molecules at work.

Single-molecule imaging showed the enzyme first binding the collagen fragment through a particular region, then engaging it for cutting. Rosenblum and colleagues could watch recognition, binding, and digestion as separate steps rather than inferring them from bulk chemistry. Seeing the mechanism directly matters because these proteases drive arthritis, cancer spread, and wound problems, yet drugs blocking them broadly have failed; precise knowledge of the grip may enable smarter inhibitors.
plos-pone-0011143:
Matoba, Husk, Barnett and colleagues grew an HIV blocking protein in plants for PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, from a sea organism, grabs the sugary coat of HIV and can stop the virus. The team made it in plant leaves and tested how well the plant made version blocked HIV.

The plant grown protein kept its blocking power and lacked a harmful side effect seen in similar proteins. Growing medicine in plants could lower cost and raise supply. That matters for prevention tools meant for wide use in poor regions. The study is an early step toward plant made HIV prevention.
plos-pone-0011243:
Almanza, Fernandez, Volinia and colleagues studied immune memory in mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. After infection, some killer T cells settle into a central memory pool that guards the body for years. The team asked whether small RNAs help decide which cells take that long term path.

Selected small RNAs did help define that fate choice in mouse memory cells. Fate programming at the RNA level gives vaccine science a new handle. If memory fate can be steered, vaccines might last longer with fewer boosters. The finding links tiny regulators to one of the immune system's most valuable outcomes.
plos-pone-0011343:
Dana Dunne and colleagues compared immune responses in adults with weakened immunity in a 2010 study. More people now live with conditions or drugs that suppress the immune system, and they face higher risk from infection. Yet suppression does not simply turn every defense down, and the details of the first, fast line of defense were poorly mapped.

The team measured a germ sensor on immune cells and the alarm chemicals released after it is triggered. Adults with suppressed immunity showed more of the sensor and produced more of those alarms than adults without suppression. That surprise suggests their early defense may be over-primed even while other defenses are weak. Clinicians who know this pattern can read infection signs in these patients more wisely and avoid assuming their responses will match textbook cases.
plos-pone-0011443:
Christophe Galichet, Robin Lovell-Badge, and Karine Rizzoti issued a caution in 2010 about a widely used mouse line. Nestin-Cre mice let researchers switch genes on and off in nerve cells, and thousands of studies rest on them. The team found that the line carries an unexpected flaw: an underactive pituitary gland, the master hormone gland under the brain.

They showed the flaw is not caused by the gene switch acting inside the pituitary itself, which rules out the obvious explanation and makes the trait harder to dodge. A hormone flaw can quietly distort growth, stress, and behavior results blamed on the gene under study. The paper warns labs to check for this confound before trusting results from the line. It is a reminder that a research tool's hidden traits can shape findings across an entire field.
plos-pone-0011543:
Lucas Silva, Madhur Anand, and Mark Leithead documented in 2010 a paradox for climate science: tree growth is declining widely even as the air grows richer in carbon dioxide. Extra carbon dioxide should fertilize plants, and many climate plans quietly count on forests growing faster and soaking up part of humanity's emissions. The team assembled growth records to test whether that hopeful assumption holds in real forests.

Trees across their records showed recent, widespread growth decline despite the rising carbon supply. Heat, drought, or other stresses appear to outweigh the fertilizer effect in the places measured. The warning is direct: carbon budgets that bank on a greening world may be overdrawn. Forests remain vital to protect, but as stressed systems needing help, not as a bottomless sink that forgives continued emissions.
plos-pone-0011643:
Nicholas Fischer and co-authors built uniform nanoscale discs for laboratory use, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Nanolipoprotein particles are tiny discs of fat membrane held together by proteins. Labs use them to hold membrane proteins still for study and for other small-scale technology tasks, but batches often vary in size.

The team assembled the discs with a protein called apolipophorin-III and measured the results. They obtained particles of discrete, even sizes and tested how stable the discs stayed over time. Dependable, uniform particles give researchers a more reliable platform for studying membrane proteins and building nanoscale devices.
plos-pone-0011743:
Ksenija Jovanovic, Angel Pastor and Michael O'Donovan traced spinal circuits in newborn mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The newborn mouse is a standard model for studying how the lower spinal cord produces walking motions. Yet the wiring of the network that runs those motions was still poorly mapped.

The team used a tracer virus, PRV-Bartha, which jumps back across nerve links, to map inputs that reach the motor neurons of the lower cord. The traced circuits reveal the control web behind early leg motions. A clearer wiring map guides work on restoring movement after spinal injury.
plos-pone-0011843:
Katerina Gkirtzou and co-authors introduced in 2010 a computer program called MatureBayes. MicroRNAs are short RNA pieces that fine-tune the activity of thousands of genes. Each one starts as a longer folded precursor, and only a small part of that precursor becomes the working microRNA, so finding the exact mature piece is a common bottleneck.

MatureBayes uses probabilities learned from known examples to judge where the mature sequence sits inside a new precursor. Better placement helps researchers confirm real microRNAs among many look-alike candidates in genome data. Since these small RNAs shape development and disease, a more accurate finder speeds up every study that depends on knowing exactly which piece does the work.
plos-pone-0011943:
Hendrikus Hendriksen and co-workers tested in 2010 whether a richer living space could help animals recover from a trauma-like condition. Post-traumatic stress can be seen as a failure to recover after a frightening event. The team used rats that model PTSD and, importantly, do not respond well to antidepressant drugs.

Given enriched surroundings, with or without a running wheel, the rats showed behavioral recovery and increased growth of new cells in the hippocampus, a brain area tied to memory and stress. Recovery in a drug-resistant model gives the environment itself standing as a treatment factor. The work supports therapies built around activity and surroundings, not pills alone.
plos-pone-0012043:
Joseph Olberding and co-workers treated in 2010 the cell's grip points as a problem in physics. A focal adhesion is built from molecular complexes, each a ligand outside, an integrin spanning the membrane, and plaque proteins inside. Binding and unbinding of those complexes set how the adhesion grows, slides, or dissolves.

Applying non-equilibrium thermodynamics and kinetics, the team modeled the energy changes driving that turnover. Cells must constantly renegotiate their grip to move, divide, or hold tissue together. A physics account of the grip explains behaviors that pure biochemistry lists but cannot predict, such as why adhesions strengthen under pull.
plos-pone-0012143:
Macarena Morillo-Huesca, Marta Clemente-Ruiz, Eloísa Andújar, and colleagues studied a yeast protein complex in PLOS ONE in 2010. The complex swaps a standard histone, a spool protein that DNA wraps around, for a variant form at chosen spots on chromosomes. That swap helps control which genes are read, how chromosomes split, and how DNA is repaired.

When the variant is missing, the swapping complex turns harmful, the team found. It stirs genome-wide mistakes in gene reading and leaves the DNA unstable. The lesson is that a machine built to fine-tune genes needs its usual partner present, or its activity does damage instead. Such details matter for understanding chromosome faults in disease.
plos-pone-0012243:
Felix Rückert, Gihan Dawelbait, Christof Winter, and co-authors modeled cell-death signaling in pancreatic cancer by computer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. This cancer remains one of the deadliest, largely because its cells refuse the death orders that chemotherapy delivers, growing and spreading aggressively instead. The team set out to characterize the whole death-signaling pathway in these tumors rather than one protein at a time.

A computational model of the pathway can show which broken link most protects the cancer, and which drug combinations might restore the death signal. Testing combinations in a model first saves years of trial and error in the lab. For a cancer with so few working treatments, smarter targeting of effort is itself valuable.
plos-pone-0012343:
Xiao Xiao Tang, Hao Chen, Sidney Yu and co-workers reported a cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010 on the seals that line the gut and other body surfaces. Those seals, called tight junctions, sit between neighboring lining cells and control what slips through. The team asked whether white blood cells called lymphocytes can speed up the building of these seals, and what role a cell energy sensor named AMPK plays.

They found that lymphocytes do help the seals form faster, and that AMPK is part of the signal that drives the effect. A faster seal means a stronger barrier against germs and leaks. The result links immune cells to barrier repair in a direct way, which matters for gut diseases where the lining leaks and heals poorly.
plos-pone-0012443:
Adrien Weingärtner, Björn Drobot, Andreas Herrmann and colleagues disabled a fat-moving machine in the parasite Leishmania donovani, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Cell membranes keep different fats on their inner and outer faces, and a protein pair called LdMT-LdRos3 flips fats to hold that balance. The parasite causes leishmaniasis, a disease spread by sand flies.

Breaking the pair scrambled the parasite's membrane balance, as expected, but did not stop it invading host cells. The result rules out one assumed job for the machine and redirects drug hunters. A parasite protein that is not needed for invasion makes a weaker drug target than first hoped.
plos-pone-0012543:
Claire Ward, Diana Kuehn, Roberta Burden and colleagues aimed antibodies at a vessel-feeding enzyme, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Tumors cannot grow without new blood vessels, and blocking vessel growth is a proven cancer strategy. The enzyme cathepsin S helps tumors build those vessels, while the standard anti-VEGF drugs block a different signal, so the two might combine well.

Antibody targeting of cathepsin S inhibited vessel growth and, paired with anti-VEGF treatment, worked better than either alone. Synergy between two vessel attacks could help tumors that escape single drugs. The study supports clinical development of cathepsin S antibodies for cancer.
plos-pone-0012643:
Wu, Liu, Reedy and co-authors took three-dimensional pictures of insect wing muscle mid-contraction. Holding a muscle at fixed length traps its tiny motors in many states at once, which makes the structure hard to read. Their 2010 study froze fly muscle in that state and imaged it with electron tomography.

The images revealed fresh ways the two motor proteins, actin and myosin, meet during a contraction. Those meetings are the very steps that make force, in insect wings and in human muscle alike. Seeing them clearly sharpens the basic science of movement.
plos-pone-0012743:
Egusa, Okita, Kayashima and co-authors made stem cells from an unlikely source, gum tissue. Induced pluripotent stem cells can be grown from many body tissues, and easy sources help medical use. Gum tissue is often cut away during routine dental work and thrown out.

Their 2010 study reprogrammed gingival fibroblasts from that discarded tissue into stem cells. A waste source that patients give up painlessly could supply personal stem cells for many people. The work widens the menu of tissues that clinics might bank for future care.  The resulting cells passed the standard tests for pluripotency.
plos-pone-0327443:
Yan Zeng and three co-workers tracked blood counts in old patients with sepsis, a grave whole-body infection. They used a big US hospital data set with near five thousand old cases. The team sorted the counts into three paths. One stayed low. One sat mid-way and slid down slow. One fell fast from a high start.

Both the low path and the fast fall path died more in four weeks. The mid path fared best of the three. The fast fall warned of death most in men. The team says the shape of the curve holds clues that a lone count can miss.
plos-pone-0329343:
Andrew Christopher Slater and co-authors tested whether satellite data can forecast which birds live in Peru's Amazon forests in 2026. Satellites track forest loss well, but whether their signals capture which birds live below the canopy was open.

The team used more than three thousand bird surveys gathered over sixteen years in the Tambopata forest. Models fed with satellite reflectance and vegetation measures beat models using simple habitat classes at predicting where each of many species occurs and how communities are composed. The result opens a path to mapping wildlife change from space, where field surveys cannot reach every year.
plos-pone-0332243:
Nathan Seegert and colleagues use mask rules from the COVID years to test how policy signals move spending. Their idea is simple: a mask order tells the public how risky officials think local conditions are, and a statewide order may send a cleaner signal than a patchwork of county ones. The team built a county dataset from the middle of 2020 and compared phone movement and card spending right around each order's start.

State orders were followed by a rise in movement and in spending per person, while county orders showed no clear effect. Seegert and colleagues read the contrast as evidence that broader orders carry clearer information. The study speaks to how governments communicate risk, beyond masks alone, during fast-moving crises.
plos-pone-0339543:
Esraa A Salim led a team of seven authors hunting drug combinations against a rare breast cancer, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Inflammatory breast cancer is uncommon and aggressive, and new treatment options are badly needed. The team began with computer predictions, then tested the best candidates in real cancer cells.

Salim's pipeline identified drugs and paired combinations that slow the growth of these cancer cells, with synergy between partners. Moving from in silico screening to lab validation in one study strengthens the claims. The candidates now merit further testing toward clinical use. For patients with few options, a disciplined route from computation to bench evidence is exactly how new therapies start.
plos-pone-0339943:
Wenhao Guo and co-workers study why women in China sign up for adventure sports trips such as skiing, surfing, and rock climbing. Such travel is growing, yet social expectations still hold some women back. Their 2026 paper surveys more than five hundred women at well-known activity sites and asks how drive, confidence, and sense of standing shape their plans.

Both inner enjoyment and outer rewards raised plans to take part, but through different routes. Inner drive worked mainly through personal confidence and a sense of public standing. That standing, understood as earning respect and a fair place, proved the strongest path of all. Feeling that a sport was risky weakened these links, so safer planning may help more women join in.
plos-pone-0340243:
Corentin Lucas and six co-authors try a deliberately simple idea for finding Crohn's disease lesions around the anus on MRI scans, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Such lesions usually sit on one side, so the team measured how lopsided each scan looked in shape and brightness. Their features were designed to work across different scan types, which often trip up automated tools.

On a small, clear-cut test set the method performed strongly, but accuracy fell on harder validation cases, especially lesions wrapped around both sides. The authors present the work as proof of concept: asymmetry is a real signal, yet not enough alone for a dependable clinical tool.
plos-pone-0342143:
Changrong Lu and co-authors argue that large digital platforms quietly discipline public emotion and behaviour. Their 2026 study links interface design, recommendation systems, and feedback loops to standardised behaviour and growing dependence on platform cues. They built a daily measure of emotional polarisation from news sentiment and compared it with the research output of big technology firms.

Treating 2020 as a turning point, the analysis traces how platform governance tracks sharper emotional splits between online groups. The authors are careful that their measure reflects the information environment, not individual minds. Lu and colleagues frame platform design as a form of soft power that shapes how publics feel and argue, with consequences for democratic debate.
plos-pone-0342443:
Guido Catalano and colleagues survey in 2026 how well children and teenagers with impaired vision manage daily life, feelings, and quality of life across five specialist centres. Caregivers for about ninety young people completed trusted questionnaires on independence, behaviour, and life quality, split into younger and older age bands. Vision shapes social life, school inclusion, and self reliance from early years.

Both age groups scored in a medium to high range for independence and showed sound emotional and life quality scores. Teenagers scored lower on independence than younger children overall. Greater independence tied strongly to better life quality and fewer behaviour problems, making it a key rehabilitation target.
plos-pone-0343143:
Federico Zilia and three co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study on turning leek waste into a plant-boosting extract for greenhouse lettuce. The work pairs two tasks. First, the team measured the full footprint of making the extract. They also measured the footprint of growing lettuce with it. Second, they asked how a firm could actually sell such a product.

Lettuce grown with the extract scored better on most measures of harm. Gains included less acid rain impact and less water toxicity. Making the extract itself carried some costs in resource use. The authors then mapped each problem spot to the actor best placed to fix it. The actors ranged from processors to farmers. They also sketched ways to pay for checks and upgrades. The approach links hard data to business choices for residue-based farm goods.
plos-pone-0343243:
Melissa Allen and colleagues test how age affects the split-second act of reading gender from a face, in this 2026 PLOS ONE psychology study. Six hundred adults aged eighteen to sixty-nine saw faces paired with the pronouns he or she, sometimes matching the face's stereotype and sometimes not, while the team timed their answers.

Older participants answered more slowly overall and reported more negative, more conflicted feelings about pronoun use, though also fewer worries about it. Crucially, the slowdown when pronoun and face mismatched was no bigger in older adults than in younger ones. Automatic gender reading, it seems, stays stable across adulthood even as stated attitudes shift with generation.
plos-pone-0344143:
Negar Mottaghi-Dastjerdi and Mohammad Soltany-Rezaee-Rad analyzed gene activity in stomach cancer tissue to show how the cancer rewires the organ at a structural level. Stomach cancer is a major killer worldwide and is hard to catch early. Their network approach linked gene expression data with clinical details such as stage, spread to lymph nodes, and metastasis.

Across patient groups the same signature appeared: the cancer switched on developmental genes, most notably the HOX family that normally pattern the embryo, while losing the identity genes of healthy stomach lining. In effect, tumor tissue partly reverts to an early developmental program. Signatures like this help explain the disease's behavior and may point to stage-specific markers worth testing in the clinic.
plos-pone-0345043:
Cao and Zha, in a 2026 paper, tackle a hard choice in instant delivery: some orders cost more to serve than they are worth. When fleets are stretched, trying to serve everyone can raise costs and break time promises. Their model lets a platform drop a small share of costly customers on purpose.

The team built a routing plan that weighs vehicle costs, travel costs, and penalties for late arrival. They solved it with an improved genetic algorithm, a search method that breeds better routes over many rounds. In a case study, their solver beat a standard genetic method and a tabu search on speed, cost, and stability, with no missed time windows. Dropping a small share of hard orders cut total cost sharply, mostly by shrinking the fleet. Tests at larger scale showed the same pattern. The authors argue that planned, selective refusal can use scarce delivery resources better.
plos-pone-0345143:
Matthew Boot and co-authors studied how a parasitic guest ant keeps the peace inside its host's nest. The guest lives long-term inside a fungus-farming ant colony, taking resources while also defending the shared home. Their 2026 study staged encounters, measured venom doses, and quantified how the guest presents its sting chemistry.

Guest ants make conspicuous, costly displays of venom during meetings with hosts. Because the display is expensive to fake, the authors read it as an honest signal rather than a bluff. Signalling may calm conflict by advertising the guest's value as a defender. Boot and colleagues argue parasite signals deserve study as negotiated communication, not only as manipulation, when both sides gain from calm.
plos-pone-0345343:
Victoria Manasevich, Daria Kostanian, Anton Rogachev, and Olga Sysoeva wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It is a systematic review of the EEG signs that track how the brain handles the rise time of sounds. Rise time is how quickly a sound swells from silence, a cue the brain uses in hearing speech and music.

EEG records the brain's electrical activity, and correlates are the brain signals that track rise time changes. Gathering the scattered studies into one review shows what is firmly known and what is still guesswork. Hearing scientists and speech researchers, including those studying reading disorders tied to rhythm perception, are the audience.
plos-pone-0345843:
Celine Brooks led a team of eight authors on this 2026 mouse study of a protein-folding machine inside the eye's light-sensing rod cells. The machine, called TRiC, folds many proteins these cells depend on. Using mice engineered so the machine could be fished out of retina tissue, the team catalogued over two hundred partner proteins.

Blocking the machine cut levels of its known folding clients and disturbed energy metabolism proteins. Brooks links proper folding to the rod cell's power supply, and shows how overloading the machine can tip the eye toward degeneration.
plos-pone-0347343:
Xiaoyu Huang and co-workers build a phone-based system that watches transplanted tissue flaps after surgery and warns of trouble early. A flap fails most often when blood pools and cannot drain, and fast rescue saves it. Their 2026 study trains a deep learning model on photos from hundreds of patients and wraps it in a phone app for remote checks.

In testing at the home hospital and beyond, the model sorted healthy and troubled flaps with high accuracy. It caught nearly all cases of dangerous congestion while raising few false alarms. In live ward use it kept that record. Nurses could check flaps from afar and act sooner, which matters most where specialists are few.
plos-pone-0347443:
Jaeeun Yoo analyzed immune patterns in lupus across several cohorts, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Lupus patients have immune systems already on edge, and transfused donor blood can provoke reactions called alloimmunization. Yoo linked the strength of the type I interferon signature, a marker of immune activation, to gene programs tied to that risk.

The analysis suggests the signature may predict which patients will react badly to transfusions before blood is given. A warning like that lets doctors choose blood products more carefully or watch high-risk patients closely. Multi-cohort work strengthens the claim, since the pattern held across groups. Transfusion is common in lupus care, so a predictive marker has everyday value.
plos-pone-0347643:
Yan Yan, Mingxie Chen, Chuanyong Tang, and Sheng Wang mapped soil erosion across the world's karst regions, the limestone landscapes that cover about fifteen percent of Earth's land. Thin soils and underground drainage make these areas unusually fragile. Using a standard ecosystem model plus satellite-era data, the 2026 study tracked erosion from 2000 to 2020 and separated the roles of climate and human activity.

Erosion eased worldwide overall, though it stayed harsh across the south-west of Asia and the south of Europe. In North America the worst losses sat in the north-west, and that region's rate actually rose. Rainfall drove erosion most strongly, while scenario tests credited human activity with nearly half of the changes. Russia, China, and Europe led the reductions, the authors report.
plos-pone-0347943:
Robert W. Hurley, Daniel Guth, Elaine L. Hill, and Meredith C. B. Adams checked whether a diagnostic code on insurance claims actually identifies patients on long-term opioid therapy. Researchers and regulators often treat the code as equivalent to pharmacy records showing ninety days of prescriptions. Using complete Medicare and Medicaid claims from 2016 to 2022, covering well over a hundred million people, they tested the code against the prescription standard.

The code missed about two-thirds of true long-term users in both programs, though it rarely flagged the wrong people. Worse, patients found by code alone carried different risks, with more opioid use disorder diagnoses than those found by prescriptions. The authors warn that code-based surveillance badly distorts the picture.
plos-pone-0348143:
Fah Lertkulvanich and two co-workers read the full gene sets of four spiders that live in a plant trap. The plant is a pitcher plant in a Thai park. Its cups hold fluid that digests bugs. These spiders live in the cups, eat the trapped bugs, and are not digested. Three are crab spiders, and one is a huntsman.

Some genes for cell power had changed fast in these spiders, a mark of life in a strange home. The crab spiders also held rare shifts in gene order. One had a doubled control stretch. The work gives fresh facts for kin charts and for the study of life in odd homes.
plos-pone-0348443:
Mohammed Abdullah Hamad, Ahmed J. Alfahdawi, and Basim Mohamed Manswr characterize a fowl adenovirus strain taken from Iraqi chicken farms. The virus causes a liver disease that threatens broiler flocks, and this type has been reappearing in several regions. Their 2026 study infects young broiler chicks with the local isolate and examines organs and virus levels three weeks later.

Infected birds developed swollen, pale livers and enlarged dark spleens, with milder changes in kidneys and little in hearts. Virus copies ran highest in the liver, matching the damage pattern. No birds died, which points to a mild strain. Regional data like this helps farms watch for the right virus types and plan protection that fits local strains.
plos-pone-0348843:
Haiyan Zhang and colleagues designed TransitNet, a compact computer vision network that labels every part of a street scene, such as roads, cars, and sidewalks. Large labeling networks are too heavy for the small computers inside vehicles. TransitNet aims to stay accurate while using far fewer resources.

Built on an existing design, it adds modules that link distant parts of a scene and blend fine detail with broad context. A star-shaped backbone keeps the parameter count low. The network also adapts across different kinds of scenes, from traffic views to remote sensing images. Lightweight scene understanding like this is what driver-assistance systems and roadside cameras need to run in real time.
plos-pone-0348943:
Sofie Meijer and colleagues compared the gut microbes of Swedish women with the two forms of preeclampsia, the dangerous pregnancy blood-pressure disorder that arrives either early or late, against healthy pregnancies. Earlier studies lumped the forms together and used shallow sequencing. Thirty-seven women in late pregnancy gave samples read by deep shotgun sequencing, which names species and functions rather than broad groups.

Both preeclampsia groups' gut communities differed measurably from controls', surviving adjustment for age and body size, with the late-onset form showing the stronger shifts and lower diversity. A few named bacteria emerged as leads, though none survived the strictest statistical correction, and function-level differences washed out entirely. The careful, mostly negative detail matters: microbiome links to this disorder are real but subgroup-shaped, and small studies should stop promising simple signatures.
plos-pone-0349343:
Youming Huang and colleagues show that the plant hormone abscisic acid controls how rice flowers close, a detail that matters greatly in hybrid seed production. Rice spikelets open and close on a daily rhythm, and poor closure wastes pollen and cuts seed set. The team sprayed fertile and sterile rice lines with the hormone and with a blocker of its production, at several strengths.

The hormone sped closure, shortened the open window, and raised final closure rates, with a middle dose range working best; the blocker did the opposite. Gene sequencing of the tiny organs that push the flower open confirmed the hormone's pathway was active. In breeding fields, combining the hormone with a second treatment improved seed setting, a direct yield lever for hybrid rice.
plos-pone-0349643:
Marta Sfulcini, Erminio Trevisi, and co-authors studied how weaning hits dairy calves' immune systems, and why some calves grow poorly through the transition. Weaning stacks diet change, separation, and new surroundings into one stressful week. Their 2026 study split forty female Holstein calves into high and low growers over the ten days after weaning and compared blood chemistry and immune gene activity in white blood cells.

Weaning switched on innate immune pathways in all calves. Low growers, though, mounted a bigger immune response and showed blood signs of energy shortage, burning protein for fuel. High growers passed through with a quieter profile. The authors say the difference points to unequal resilience, and that spotting vulnerable calves early could let farmers support them through weaning.
plos-pone-0349943:
Crowded sea lanes raise the risk of ships colliding, and Minmin Zheng and co-authors combine two methods to plot safer courses. Their 2026 PLOS One paper pairs a rule-based reasoning system with a velocity obstacle method, a geometric way of finding paths that miss moving ships.

First, ships moving alike and sailing close are grouped, so the planner handles fewer targets. Safety zones around each ship or group scale with vessel length. The path method then draws avoidance routes toward the destination. Tests in two busy scenarios showed safer, smoother sailing. The authors offer the approach as a step toward smarter bridge decision support.
plos-pone-0350043:
Machines that caption sounds learn from human-written descriptions, and Laura Hekanaho and colleagues compared those descriptions in English and Finnish. Their 2026 PLOS One study is among the first to inspect this training data as language, including descriptions written by blind and sighted Finns.

The Finnish collections varied far more than the English one, which the authors trace partly to English writers working in a second language. A close reading of one hundred fifty descriptions showed what people choose to mention about a soundscape and what they leave out. The findings matter for accessibility tools, since captions trained on thin descriptions will describe the world thinly.
plos-pone-0350343:
Yoann Zafiriou and co-authors tested whether resilience protects anaesthesia staff during a simulated crisis in 2026. The specialty carries high burnout, and resilience is often promoted as a shield, but its link to the body's stress response was untested.

Thirty-four anaesthetists, trainees, and nurse anaesthetists completed a resilience scale, then faced a high fidelity child airway emergency simulation. Heart rhythm measures and self rated stress were tracked. Resilience scores sat in a mid range, yet neither body nor mind stress responses tied significantly to them. The result questions easy claims that resilient staff simply stay calm under fire.
plos-pone-0350643:
Jorge Maurino and co-authors studied procrastination among clinicians who manage spinal muscular atrophy in Spain in 2026. Delaying hard decisions is a known failure of self control, worsened by stressful clinical work, and the team linked it to burnout and regret.

Thirty-seven professionals from a national registry completed standard scales for delay, regret, attitudes to evidence, and burnout. About a third showed moderate to high procrastination. Modelling explored whether burnout feeds delay through regret over past choices. Even a small study matters here: if delay is common in rare disease care, systems, not just willpower, need redesign.
plos-pone-0350743:
Ivan Nirmalaraj, Nicholas Sookhan, and J. Scott MacIvor test a new way to measure how worn a bumble bee's wings are, in this 2026 study from a Toronto-area national park. Wings fray with flight, so wear hints at a bee's age and foraging effort, but existing scoring is coarse and subjective. The team photographed the forewings of more than two hundred sixty worker bees from three species and measured edge complexity using fractal geometry.

Fractal scores tracked human visual wear grades more closely than a simpler perimeter-to-area measure, and unlike that measure they were not distorted by body size. Undamaged wings also differed between species, giving each a baseline. The authors propose fractal dimension as a sensitive, objective tool for judging bee condition in field studies, useful for tracking colony stress and pollinator health.
plos-pone-0350943:
Maria Clara Ferreira, Frederico Kremer, and Vanessa Galli built a software tool that guesses which circular RNAs, a loop-shaped class of RNA, help plants weather cold and drought. Loops are hard to study one by one, so prediction narrows the field. Their tool reads the RNA's letter sequence, chops it into short fragments, and turns those fragments into numbers using a technique borrowed from language software, then classifies with a random forest.

Trained on rice and maize loop RNAs with known stress links, the tool sorted independent test sets well enough to serve as a screening instrument. Breeders hunting stress-resilient crops face thousands of candidate molecules; a ranked shortlist from sequence alone saves seasons of bench work. The authors offer the tool as an open starting point for a corner of plant biology that lacked one.
plos-pone-0351143:
Adults and children may not value the same rewards. Money means a lot to adults. Its pull on children is less clear. Sebastijan Veselic and colleagues compared fifty-one adults with thirty-nine children. The children were aged seven to twelve. Three tasks tested value, effort, and attention control. The study appeared in PLOS One in 2026.

Adults responded more strongly to money-like rewards. Children reacted about equally to both reward kinds. Food and treats counted as primary rewards here. Tokens and money counted as secondary rewards. The gap suggests learned rewards gain power with age. The authors add a caution. The two reward types were not perfectly matched. Age studies must weigh what a prize means to each group.
plos-pone-0351243:
Christoph Steup and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One genomic study of bowel cancer that has spread to the liver and been treated with antibody drugs targeting the EGFR pathway. Such treatment can shrink initially inoperable tumors enough for surgery, but resistant cell clones may grow meanwhile. The team sequenced tumor samples from thirty patients, taken before and after treatment, and compared them with public cancer genome datasets.

Samples taken after treatment carried resistance-linked mutations more often, spread thinly across many genes rather than concentrated in a few. Neither the total mutation count nor the well-known RAS status predicted whether tumors became operable. Reassuringly, even where resistance mutations appeared in subclones, they did not block successful removal of the liver tumors. The authors question how much routine profiling adds in this setting.
plos-pone-0351543:
Many insects stop eating as adults, living only to mate, and their guts fill with air instead of food. Hollister W Herhold and colleagues scanned such insects with micro CT imaging to measure that hidden air, in this 2026 PLOS One study spanning several insect orders.

The inflated gut was known from mayflies and one other group; scans now show it in stoneflies, webspinners, dobsonflies, moths, and true flies too. Species that had lost adult feeding carried strikingly more gut air, a link statistics confirmed strongly. Why the air helps is unsettled: buoyancy, display, or flight balance are candidates the authors weigh for future tests.
plos-pone-0351643:
Ju Zhao and colleagues sharpened satellite estimates of soil moisture over China's Wujiang River Basin, a rugged karst landscape where fields and rock fracture the ground. A NASA satellite reads moisture coarsely, and one model for all seasons fits none of them well there. The team trained separate seasonal models, mixing satellite drought indicators with terrain data, and compared five learning algorithms.

The seasonal CatBoost models beat single-model baselines, doing best in spring and autumn. Reading the model's reasoning showed its logic shifting with the year: winter estimates leaned on terrain, summer ones on heat and water signals. That rotation matches how moisture actually behaves in the basin. Better seasonal soil moisture maps feed drought warnings and water planning in mountain country where ground sensors are sparse.
plos-pone-0351943:
Edita Garskaite and seven colleagues turn eggshell waste into fire-resistant wood. Their 2026 study closes a loop: shells that bakeries discard become mineral protection for timber. First, water-insoluble proteins were extracted from shell membranes and fragments by boiling with denaturing agents. The mineral shell was converted into a calcium solution. Pine sapwood then soaked in two baths, phosphate first, calcium second. Inside the wood, the two met and grew a bone-like mineral, carbonated hydroxyapatite, in place.

Microscopy showed modest saturation: the wood's channels stayed mostly open. Element maps, though, showed calcium and phosphorus spread evenly throughout. Diffraction confirmed the mineral's identity and its carbonate substitution. Fire behaviour was measured with two calorimeter instruments. Timber construction is booming as a low-carbon choice, but wood burns. A waste-derived mineral grown inside the fibres, rather than coated on top, could protect buildings while giving eggshells a second industrial life.
plos-pone-0352143:
Zhiqiao Cheng, Ping Li, and Jingsheng Pan ground steel slag asphalt under accelerated wear to learn how its skid resistance ages, and how much slag a road crew should use. Steel slag, a steelmaking waste, grips tires well but roads must stay grippy for years at real temperatures. The lab program crossed three slag contents with three temperatures and measured two standard grip indicators as abrasion cycles piled up.

Both grip measures fell steadily as wear accumulated, and heat sped the decline sharply, a warning for hot-climate highways. The two indicators moved together closely, so either can track the other in monitoring. With wear curves in hand, engineers can set slag doses by climate zone instead of habit, and schedule resurfacing before a polished road turns treacherous in the rain.
plos-pone-0352243:
Xiaorong Bai and five colleagues run a brisk walking trial for overweight older women in China. Their 2026 study is a cluster-randomised trial with fifty-four women aged sixty to sixty-nine. Half walked briskly three times a week for twelve weeks. Sessions ran from thirty-five to sixty minutes. The other half kept their usual routines. Fitness, balance, and life satisfaction were measured at the start and the end.

Walking delivered broad gains. Heart and lung fitness, flexibility, strength, and endurance all improved significantly. Balance got better too, a serious benefit at this age. Life satisfaction rose with the physical gains. Body composition, though, did not shift in twelve weeks. Between-group differences reached significance clearly only on the chair stand test of endurance, while effect sizes grew across measures. The prescription is refreshingly plain: regular brisk walking, no equipment, measurably rebuilds fitness and mood in older women.
plos-pone-0352443:

Direct measurements are missing for most species, blocking models of how disturbance affects populations. McHuron gathered published milk intake rates and milk energy values from marine mammals and their land relatives, tracking how both change across the nursing period.

Milk intake per body weight fell over time in all groups, fastest in bears and kin, slowest in seals. Whales and dolphins drank heavily early, then dropped fast. The patterns give modelers grounded estimates for species never measured.
plos-pone-0352643:
Mary Bitta and seven colleagues report a large trial of bringing mental health care into ordinary clinics in rural Kilifi County, Kenya, published in 2026. Specialists are almost absent in such regions. The team therefore trained non-specialist primary care workers using the World Health Organization's intervention guide. They then rolled the program out across more than one hundred public facilities in a randomized stepped sequence, with refresher supervision each quarter.

Detection rose sharply once facilities crossed over. Monthly diagnosis rates for epilepsy roughly doubled, while depression, dementia, and substance misuse diagnoses climbed from near zero, all statistically robust after adjustment. Psychosis and suicidality showed raw gains that did not survive adjustment. Health worker stigma fell and patient outcomes improved. The authors call the scale-up feasible and effective, while asking for tests in other settings before general claims.
plos-pone-0353143:
Li and colleagues combined several data layers to find drivers of irregular heartbeat caused by a cancer drug in a 2026 study. The drug, widely used against cancer, can trigger atrial fibrillation, a serious rhythm problem. The team started with drug safety reports, then layered gene, protein network, and immune data.

Candidate targets emerged where drug targets, disease genes, and changed genes overlapped. Hub genes were checked in independent data sets, and docking tests probed direct binding. Naming the mediators could lead to heart-protecting companions for the cancer drug, so patients gain the cancer benefit with less rhythm risk.
plos-pone-0353343:
Altınalan and colleagues combined gene studies of a benign inner-ear tumor in a 2026 analysis. The tumor grows on balance and hearing nerves and often causes gradual hearing loss. Pooling four public data sets let the team find gene changes too faint in any single study.

Thousands of genes differed between tumor and normal tissue, even under strict cutoffs. Changed genes clustered around tissue scaffolding, hearing and nerve signaling, immune activity, and cell growth. Some changed genes already have known drugs that act on them. The map offers fresh leads for biomarkers and drug ideas for a tumor that today is handled mainly by watching or surgery.
plos-pone-0353743:
Chen and colleagues, in a 2026 study, profile the chemistry of backfat in Ningxiang pigs, a prized local breed in China, as the animals fatten. Backfat chemistry shapes pork quality, yet the fattening months, from about six months to a year old, were poorly charted. Samples at four ages were scanned for small molecules and matched against carcass traits.

More than one hundred fifty compounds shifted significantly with age, including fats tied to appetite control and fat burning. Plant-derived and vitamin-like compounds built up over time, which the authors read as the fat quietly recording diet and environment. Some man-made chemicals from feed or surroundings also accumulated, a possible flag for pork safety. One network of compounds tracked carcass traits strongly, with an obscure plant alkaloid at its center. The team offers these molecules as candidate markers for breeding and quality checks.
plos-pone-0353843:
Patryk Ziobro led a team of seven authors on this 2026 mouse study of exercise wheels and social behavior. Female mice raised with a running wheel in the home cage from weaning were tested as adults meeting unfamiliar females, and compared with mice given a simple paper hut.

Wheel-raised females spent less time investigating newcomers and called less during meetings, and two weeks without the wheel did not undo it. Surprisingly, even a locked, immobile wheel produced the same effect, so the object itself, not running, changed social motivation. Ziobro warns mouse study designs to account for cage furniture.
plos-pone-0353943:
Michael Bazaco and colleagues track in 2026 how foodborne outbreaks in the United States changed over two decades, sorted by food type and germ. Four priority germs and seventeen food groups were followed with a Bayesian trend model that handles rare events and hard attribution. Prevention teams need such trends to see which foods are emerging as risks.

Listeria outbreaks tied to dairy rose while those tied to meat and poultry fell. A gut germ's outbreaks tied to dairy and poultry also rose, while a toxin producing gut germ tied to meat fell. Salmonella outbreaks tied to eggs fell as well. The method itself is offered as a reusable trend tool.
plos-pone-0354143:
Kim and Kim, in a 2026 computer study, mine the genomes of African swine fever virus for pieces that could serve in vaccines. The virus kills pigs in huge numbers across Africa, Europe, and Asia, and its strains differ a lot by region, which frustrates one-size vaccine design. The team looked for protein fragments that are common within one country's strains.

Genomes were chopped into short overlapping pieces of four lengths, and pieces enriched in each country with enough genomes were kept. Italy yielded the most pieces, while Russia's pattern differed oddly. The kept pieces were screened as candidate targets for three arms of the immune system, and many were predicted to provoke a response. They came from shell proteins, copying machinery, and large gene families. The resulting library is meant to help design vaccines tuned to each region's virus, and tests of diagnostics as well.
plos-pone-0354243:

These authors asked instead whether the web of a person's psychological traits hangs together less tightly when sleep is poor. They surveyed about four hundred Iranian university students, roughly split between good and poor sleepers.

Each student's answers on twenty-seven mental traits were turned into a network, with traits as nodes and links as their ties. Poor sleepers' networks were sparser, with more isolated traits and traits that were harder to predict from their neighbors. Overall network strength, however, did not differ. In good sleepers, thinking-related traits sat closer to the center of the web. The authors suggest insomnia may mark a mind whose parts talk to each other less, a shift in how care might be aimed.
plos-pone-0354343:

Strength exercise is a core part of youth health advice, yet its drivers are less mapped than aerobic activity's. Their 2026 study drew on a national youth risk survey of about twenty thousand high school students.

About three in five students met the guideline of strengthening on at least three days weekly. The model sorted students well. Overall physical activity level was the top predictor, followed by sex and fruit intake. Explanation plots showed how each factor bends the prediction. Ge and Bi say explainable models can help schools target the habits that travel with strength training.
plos-pone-0354743:

The joint problem resists direct solution, so they split it into three smaller problems and solved them in turn with approximation methods. Simulations showed the algorithm settling quickly and steadily on its answer.
plos-pone-0355043:

The team newly sequenced the full mitochondrial genome of one rare flying squirrel species and lined it up against published genomes from both flying and tree squirrels. Basic organization, gene order, and composition proved highly conserved across the family.

Beneath that stability, four energy-related genes evolved faster in the flying squirrel lineage, and codon usage bias ran stronger there too. These are signs that natural selection pulled the two lineages differently, plausibly matching their energy demands. The reconstructed family tree settled into four subfamilies with strong support and placed flying and tree squirrels as sister groups. The authors offer the genome as a foundation for future work on squirrel evolution.
plos-pone-0355343:

Doctors usually track a blood marker for this cancer, but that marker can mislead in both directions. Their scan uses a tracer that sticks to a protein common on cancer-supporting tissue, and they compared scan results against the blood marker in patients checked over about three years.

The scan judged cases more accurately than the blood marker in patients whose hormone levels were held low, and it was flawless in a smaller group tested under stimulation. It also found spread in several patients whose blood marker read negative, mostly in neck lymph nodes. Mou and colleagues say the scan can catch disease the standard marker misses.
plos-pone-0355543:

The display was built for children aged five to ten and mixes hands-on stations with more traditional presentation. Over two and a half months the researchers watched hundreds of interactions involving more than two thousand visitors. Older children engaged more deeply, but they made up less than a quarter of the child visitors; most were younger than the intended audience. Many of those younger children seemed to struggle with the exhibition's open-ended design. The authors suggest ways to better match the content to the children who actually come.
plos-pone-0355743:

Pelleting raised how much dry matter and nitrogen birds kept and raised usable energy for all ingredients. Adding the enzyme also helped, most for the coconut and palm meals rich in that fibre. Both steps could let feed makers use fibrous byproducts more fully.
plos-pone-0355843:

Newborn meningitis kills and disables many infants in low-income settings, yet local outcome data were scarce. Their 2026 study extracted records for about five hundred admitted newborns across four years.

One third of the babies had a poor treatment outcome. Risk climbed with assisted vaginal delivery and with laboratory-confirmed spinal fluid infection. Very high white cell counts in spinal fluid also tracked with poor outcomes. Yirsaw and colleagues argue earlier recognition and closer watch on these flagged babies could improve survival in similar hospitals.
plos-pone-0355943:

A device called a DSTATCOM is meant to smooth that output, but it only works well when it can estimate the load current accurately.

The authors propose a new control method built around an improved phase-locked loop, a circuit that tracks the timing of the electrical signal. Their design filters messy load currents more cleanly, so the compensator can keep the source current balanced and smooth. Tests using real-time hardware simulation, including changing wind speeds and noisy measurements, showed the controller held up well.

Site changed the oil's character clearly: Hebron oil leaned rich in thymol, while Bethlehem oil leaned rich in carvacrol. All oils fought oxidation modestly and blocked bacteria across a useful range, with the strongest antifungal effects against the crop fungi tested. Bsharat and colleagues say origin and drying must be stated when such oils are sold or studied, since both shift performance.

Accuracy reached roughly ninety-one percent for attrition and eighty-seven percent for churn, with well calibrated confidence scores. The explanations scored high on fidelity checks, and the suggested actions cost less than those from comparison methods.
