Zhang presented Gctf in 2016, a program for cryo electron microscopy, or cryoEM. To rebuild a molecule's structure at near-atomic detail, researchers must estimate the contrast transfer function, which describes how the microscope blurs each image. Errors in that estimate blur the final structure.

Gctf uses graphics processors to determine and correct this function in real time, as images are collected. Speed and robustness are its main aims, since modern sessions gather huge numbers of images. A fast, accurate correction lets labs judge data quality on the spot. That real-time feedback transformed cryoEM workflows during its rise.
pmc-5023043:
Franke and Svergun presented DAMMIF in 2009, a program for small-angle scattering work. Small-angle scattering lets researchers probe the low-resolution shape of a molecule in solution. DAMMIF determines that shape from scratch, a task called ab initio shape determination, using the scattering data alone.

DAMMIF is a much faster, improved version of the earlier program DAMMIN. Speed matters because shape runs are repeated many times to check stability of the result. A faster program lets labs test more models and larger systems in the same time. Structural biologists use such shapes as a first model of proteins and complexes that resist crystallization.
pmc-5956843:
Nicholas Bokulich, Benjamin Kaehler, Jory Rideout, and colleagues described a QIIME 2 plugin for naming microbes in 2018. Marker-gene studies must assign each DNA sequence to a known group. That naming step shapes every later claim about a community.

The plugin offers machine learning and alignment methods and a way to test which works best on known samples. Honest testing matters because accuracy drops on new sample types. The authors show how to tune the classifier rather than trust defaults. Microbiome researchers use the tool to keep species calls as sound as the data allow.
pmc-6202443:
The GBD 2016 Lower Respiratory Infections Collaborators published this global study in 2018. Chest infections such as pneumonia remain a leading cause of sickness and death worldwide. They strike hardest at very young children and older adults.

The analysis gives illness and death figures plus the likely germs behind them for nearly two hundred countries. Streptococcus pneumoniae stands out as the top killer among the causes studied. Trends show progress in child deaths but stubborn totals overall. Vaccine and treatment programs use these estimates to choose where new tools will save the most lives.
pmc-6618143:
Antonella Viola, Fabio Munari, Ricardo Sánchez-Rodríguez, and coauthors reviewed macrophage metabolism in 2019. Macrophages are immune cells with many jobs, from eating germs to healing tissue. Their behavior depends on how they fuel themselves.

Different tasks call for different metabolic settings inside the cell. Inflammatory macrophages lean on fast sugar burning, while healing types favor slower, oxygen-based routes. The review maps these signatures and the signals that flip them. Reprogramming metabolism may one day steer macrophages in diseases from arthritis to cancer. The authors close by naming the metabolic questions that single-cell methods may soon answer.
pmc-7090843:
Jianbo Lai, Simeng Ma, Ying Wang, and coauthors studied mental health in Chinese health care workers during COVID-19 in 2020. Frontline staff faced heavy exposure, long hours, and fear of infecting family. Their psychological state was a pressing concern.

Surveying staff across dozens of hospitals with fever clinics or COVID wards, the team found widespread depression, anxiety, insomnia, and distress. Nurses, women, and frontline workers reported the heaviest burden. The authors urge protected rest, clear support channels, and screening for staff. The study became a reference point for workforce care in later outbreaks.
pmc-7094943:
Fan Wu, Su Zhao, Bin Yu, and coauthors reported a new coronavirus tied to human respiratory disease in China in 2020. Emerging infections like SARS and Zika remain a major public health threat. Where and when new ones appear is still hard to foresee.

The team isolated and sequenced the virus from a patient in Wuhan with severe pneumonia. Its genome marked it as a new member of the coronavirus family, related to SARS-like bat viruses. Sharing the sequence let labs worldwide build tests at once. The paper is one of the founding reports of the COVID-19 pandemic.
pmc-7222643:
Laure Wynants, Ben Van Calster, Gary Collins, and coauthors appraised COVID-19 prediction models in 2020. Models to diagnose the disease, forecast patient outcomes, or flag high-risk people appeared at great speed. Decisions based on weak models could do real harm.

Reviewing published and preprint models against reporting and bias standards, the team found all of them at high risk of bias. Small data sets, poor handling of missing values, and rosy validation were common. The authors urged that none be used in practice yet. Their verdict became a widely quoted guardrail for pandemic modeling.
pmc-7692443:
Spase Stojanov, Aleš Berlec, and Borut Štrukelj examined in 2020 whether probiotics can shift a widely watched balance in the gut. The two largest bacterial groups in the intestine, Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes, draw attention because their ratio is thought to help keep the gut in a healthy state. Changes in that ratio have been linked to obesity and to inflammatory bowel disease.

The authors review studies in which probiotic products were used to treat those two conditions, asking whether the ratio moved and whether patients improved. They weigh the strains and study designs behind the claims. Their account gives readers a sober measure of what friendly bacteria can and cannot yet do for these common conditions.
pmc-7857443: Lafta and colleagues measured how rear wheel position affects arm kinematics in 2018, the wheelchair biomechanics, the rehabilitation. Therapists will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it.
pope-dunciad-1743:
Alexander Pope first published The Dunciad in 1728 to mock the bad writers and hacks who had attacked him. He kept expanding it for fifteen years. The final four-book version, printed in 1743, replaced his original target with the critic and playwright Colley Cibber as hero of dullness.

The goddess Dulness holds her games for the worst poets, divers, and critics in London. Pope names real rivals and buries them in mock-heroic verse, with learned notes adding fake scholarship. Beneath the jokes lies real anger at a culture of print for profit. The poem ends with Dulness swallowing art, science, and morality in one great yawn of darkness.
prescott-conquest-mexico-1843:
William H. Prescott published History of the Conquest of Mexico in 1843, a classic of American romantic history. Prescott, nearly blind, worked from Spanish archives copied for him. He tells of the Aztec empire under Montezuma and its fall to Hernan Cortes. Battles, marches, and the siege of Tenochtitlan form the climax.

Prescott writes Cortes and Montezuma as epic figures in a vast drama. His scenes of Aztec temples, markets, and sacrifice drew wide wonder. Modern scholars correct many details and stress native sources he lacked. Yet the narrative power remains unmatched in English. The book made Prescott famous on two continents.
prudentius-psychomachia-1743:
Prudentius, a Christian poet of Roman Spain, wrote the Psychomachia around 405 CE: a war for the soul fought by personified Virtues and Vices. The English verse translation here dates to 1743. His short epic was the first full Christian allegory, and the Middle Ages loved it above almost any other poem.

Faith wrestles Idolatry, Chastity meets Lust, and Patience stands unmoved while Wrath breaks itself on her shield. Each duel ends with a moral drawn tight. The poem's scheme shaped medieval art, where the Virtues and Vices still fight on church walls. Prudentius turned Roman epic inward, to the battlefield of the heart.
psychography-or-the-embodiment-of-though: Psychography, or The Embodiment of Thought, 1843. The thought embodiment. This book preserves that work. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
ptolemy-geography-greek-nobbe-1843:
Ptolemy's other great book maps the earth as the Almagest maps the sky. Claudii Ptolemaei Geographia, in Carl Nobbe's Greek edition of 1843 to 1845, prints the Geography in three volumes. The second-century work holds eight books of place lists and map craft.

Ptolemy gives star-based places for some eight thousand towns, with rules for drawing the world on a grid. The maps drawn from his lists taught the late Middle Ages the shape of the earth. Columbus and his age sailed with Ptolemy's world in mind. Nobbe's text gives the work in its own Greek tongue.
ptolemy-geography-nobbe-1843: Ptolemy's Geography, in C. F. A. Nobbe's 1843 Greek edition, mapped the known world with coordinates for thousands of places. Its eight books shaped mapmaking for 1,500 years. This three-volume edition is the public-domain standard text.
rolle-fire-of-love-1343:
Richard Rolle wrote the Incendium Amoris, the Fire of Love, in Latin. Richard Misyn turned it into English in 1435, close to Rolle's own day. Rolle was a hermit in Yorkshire who wrote for nuns and lone souls. The work dates to the last years of his life.

Heat, song, and sweet taste mark God's touch in Rolle's scheme. He tells how the soul burns more hot as it climbs to full love. Warnings to false hermits and cold priests spice the text. The book is the chief work of the great English mystic of his age.
stukeley-abury-1743:
William Stukeley surveyed the great stone circles of Avebury in Abury, printed in 1743. The full title calls the place a temple of the British Druids. Stukeley walked the fields, measured the stones, and drew the vast plan. He read the avenues of stones as a serpent formed in the landscape.

Druid priests, in his account, built the temple, with roots he traced toward Phoenicia. His Stonehenge of 1740 is the companion to this survey. Together the two books invented the Druidic reading of Britain's megaliths. Later ages corrected his dates but honored his fieldwork. The Gutenberg text keeps his plates and reasoning. Avebury still bears his stamp.
sunderland-magnet-1843:
In 1843 La Roy Sunderland started The Magnet, a journal for the young American mesmerist movement. He edited its pages himself in the heat of public debate. Readers sent in case reports, claims, and sharp attacks on rival healers.

Month by month, the journal tracked trances, cures, and tests of magnetic sleep. It also printed fierce quarrels among believers who split over method and fame. Few sources show the birth of mesmerism in America so close up. The excitement, hope, and hype of a new mind science fill every issue, just as its first fans lived it.
sunderland-pathetism-1843:
La Roy Sunderland published Pathetism, with Practical Instructions in 1843, at the start of his American career. The short book laid out his core claim in plain terms. He held that one mind can act on another through sympathy alone.

Half the book gives doctrine, and half gives direct how-to steps. Readers learn how to put a subject into magnetic sleep and what to do next. Sunderland wrote with total faith in his method and his gift. His manual lets modern readers see early mesmerism as its founder taught it, step by step, in his own confident voice.
the-merchant-of-venice-pg2243: The trial scene holds the stage in this edition: Shylock whets his knife for the pound of flesh, and Portia's mercy speech turns the law against him. Venice's Christians and Jews clash in Shakespeare's most debated play. Brilliant, troubling, and endlessly discussed.
tob-0043:
Five books on CIA programs and mind control are gathered in this collection, assembled in 2020 from the literature of the declassification era. The set mixes documented history with speculation. Its titles range from John Marks's The Search for the Manchurian Candidate to Victor Marchetti's The CIA and the Cult of Intelligence.

Chan Thomas's Adam and Eve Story, Fritz Springmeier's Bloodlines of the Illuminati, and Ron Patton's history of Project Monarch complete the shelf. Together they show the genre that grew from real revelations, above all MKULTRA, into a wide literature of covert plot. Readers can weigh sourced expose against conjecture within one holding, which is the collection's research use.
tob-10043:
Israel Abrahams, a leading scholar of Judaism, gathered essays on Jewish life, history, and literature in The Book of Delight and Other Papers. Subjects range from medieval poetry to the folk customs of ordinary people. The title piece celebrates the delights of learning itself.

Written with wit and deep knowledge, the papers move between scholarship and everyday culture. Abrahams shows how books, festivals, songs, and habits carried Jewish identity across centuries and countries. For general readers, the volume opens a window on a culture often seen only through its major texts, and it does so through small, human details as much as grand events.
tob-10543:
Max Arthur Macauliffe, a British official in India, spent years with Sikh scholars preparing The Religion of the Sikhs. His work grew to six volumes of translation and history. He learned Punjabi and won the trust of Sikh teachers who checked his renderings.

The volumes translate hymns of Guru Nanak and the later Gurus and tell the lives of all ten Gurus. Macauliffe aimed to give Sikhs a faithful record in English and to correct poor accounts then in print. His edition brought Sikh scripture and history to Western readers and is still quoted by students of the faith.
tob-13143:
Swami Vivekananda's lectures on Karma Yoga came out in 1896, drawn from talks he gave in New York. They teach the yoga of action, one of the four paths he set before Western pupils. Of those paths, this is the one aimed at daily work.

The secret, he says, is to work without clinging to results, offering each act rather than grasping its fruit. Duty, charity, and even hard or dull jobs become training for freedom when done in that spirit. Karma Yoga remains the most practical of his books, read by people with no wish to leave the world.
tob-13643:
The 1908 Hermetic primer The Kybalion appears in this edition under the Three Initiates name, an authorship commonly attributed to New Thought writer William Walker Atkinson. Seven rules unfold as laws of mind: mentalism, correspondence, vibration, polarity, rhythm, cause and effect, and gender. Each is stated as an axiom, then explained and applied.

Atkinson's hand, if the attribution holds, fits the book's practical tone: ancient Egypt and Greece supply the pedigree, but the intended use is modern self-mastery. V1 evidence calls it the occult bestseller that never went away. A century of reprints, study groups, and arguments over its sources supports the claim.
tob-14243:
An early Christian letter found at Nag Hammadi in Egypt, the Treatise on the Resurrection, answers a man named Rheginos who doubted the teaching. Its unknown author writes as a teacher to a pupil. The letter is short, calm, and sure of its case.

Resurrection, the author argues, is not the flesh rising as flesh, but a spiritual reality the believer already shares in Christ. The world is an illusion that death exposes, while the risen life endures. The letter gives a clear, compact case for the Gnostic view of resurrection and shows how early Christians argued over the body's fate.
tob-4043:
Friedrich Schiller, the playwright of German classicism, turned thinker in his aesthetical essays, above all On the Aesthetic Education of Man. Writing in letters to a patron, Schiller asks how human beings divided between sense and reason can become whole, and how whole people might make a free state. His answer runs through beauty.

Play, in Schiller's famous play-drive, reconciles our warring natures: form and feeling meet, and only lovely souls, he argues, make free citizens. Other essays treat the sublime, grace, and tragedy. The collection shaped German classicism and influenced readers from Coleridge to Marcuse, wherever art's power to educate humanity is claimed.
tob-4243:
Lady Charlotte Guest's edition of the Mabinogion in its 1849 to 1877 form presents the complete Welsh tales in the translation that made them English classics. The Four Branches of the Mabinogi, Culhwch and Olwen, and the Arthurian romances are all included, with Guest's notes preserving the Wales of storytellers, scholars, and vanished customs behind the texts.

Guest learned Welsh as an English aristocrat married into Welsh industry, an unlikely path to founding a literature's modern fame. Her Mabinogion is often called the Celtic Twilight's founding text in English. Readers get the tales whole, with the apparatus of the edition that first carried Welsh myth across Europe.
un-ga-res-43:
Long before the Universal Declaration of Human Rights took shape, the UN General Assembly passed Resolution 43 on 11 December 1946. The Economic and Social Council had set up a Commission on Human Rights that year. Its charge was to draft plans for an international bill of rights. A draft Declaration on Fundamental Human Rights and Freedoms was already in hand.

The Assembly sends that draft to the council, for the commission to use as it drafts the bill. It also voices the hope that the question will come back to the Assembly in time for its second regular session. The path from this referral led, two years later, to the famous 1948 declaration.
un-ga-res-a-69-43:
A timed plan to end nuclear arms is urged in Resolution A/69/43, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls a chain of votes since 1994 on the step-by-step cut of the nuclear threat. It holds that the mere life of such arms puts mankind and all life on earth at risk. The sole sure defense, it argues, is their total end, with a pledge they will never be made again.

The pledges of the nuclear states are spelled out: the firm vow of 2000 to wipe out their arsenals in full. Deep concern at the toll of any use of such arms runs through the vote. The Conference on Disarmament is pressed to open talks on a phased plan, with a set frame of time.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 43 was adopted on 11 December 1946, at the fifty-fifth plenary meeting. It fed a draft text into the making of an international bill of rights. The Assembly sent the draft Declaration on Fundamental Human Rights and Freedoms to the Economic and Social Council. It was for passing to the new Commission on Human Rights. The Assembly voiced the hope that the question would come back to it for the second regular session.

General Assembly resolution 69/43 (2014) follows up the International Court of Justice's 1996 advisory opinion on nuclear weapons. The Assembly stresses the Court's unanimous conclusion. States are obliged to pursue negotiations in good faith. They must bring them to an end leading to nuclear disarmament under strict international control. It calls on all states to fulfil that duty at once. They should start multilateral negotiations toward an early nuclear weapons convention. The convention would ban the weapons and provide for their elimination.
un-sc-res-1343:
The Council adopted Resolution 1343 on Liberia on 7 March 2001. United Nations experts had found hard proof of Liberian support for Sierra Leone's rebels, the RUF. Rebel diamonds moved out through Liberia, with top officials involved. That trade paid for guns, fuel, and training across the border.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council first ends the old 1992 arms embargo on Liberia, its war now over. It then sets a fresh arms embargo for fourteen months. Liberia must expel RUF members, halt all money and military help, and stop uncertified diamond imports. A ban on Liberian rough diamonds and a travel ban on senior officials follow in two months unless Liberia complies.
un-sc-res-143:
Days after the Republic of the Congo gained independence, its government asked the United Nations for military help, and Belgium still had troops on Congolese soil. Resolution 143, adopted on 14 July 1960, was the Security Council's first answer to the Congo Crisis. The vote was eight to none, with three abstentions.

The Council calls on Belgium to withdraw its troops from the Congo. It authorizes the Secretary-General, in consultation with the Congolese government, to provide military assistance until Congo's own security forces can fully do their job, with UN technical help. He must report back to the Council. The decision launched one of the UN's largest early peacekeeping efforts.
un-sc-res-1443: The Council spoke on Iraq's oil-for-food program through Resolution 1443, adopted unanimously on 25 November 2002. The program let Iraq sell oil to buy food and medicine under sanctions. Its current phase was about to lapse. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the standing rules for just nine days, until 4 December 2002. The short bridge keeps aid flowing while members finish talks on the next phase. Nothing else in the sanctions setup changes.
un-sc-res-1543:
Timor-Leste's support mission was reshaped by the Security Council on 14 May 2004. The foreign minister of Timor-Leste had asked in February for a one-year extension of UNMISET. The Secretary-General advised a one-year consolidation phase, though with a smaller mission. The country's institutions were still forming, above all in justice, public administration, and policing.

The Council extended UNMISET for six months, with a view to one further final period of six months. The mission would shrink and take on revised tasks drawn from the Secretary-General's April report. Its new shape included up to 58 civilian advisers, with police and military parts scaled to the plan. Human rights principles had to stay at the core of its training work. The Secretary-General would report often and advise on the police and military shape ahead. The Council also restated the need to fight impunity for the crimes of 1999.
un-sc-res-1643:
Côte d'Ivoire's sanctions were renewed and widened on 15 December 2005. The African Union's October decisions and resolution 1633 (2005) had set the road map for the transition's final year. An international working group now watched the process. The arms embargo and targeted measures of resolution 1572 (2004) were nearing their first term. Peacekeepers' freedom of movement still met blocks.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renewed the arms embargo and the travel and asset measures of resolution 1572 to 15 December 2006. Any grave block on UNOCI's movement would itself draw the targeted measures. All states were ordered to bar the import of rough diamonds from Côte d'Ivoire, in line with the Kimberley Process bar on Ivorian stones. States in the region had to report on the steps they took. The Secretary-General and France were to keep reporting on breaches and obstructions.
un-sc-res-1743:
On 15 February 2007, the Council adopted Resolution 1743 on Haiti. Elections in 2006 had restored an elected government after years of turmoil. Armed gangs still ruled parts of Port-au-Prince, the capital. United Nations troops, called MINUSTAH, worked beside the Haitian police.

The text extends the mandate of MINUSTAH until 15 October 2007. The mission must keep up strong operations against armed gangs, above all in the capital. It should shift its disarmament work toward cutting violence in poor districts. The Council also asks for faster police, court, and prison reform, and for job projects that show quick results.
un-sc-res-1843: Resolution 1843, from 2008, is a Security Council decision held in this collection in official-record form. Its source transcription comes from English Wikisource. The document's two registers are easy to hear: the preamble's diplomatic weighing, then the operative part's plain commands and requests. The entry keeps both registers complete and in sequence.
un-sc-res-1943:
The Council's vote on 13 October 2010 produced Resolution 1943 on Afghanistan. The London and Kabul conferences had set a shared plan for the country's future. A joint board would start handing security duties to Afghan forces. The shared aim was Afghan command of most operations by the end of 2014. Civilian deaths stayed high, most caused by insurgent attacks.

The Council extends the International Security Assistance Force until 13 October 2011. States in the force may take all necessary measures for the mission. Members are urged to add troops, gear, and funds. Training Afghan soldiers and police comes first, so the handover can hold. The force must report to the Council every three months.
un-sc-res-243: Under number 243, the catalog lists a Security Council resolution dated to 1967 in the official UN record. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-343:
Cyprus kept its United Nations peacekeeping force under a Council decision of 14 December 1973. The Secretary-General's report of 1 December held that the force was still needed if peace was to be kept on the island. The Government of Cyprus agreed the force should stay past 15 December 1973. The Council also took note of the conditions then prevailing across the island.

The Council reaffirmed the long line of Cyprus resolutions back to resolution 186 (1964), which created the force. It urged the parties to show the utmost restraint. Both communities were told to press on with joint efforts toward the Council's goals while the climate was favorable. The force's stationing was extended to 15 June 1974. As in each renewal, the Council voiced the hope that progress by then would allow a withdrawal or a large reduction of the force.
un-sc-res-43:
Violence and disorder were rising in Palestine in the spring of 1948. On 1 April 1948 the Security Council said an immediate truce was urgently needed. It acted, the text notes, under its chief duty for world peace. The call went to both national movements. The Jewish Agency and the Arab Higher Committee had to send representatives. Their task was to arrange a truce between the two communities.

Any party that failed to uphold a truce would bear heavy blame. Arab and Jewish armed groups had to stop all acts of violence at once. The resolution came six weeks before the British mandate ended. The truce it sought did not hold.
un-sc-res-443:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force came up for renewal again in December 1978. On 14 December 1978 the Security Council extended UNFICYP until 15 June 1979. The Secretary-General had reported on the operation at the month's start. The parties agreed the force should stay. Cyprus's government said conditions on the island still required it. The Council restated the terms set when the force was created in 1964.

The Secretary-General had to keep his good offices mission going. That meant quiet work to bring the two communities toward talks. He owed the Council a report by 31 May 1979. It would cover progress and the use of the resolution. China did not take part in the vote.
un-sc-res-743:
A United Nations Protection Force for Yugoslavia was created in February 1992. The Secretary-General's report of 15 February found the conditions met for early deployment. Yugoslavia's government had asked for a peacekeeping operation. The Secretary-General and his personal envoy had worked to open the way. The Council judged the Yugoslav crisis a threat to international peace and security.

The Council approved the report and the United Nations peacekeeping plan for Croatia. It decided to establish UNPROFOR under its own authority. The Secretary-General was asked to take the steps needed for the earliest possible deployment. The force would serve an initial period of twelve months. The arms embargo of resolution 713 (1991) would not cover weapons meant solely for the force. All states were asked to support UNPROFOR and to ease the transit of its staff and equipment. The force grew into the largest peacekeeping deployment of its era.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Liberia is sanctioned for backing Sierra Leone's rebels in Resolution 1343, adopted unanimously on 7 March 2001. A UN Panel of Experts found that diamonds were the Revolutionary United Front's main income. Most left through Liberia, and Liberia's government supported the RUF at the highest levels. Liberia had announced corrective steps after the report.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council first ends the old 1992 arms embargo on Liberia, its conflict being over. It demands Liberia expel all RUF members, cut off financial and military support, and stop importing uncertified Sierra Leone diamonds. It demands that Liberia freeze RUF funds and ground its registered aircraft pending a corrected register. New measures follow: an arms embargo for 14 months, plus a ban on Liberian rough diamonds and travel by senior officials. Both run for 12 months starting two months later unless Liberia complies first. A Sanctions Committee runs the regime.

Congo's new republic was independent for only days when it asked the United Nations for military help, as order broke down. Belgian troops were on Congolese soil, and the government in Leopoldville wanted them out. This text of 14 July 1960 is the founding act of the United Nations operation that followed.

Belgium is called on to withdraw its troops from the Congo. The Secretary-General is authorized, working with the Congolese government, to give the country the military assistance it needed. That help would last until Congo's own security forces could fully handle their duties with United Nations technical support, and the Secretary-General was asked to report back as events required.

Iraq's oil-for-food programme was nearing a deadline in late 2002. Resolution 1443, adopted unanimously on 25 November 2002, gave it a short reprieve. The programme let Iraq sell oil under UN control. The money bought food and medicine for ordinary Iraqis. All this happened while sanctions stayed in force.

Members extended the governing rules, last set in Resolution 1409, until 4 December 2002. The extension lasted only nine days. It was a bridge while the Council debated the programme's future. The text stresses that the aim was easing hardship for civilians. It also reaffirms Iraq's sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Resolution 1543, adopted unanimously on 14 May 2004, gives Timor-Leste's support mission one more year, in a deliberate wind-down shape. Timor-Leste's foreign minister had asked for the extension that February. The Secretary-General recommended a one-year consolidation phase so UNMISET could finish key tasks and lock in the gains made since independence in 2002.

The Council agreed, keeping UNMISET until May 2005 at a reduced level. It praised the progress Timorese institutions had made in administration, policing, and defense in a short time, and thanked the states supplying troops, police, and support staff. The consolidation model, shrinking a mission instead of ending it abruptly, was meant to leave behind a state that could stand alone.

Resolution 1643, adopted on 15 December 2005, renews the sanctions architecture on Côte d'Ivoire for another year. The arms embargo, the ban on rough diamond exports, and targeted travel and money measures dated from late 2004 and early 2005. A string of peace deals, from Linas-Marcoussis to Pretoria, and an African Union decision that October framed the politics, and regional leaders from Nigeria, South Africa, and Niger had all mediated.

The Council extended the embargo and diamond ban into December 2006. It also renewed the group of experts who investigated violations and reported on the sanctions' effect. The measures, the Council repeated, existed to support the peace process rather than punish the country.

Haiti's fragile recovery after its 2006 elections shapes Resolution 1743, adopted on 15 February 2007. The UN Stabilization Mission, MINUSTAH, was helping the government keep order, but armed gangs still operated in Port-au-Prince. Police, courts, and prisons all needed deep reform, with long pretrial detentions and overcrowded jails. Security, rule of law, and development were tied together.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MINUSTAH until 15 October 2007, intending further renewals. It asks the mission to keep up operations with the Haitian National Police against armed gangs and to shift its disarmament work toward a community violence reduction programme. It backs the police reform plan and calls for matching reform of courts and corrections to end impunity. It also urges quick-impact projects and job-creating work, support for the coast guard against drug and arms trafficking, and a full report before the mandate expires.

Fighting had flared again in the Kivus, and in November 2008 MONUC, the Congo mission, is temporarily strengthened. The Secretary-General had written on 31 October asking for more capacity so the mission could carry out its mandate. MONUC's existing mandate was due to expire on 31 December 2008.

Up to 2,785 extra military personnel and up to 300 more formed police are authorized for the mission. The added forces could deploy at once and were approved until 31 December 2008, with the Council intending to extend them when it renews the mandate. How long the reinforcements stay was tied to the security situation in the Kivus, the focus of the renewed violence.

Afghanistan's transition planning shapes Resolution 1943, adopted on 13 October 2010. The London and Kabul conferences had set priorities. A Joint Afghan-NATO Inteqal Board was being set up to judge when provinces could pass to Afghan control. The aim was Afghan security leadership by the end of 2014. Civilian casualties were rising, most caused by the Taliban and other extremist groups.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the authorization of the International Security Assistance Force, ISAF, for twelve months until 13 October 2011. It authorizes its member states to take all necessary measures. It calls for more personnel and equipment, and presses partners to train and mentor the Afghan army and police toward self-sufficient, accountable, ethnically balanced forces. ISAF must consult closely with the Afghan government and the UN mission UNAMA and report quarterly through the Secretary-General.

A new state asked to join the United Nations in December 1967, and the Council answered on 12 December that year. Resolution 243 was adopted unanimously. The Council had examined the application of the People's Republic of Southern Yemen for admission to membership. It recommended to the General Assembly that Southern Yemen be admitted as a member of the United Nations. That single recommendation is the whole text of the resolution.

Resolution 343, adopted on 14 December 1973 by fourteen votes to none with China abstaining, keeps the UN force in Cyprus for another term. The Secretary-General's December report judged the force still necessary if peace was to hold on the island. Cyprus's government agreed the force should stay beyond 15 December, given conditions there.

After reaffirming a decade of Cyprus resolutions reaching back to 1964, the Council urged the parties to show the utmost restraint and to keep working toward a settlement. The force's stationing was continued for the next six-month period. Six months later the island would be convulsed by a coup and invasion, and the quiet force this text renewed would find itself holding a new dividing line.

Fighting between Arab and Jewish communities in Palestine was worsening as British rule there neared its end, and on 1 April 1948 the young Security Council responded with Resolution 43. The text was passed unanimously. Members said an immediate truce was a matter of the utmost urgency.

The Council asked the Jewish Agency and the Arab Higher Committee to send representatives who could negotiate a truce between the two communities. It warned that any side refusing to honor a truce would bear heavy responsibility. Armed groups on both sides were told to stop all acts of violence at once.

Good offices joined the troop watch in this Cyprus text of 1978. On 14 December, the Council adopted Resolution 443. Fourteen members voted yes and none voted no. China took no part. The parties had backed the Secretary-General's advice to extend the force. Cyprus agreed it must stay past mid-December. Four years had passed since the island split.

The text restates the founding decision, Resolution 186 of 1964. It extends the posting to 15 June 1979. It also asks the Secretary-General to press on with his mission of good offices. He must keep the Council briefed on progress between the two peoples. A report on the text's working is due by the end of May 1979.

Resolution 743, adopted in February 1992, creates the United Nations Protection Force for Yugoslavia. The Secretary-General's report of 15 February judged that conditions finally allowed the force, requested by Yugoslavia itself, to deploy quickly. Five earlier resolutions had built toward this step as Croatia's war ground on and a ceasefire plan brokered by the Secretary-General's envoy took shape.

The Council established UNPROFOR with immediate effect, as the Secretary-General recommended, for an initial period of twelve months. The force's first task was to hold protected areas in Croatia while a political settlement was negotiated. It grew into one of the largest and most troubled UN operations of the decade, spreading later into Bosnia.
zoist-vol-01-1843:
John Elliotson founded The Zoist in 1843, a journal of cerebral physiology and mesmerism. Volume one runs from March 1843 to January 1844. Elliotson, a London hospital doctor, had staked his name on mesmeric practice. His journal became the first and most important English voice of the movement.

Surgical cases done under mesmeric sleep fill many pages. Somnambulist reports, cure stories, and fierce letters crowd beside them. Opponents attacked, and the journal printed its answers in full. Thirteen volumes in all would form the movement's complete primary record. Volume one shows the campaign at its bold start. The mesmerism to hypnotism debate begins here.
